text: The content-root-consumer residue class has a production fix now, in the SOURCE repo, commit 285a7a957. Root cause, one sentence: the split gave MSBuild the workspace roots and the running program none. Directory.Build.props grew GkDataRoot/GkContentRoot so the build is green, while SeedImportRunner.FindUp still walked up from the current directory - and after the split that walk stops at the gk-core checkout while data/seed lives in a sibling gk-data pack. It reached data/tuning by luck because gk-core owns that, which is why nothing looked broken until content was read. The contract already existed and was correct (tools/seedsmith/seedsmith/workspace_roots.py, which even names its twin and says 'a root is never guessed'); what was missing is that tests/Shared/KeepverseRoots.cs was the ONLY C# implementation and it is linked into *.Tests alone. A resolver only the tests can see is a resolver the product cannot use. ADDED src/FusionRpg.Core/Workspace/KeepverseRoots.cs (net6.0, Unity-free, no SQL; guard-dal and guard-secondary-no-unity both OK), mirroring the Python contract exactly. One deliberate difference, documented in the type: Roots() returns BOTH candidate roots, because FindUp is handed data/seed and data/tuning by different callers, cannot tell which owns a path, and they live in different repositories after the split - so the filesystem decides and no convention is hardcoded. SeedImportRunner.FindUp gains a pre-pass and KEEPS its walk, because a monorepo checkout must return byte-identical answers and dist/FusionRpg.Server/data (a real call site in AtomImporter and CreatureSpeciesImport) is in neither root. TESTS 15 green: 9 in FusionRpg.Core.Workspace.Tests, 6 in FusionRpg.Data.Tests, both layouts and both resolvers asserted to agree. The seed subset of FusionRpg.Data.Tests is 117/117. The first draft of these tests went into FusionRpg.Core.Tests, which was wrong twice over - FusionRpg.Core.Workspace.Tests already existed and already held a KeepverseRootsTests, so it would have been a duplicate class and namespace in a second assembly. Deleted, not shipped. TWO BLOCKS, both reported rather than worked around. (1) The boundary mapping for the new files is DEFERRED: src/FusionRpg.Data/Seed/SeedImportRunner.cs is owned by NO boundary row and reaches verification only through the data-fallback and seam fallbacks, which is the unmapped-production-path defect; the mapping was written and then REVERTED because scripts/verification-boundaries.v1.json is claimed by the active session ps1-ban-manager-20260926 (direct mode, features/mega-merge, 1107 paths). The registry is byte-identical to HEAD, sha256 b9d0a8ed4e0d80bd72c0bd3a768d807788d6c2e8cfdc6787206744812b9529b1, and nothing of theirs was touched. (2) verify-change.py aborts before running ANY test on this repo: it runs the session-boundary guard unscoped and three other active sessions contribute drift that fails it, while the same guard scoped to this session exits 0 and states the drift 'does not block it'. The plan's checks were therefore run directly - dal OK, test-substrate OK, session-boundary OK (scoped), Guard.Tests 717 passed / 4 failed, all four proven independent of this change (the registry is byte-identical to HEAD and none of the four tests references any file this session touched). mark: csharp-lexer-20260930
text: A TESTED C# LEXER, because the root cause of both earlier transform failures is now named. Neither the naive brace counter nor a first-draft tokenizer handles an interpolation hole that CONTAINS A NESTED STRING LITERAL. The real cases in this repo are src/FusionRpg.Data/Sqlite/LegacyMonoMigrator.cs:197 $"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS \"{table.Replace(" ... , an interpolated string whose hole opens a nested string. A lexer that ends the literal at the hole's first inner quote leaves a real '{' outside the string, and every brace count after that point is wrong - which is the 30 CS1519 'Invalid token throw in a member declaration' from the previous row, and it is a lexer bug, not a C# syntax problem. The lexer now tokenizes comments (nested block comments included), char literals, regular, verbatim and raw string literals, and every interpolation form, and scans an interpolation hole as CODE - a hole may contain a nested literal, and that literal's quotes must not be mistaken for the enclosing literal's closer. A '{' is a hole only in a $-prefixed literal; in a plain string it is an ordinary character, and treating it as a hole made an early draft swallow real code (1782 files wrongly reported unbalanced, versus 28 now). PROOF IT BITES, because an untested parser is the thing being replaced: 14 adversarial shapes are asserted, including hole-with-nested-string, hole-with-escaped-quote, raw-interpolated-hole, verbatim-doubled-quotes, char-literal-brace and nested block comment. The naive character counter is demonstrably WRONG on 6 of the 14. Two structural properties are asserted over all 3522 .cs files: mask() preserves length exactly on 400 files, and match_brace produces a proper nesting (equal open/close counts, every '{' pairs forward, intervals never cross) on a real file. 28 real files remain unprovable, mostly raw interpolated strings and one double-dollar raw string - that residual is the reason for the refusal below rather than a reason to trust the tool more.

mark: finddatadir-two-meanings-20260930
text: FindDataDir HAS TWO MEANINGS, NOT ONE - and the test suite proved it in 27 failures, which is the most useful result of the day. Collapsing all four definitions to KeepverseRows.Content() was my hypothesis: the helper walks for a directory literally named 'data', in the split it finds gk-core/data (which exists, because gk-core owns data/tuning) and joins 'seed' onto it, and Content() is what owns data/seed. Monorepo build 0 errors. Then Atoms.Tests went 0 -> 22 failed and Items.Tests 1 -> 6. REVERTED. The cause is that the helper never meant one thing. Some callers do Path.Combine(FindDataDir(), "seed", ...) and want the pack; but tests/FusionRpg.Core.Atoms.Tests/Atoms/KindValueGuardTests.cs:186 does `var dir = FindDataDir();` and treats the result as a data directory in its own right, so collapsing it moves that call from <root>/data/... to <root>/... . This is the SAME two-roots-in-one-helper defect the whole collapse programme exists to remove, and I reintroduced it from the opposite direction by assuming a single meaning instead of reading every call site. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE REMAINING 51 NAMES, and it changes the plan: this is NOT a mechanical rewrite. Each helper must be classified by what its CALL SITES join onto it - 'seed' or 'generated' means Content(), 'tuning' or a bare directory means Core(), and a helper serving both must be split into two named helpers with the call sites divided between them. The call-site census is per-helper and must be read, not inferred from the name. The measured cost of guessing instead of reading: 27 tests, one revert, and a build cycle.

mark: helper-decision-table-20260930
text: THE CALL-SITE DECISION TABLE, which is what the previous row said was required. Built with the tested lexer; the tool and its output are committed at docs/migration/repo_root_helper_census.py, docs/migration/kvcsharp.py and docs/migration/repo-root-helper-census.txt. 55 helper names, 590 definitions. It classifies each helper on TWO axes, because one axis is not enough: a helper that NAMES ITS OWN TREE (RepoTuningDir's body is a root plus 'data','tuning') is decided by its body, while a BARE ROOT (RepoRoot, FindDataDir) is decided by what its CALLERS join onto it. Classifying everything by call sites reports RepoTuningDir as bare, because its callers join a bare filename - the wrong question. THE TABLE: 505 definitions across 26 helpers already delegate to a KeepverseRoots accessor and are done. 58 definitions across 13 helpers are CORE: RepoTuningDir(19), FindScenariosDir(12), FindSourceFile(10), ReadCoreFile(6), ScopeDir(2), TimelineDir(2), CoreSrcDir(1), DelveDir(1), FindCoreFile(1), FindShippedFile(1), RepoSourceRoot(1), RungsSourceDir(1), SrcDir(1). 4 definitions across 4 helpers are CONTENT: BaseTypesDir, ItemsDir, SuppliesDir, ReadItemDataFile. 7 definitions across 2 helpers are BOTH and must be split BY CALL SITE: FindDataDir(4) and RegistryDir(3). 16 definitions across 10 helpers are BARE and need a read: FindRepoFile(5), CreateTempDir, ActionsDir, Dir, MovementDir, ToolSourceDir, FindRepoDir, NewRoot, Root, TempRoot. So the remaining work is 85 definitions across 29 helpers, not the 51 names estimated before. THE TABLE INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCES THE EMPIRICAL RESULT. FindDataDir classifies as BOTH on its own - it reports joining generated, seed AND tuning - which is exactly what the 27 test failures proved in the previous row. A census derived from call sites and a suite disagreeing are two independent routes to the same fact, and that is the reason to believe the classification rather than the reason to admire it.

mark: subpath-must-survive-20260930
text: THE TRANSFORM IS NOT 'POINT THE HELPER AT A ROOT', AND THE 27 FAILURES WERE POINTING AT THIS. Most of the remaining helpers return a SUBDIRECTORY, not a root: RepoTuningDir() returns <root>/data/tuning and its callers join a bare filename (Path.Combine(RepoTuningDir(), "power-scale.v2.json")). Collapsing that to KeepverseRoots.Core() would silently drop the 'data','tuning' segment and turn 19 definitions into reads of <gk-core>/power-scale.v2.json - a new class of wrong path, and a green build, because it still compiles. The correct rewrite preserves the helper's own subpath and changes only the ROOT it is joined to: Path.Combine(KeepverseRoots.Core(), "data", "tuning"). That is also why the seven-helper collapse in 6f32776dc was safe for the names it covered - those returned bare roots, so there was no subpath to lose - and why the same mechanical move applied to these 29 would not be. SECOND RULE FROM THE SAME TABLE: a helper classified BOTH cannot be rewritten at all, only split. FindDataDir and RegistryDir need their call sites divided between two named helpers, and the division is per call site, so it is a read-then-edit change set with its own verification, not a transform.

mark: census-tool-defects-20260930
text: THREE DEFECTS IN THE CENSUS TOOL ITSELF, recorded because each produced a confident wrong answer rather than an error, which is the failure mode this whole migration keeps paying for. 1. The first version reported EVERY helper as bare, with zero signals across the board. Cause: it searched for path-segment string literals in a MASKED copy of the fragment - and masking blanks out string contents, which is the entire point of masking for brace counting and precisely wrong for finding literals. A number that reads as a confident zero. 2. The second version read all 1500 test files once PER HELPER NAME, about 67000 reads, and timed out past 30 minutes; and match_brace re-tokenized the whole file once per definition, so a file with 20 helpers cost 20 full tokenizations. Fixed by loading the corpus once and adding kvcsharp.match_in(), which matches braces in an already-masked copy. Runtime 12s. The lesson is the same one as everywhere else in this programme: a scan that is too slow to finish is not producing a slow number, it is producing no number, and a number that appears only because the scan was narrowed is not a measurement. 3. The first pass used the first string literal after a call site as the segment, which is the helper's own argument rather than the path segment, so RepoTuningDir read as bare. Axis one and axis two are not interchangeable and using the wrong one produces a clean, wrong table.

mark: loop-invariant-condition-1924-tests-20260930

FusionRpg.Data.Tests was 1924 total / 1924 failed / 0 passed - completely dead - and no solution-wide run had reported it because the project is not a member of FusionRpg.slnx. Root cause: DungeonRegistryHubTestBootstrap.Init is a [ModuleInitializer], so it runs at ASSEMBLY LOAD, and its walk-up read `while (dir is not null && !Directory.Exists(Path.Combine(KeepverseRoots.Content(), "data", "seed", "dungeon"))) dir = dir.Parent;`. The condition NEVER REFERENCES dir. KeepverseRoots.Content() returns an absolute path independent of where the walk is, so the condition was loop-invariant - false on entry - and dir stayed at AppContext.BaseDirectory for the whole method. The three tuning files were then joined onto bin/Debug/net8.0/data/tuning, a directory that does not exist. One unresolvable file, thrown at assembly load, killed every test in the assembly. Fixed at gk-core 34d2ffc by deleting the walk and naming both roots once: 1924 failed / 0 passed -> 7 failed / 1917 passed. The shape is worth carrying forward because it does not LOOK wrong: a walk-up may only decide a path by examining the directory it walks through, and naming an already-absolute root in the condition makes the walk a no-op that silently pins the result to the test output folder while still reading like a search. The detection is not a lint rule - it is noticing that the loop variable is absent from its own condition.

mark: passive-tree-corpus-has-zero-derived-atoms-20261001
text: THE LAST FusionRpg.Server.Tests FAILURE IS NOT A TEST DEFECT, AND WHAT IT EXPOSES IS BIGGER THAN ONE TEST. Post_anOwnedTierOneNodeAfterOpeningTierOne_contributes asserts that an owned node appears in ContributingNodeIds, and gets an empty collection. MEASURED, not inferred. The generated passive-tree corpus is 42 trees and 560 nodes carrying 344 atoms, and EVERY SINGLE ONE IS 'stat.modify' - zero 'stat.derived' in the entire corpus. The tree's resolvers accept only the derived kind: TreeAtomSource.TryReadOp returns false for anything whose KindId is not exactly 'stat.derived', HasReadableAtom is built on it, and ChannelLegality and PassiveTreeCatalogLoader do the same. So HasReadableAtom is false for EVERY node in EVERY tree, ContributingNodeIds is STRUCTURALLY ALWAYS EMPTY, and the resolve's derived-contribution path has no data to read. That is why the test can never pass: it is the only test in the file asserting a node contributes, and no node in the corpus can. This is the same class this session keeps finding - a value written in one vocabulary and read in another - except the two ends are in DIFFERENT REPOSITORIES: the corpus is generated by gk-forge (seedsmith's tree adapter), and the consumer is gk-core's TreeAtomSource. NOT FIXED HERE, DELIBERATELY, AND THE REASON IS THE POINT. The consumer is not the wrong side: TreeAtomSource's own doc comment is emphatic that the predicate 'must not be relaxed on the assumption that widening it would reach a channel the shared fan-in can read', naming 'stat.modify's route is UNBUILT'. And the corpus is not hand-editable - generated seed data is fixed at the generator and regenerated, never edited to turn a test green. So the two real fixes are both owner decisions: have the generator emit derived atoms for tree nodes and regenerate 42 trees, or build the primary route the consumer's comment says is unbuilt. WHICH IS TRUE IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and saying so is part of the finding: 'stat.modify' is the PRIMARY kind with its own per-channel coefficients in CoefficientTable, and BindGate reads it - but BindGate is a scope VALIDATOR that only rejects primary defense at the wrong scope, not a path that turns a tree node into an actor stat. So the claim 'the 560 nodes are inert' is NOT made; the measured claim is that the DERIVED path reads nothing and contributingNodeIds can never name a node. OWNER: whoever owns the derived-stat and passive-tree binding design (stats + progression categories). This is a content and design gap, not a migration residue, and it is named rather than guessed at.

The remaining four in that file then failed for the next reason down, and it is the one worth keeping: the resolver names the sessions-owning root by looking ABOVE this repository, unanswerable in a planted fixture. mark: resolver-ownership-consolidated-20261001
text:
The split turned 'resolve a repo-relative path' into 'ask which repository owns it', and the answer needs SIBLINGS: a path in gk-fusion is not reachable by walking up from gk-core. That question first lived inside guard-verification-boundaries.py, so only that guard could ask it, while every other caller re-derived it - root_carrying, added earlier in this program, walks ancestors and CANNOT answer for a sibling at all. Measured: root_carrying returned None for scripts/deploy-play.py, which is gk-fusion's, so the helper raised during collection - an error, not a failure, which is worse because it stops the file running.
repo_bases(start, accessors) and owning_base(rel, start, accessors) now live in the shared resolver, held byte-identical across all three copies (one distinct SHA-256). Local root FIRST, so a repository's own path is always its own. None is the fail-closed answer and every caller keeps its original behaviour on it.
The `accessors` parameter is what makes the sharing safe. guard-verification-boundaries.py imports the resolver OPTIONALLY - a copied fixture has no lib/ beside it and every accessor degrades to a stub returning None - so it passes its own accessor tuple instead of letting the shared helper use its own, which would resolve a planted fixture against the REAL workspace: the exact blindness the original fix removed. Its fallback is now one line and is not a second implementation - with every accessor absent the candidate set is provably (root,) - and the guard still warns on stderr when the resolver is gone, so a real repository that has lost lib/ stays visible.
Differential evidence: both sides loaded with RESOLVER_AVAILABLE=True, 13 paths including four owned by other repositories, 0 disagreements. In a copied fixture both sides return the fixture's own root and neither reaches for the real workspace.
TWO INVALID INSTRUMENTS, recorded because both first looked like findings. The first differential loaded the original guard without its own lib; the second loaded it without keepverse_roots.py beside it, so RESOLVER_AVAILABLE was False and it was being compared against a resolver-enabled build - 7 apparent disagreements, every one the harness. The harness now asserts RESOLVER_AVAILABLE on both sides before comparing, and normalises paths before comparing because the temp directory arrives in its short 8.3 form on one side and the long form on the other.

mark: fourteen-check-wrappers-were-false-greens-20261001
text:
THE LARGEST FINDING OF THIS PROGRAM, and it was not on the triage list.
`spec_from` accepts a wrapper declaring EITHER `CHECK` or `CHECKS` and refuses one declaring neither, documenting the reason exactly: 'a wrapper whose spec is incomplete would otherwise be a check that runs an empty command and reports success'. `execute` then built its command sequence from `spec['checks']` alone. For every wrapper using the singular `CHECK` the sequence was empty, steps [], step_count 0, verdict OK, exit 0.
MEASURED ON THE POPULATION: 14 of 16 wrappers declared CHECK and executed zero steps. The only two doing real work were the one declaring CHECKS (web-fusion-rpg-web) and the one passing its command to main() explicitly (gen-content-validate). Every generator gate in the wrappers had been green without running once - creature contract, metrics, preflight, report, species, build plan, passive tree, items gate, structure contract, resource ownership, corpus dump, item seed validator, family expand, fusion recipe.
This is worse than a red gate: a red gate sends someone to look. It also means the evidence those gates exist to produce - generators --check byte-identical to the import SHA, goldens unchanged - was NEVER PRODUCED, so any claim resting on them was inherited rather than measured. That is ADDITION 3's own failure mode reached from a new direction.
Nothing caught it: the harness had no test for execute()'s sequence building. test_web_fusion_rpg_web.py covers the harness well but only through the ONE wrapper that declared CHECKS, so every assertion it made went through the branch that worked.
With the green removed, three more resolution defects appeared, each fixed against its own documentation: (1) 8 wrappers refused WORKING-DIRECTORY-MISSING because their working directory names a sibling's tree (web/fusion-rpg-web in gk-web, tools/seedsmith in gk-forge) while root is gk-core, which has neither; resolve_owned now asks owning_base, local root first. (2) 7 dotnet wrappers declared `--project tools/X` while their OWN DOCSTRING said `--project gk-forge/tools/X`; the projects are gk-forge's, gk-core has no tools/ for them, so dotnet exited 1 in under a second and the wrapper reported 'the plan is stale'. Running the docstring's spelling exits 0 with 'clean, 904 species match'. Code corrected to match documentation, which is the smaller change and the only one that makes the check mean what its docstring claims. (3) MY OWN FIRST FIX WAS WRONG: spec['check'] is ONE argv tuple, so list(spec['check']) spread it into six one-token commands and the run tried to spawn bare `python`. An intercepted run() call printed `command: python` - six characters of argv standing in for a check.
RESULT, wrapper by wrapper: 4 exit 0, then 6 after the resolver fix below. 10 remain red and are named open items, NOT fixed here: fixing a generator audit finding is the generator owner's decision, not a side effect of making a gate able to run.
tests/tools/test_checks_common.py is new. Proven non-vacuous by three mutations each applied and VERIFIED to have changed the file: consulting only checks (the original defect), spreading the singular check into tokens, removing the owner lookup. A fourth mutation run through PowerShell reported 10 passed and was a NO-OP - the regex never matched - proving nothing about the test and everything about the harness.

mark: resolver-legacy-probe-misclassified-gk-forge-20261001
text:
ROOT CAUSE of the seedsmith failure class, and a genuine resolver defect.
`_layout` recognised the pre-split monorepo as 'a FusionRpg.slnx next to a data/seed directory'. gk-forge satisfies that BY ITSELF - it owns its own solution file and its own data/seed/creatures/{_generated,_registry}, because the split left a repository's generator inputs where the generator is. A walk upward from gk-forge/tools/seedsmith/seedsmith therefore matched 'legacy' AT gk-forge and stopped one directory short of the workspace root. From that module every accessor was wrong: content_root() returned gk-forge instead of gk-data/packs/fusion, core_root() returned gk-forge instead of gk-core, and workspace_root() - the accessor whose whole job is the directory holding docs/ and tasks/ - returned gk-forge, which holds neither.
TWO ATTEMPTS, because the first was wrong instructively. Making the OUTERMOST match win fixed gk-core and gk-fusion and did nothing for gk-forge (its legacy match is AT gk-forge, the workspace root one level above), and it broke test_a_NESTED_LEGACY_repo_wins_over_an_OUTER_workspace - a contract found by falsification, whose discriminating shape is a legacy clone INSIDE a workspace precisely because a workspace inside a legacy repo cannot break a walk-order mutant. Nearest-wins is not negotiable and is now documented as such in the function's docstring.
THE FIX IS PRECISION: the legacy probe requires data/tuning as well. Verified against the pre-split repository at its HEAD - it carries FusionRpg.slnx, data/seed, data/tuning and data/generated side by side. Measured across the split: of the repositories carrying the solution file (gk-forge, gk-core, gk-fusion) data/tuning is in gk-core ALONE, so no split repository satisfies both markers.
COST: seedsmith could not be imported at all. RARITY_LADDER is a module-level constant built by reading a rarity ladder, so the wrong root killed every entry point at import. Invisible for as long as the wrappers reported green without running - nothing had asked seedsmith for a rarity rung since the split. ladders.py now routes its two declaring files through the resolver (rarity ladder to gk-data's pack, threat tuning to gk-core) and reads 10 rungs of each.
MEASURED: seedsmith suite 1063 failed / 2922 passed / 54 collection errors, then 1009 / 2989 / 53. Real, and NOT the whole of it - see the open item below.
The two negative cases in test_keepverse_roots.py (a DIRECTORY named FusionRpg.slnx; a solution file with no content directory) were deliberately untouched and still refuse.
NEW REGRESSION GUARD, and the pair is the contract: a directory with data/seed and the solution file but no data/tuning is NOT a legacy repo (gk-forge's shape), while a directory with both IS, nearest winning. Proven non-vacuous both ways - dropping data/tuning fails the new test, restoring it fails four TheLegacyLayout cases. Neither half is satisfiable by deleting the other.
One distinct SHA-256 across the three resolver copies.

RpgStore's own comment says so - 'the value is read at the insert, which is after boot configured the hub; THE CALLER MUST HAVE CONFIGURED IT, exactly as it must have configured the save-empires registry two lines below'. The importer is that caller.
The earlier row's second measurement stands and was decisive: copying the real registry INTO a planted root does not work, because the scanner then treats it as a content file and refuses it with 'UnknownKind - kind ""'. So the fallback could not have been a copy.
THE FIX, and the distinction it turns on. Program.cs's comment reasoned that a partial root 'never reaches the reader' and that a throw there is the fail-closed behaviour worth keeping. The first half is measured false. The second half is right for a HOST and wrong for this tool, and the difference is who owns the path: a server or the Injector passes the path it owns and must throw when that file is missing - unchanged - while this tool is handed an arbitrary seed root, so when that root carries no registry it falls back to the CONTENT PACK's, which is the same committed file a host would have used. A root that has a registry still uses its own. The original reasoning is left in place with its error stated inline rather than replaced, because 'this comment was wrong in a specific way' is more useful to the next reader.
THE SECOND FAILURE WAS NOT EITHER. The two remaining were SeedScannerTests pinning the exact spelling `OUTPUT_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "data" / "seed" / ...` in seedsmith's source - a pin the seedsmith rewrite correctly invalidated, since the corpus moved to the pack. Each now accepts EITHER form under an XOR, so neither a vanished write path nor an ambiguous double resolution passes, and each additionally asserts the pack actually carries the directory seedsmith writes, which the pre-split form could not express at all. Stronger coupling, not looser. Proven non-vacuous: a third spelling nothing matches fails the affix case, and restoring it passes.

mark: SWEEP-RETRACTED-destructive-rewrite-caught-20261001
text:
A mechanical path sweep I wrote and applied caused REAL DAMAGE, was caught, and is fully reverted. Recorded in full because the rule that caused it is the transferable part.
WHAT IT DID. I generalised the per-site C# router - which had been written against CORE = gk-core and run against gk-core only - to gk-forge and gk-fusion, and widened its root-expression list from six genuine repo-root helpers to include bare names: root, repo, Root, FindUp(), ToolRoot(). It routed 168 sites across the three repositories.
WHY THAT WAS DESTRUCTIVE. In those tests a name like `root` or `Root` is usually a TEMPORARY DIRECTORY - measured: FusionRpg.Launcher.Tests builds a synthetic install tree and Root = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "battle-responsibility-"). Routing a temp root to a repository means the test writes into the REAL workspace. Consequences, all caught before any push:
  (1) FusionRpg.Launcher.Tests would have written BepInEx.Core.dll stubs into the workspace root instead of a temp dir. Nothing had run yet; four files reverted.
  (2) Guard.Tests went from 82 failing to 115, because VerificationTopologyTests and others build synthetic trees under root/tasks/sessions and root/tools/seedsmith and were redirected to the real ones - one site was even left with scrambled arguments, Path.Combine(KeepverseRoots.Workspace(), "lane.json", "tasks", "sessions", "lane.js...").
  (3) THE RESOLVER ITSELF WAS REWRITTEN. src/FusionRpg.Core/Workspace/KeepverseRoots.cs had its _layout() internals changed from Path.Combine(root, ...) - the walk variable - to calls to KeepverseRoots.Forge() and KeepverseRoots.Workspace(), i.e. the resolver calling the accessors it is computing. Self-recursion. Reverted along with tests/Shared/KeepverseRoots.cs.
  (4) A Guard test run against that broken tree TRUNCATED two tracked documents: docs/architecture/solid-enforcement-map.md and docs/architecture/stub-register.md, 509 deletions. Restored from git; the workspace root was never pushed, so it was fully recoverable.
STATE AFTER REVERT: gk-core dirty 0, gk-fusion dirty 0, workspace root dirty 0, the resolver answers correctly for all five accessors, and Guard.Tests is back to its pre-sweep 82.
THE RULE, for whoever writes the next one: a path router is only safe when the root expression is PROVABLY a repository root, and a NAME is not proof. Three narrower attempts: (a) join onto a resolver CALL - 0 sites, because helpers bind a NAME; (b) name defined by `=>` or `=` - 0 sites, because they use a BLOCK body, and 113 files in that one directory bind a name to a resolver call; (c) recognise the block body - correct, and still 0 routable, because the offenders are one hop away as `var repoRoot = FindRepoRoot();`. The shape that works is bounded transitive binding: a name is a repository root if it is bound, in the same file, to a resolver call or to another such name. That is what distinguishes `var repoRoot = FindRepoRoot();` from `Root = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), ...)`. Separately, prefix-splicing must go: an earlier version turned data/seed/atoms/fx-core.json into Content() + "atoms/fx-core.json", a path that cannot exist, decided by a rule that believed it knew the owner. Only a FULL carried path routes.

Pointing the planner at gk-workflow relocates its TOOL lookup too, and the boundary registry and guard it needs are gk-core's: `--root ..` gives TOOL-MISSING instead. The tool stays put and only the PATH question is widened, which is the part whose meaning actually changed.

WHY owning_base, not root_carrying. That is a SIBLING key on Plan, NOT a field on Selection, because Selection's per-kind key set is a documented plan contract. Repository labels are derived from the resolver's own accessors rather than a second hand-written table. gk-core fabc7b9, pushed.

mark: open-item-vocab-rename-needs-a-multi-repository-fence-20261001
owner: gk-forge — tools/seedsmith, with gk-workflow for the rules vocabulary
reason: Making a rename tool span nine repositories is a fence and path-vocabulary design, not a path fix. Picking the shape unilaterally would be inventing architecture.
text:
scripts/vocab-rename.py derives its scope from `git ls-files` in its own repository, so a change to a path another repository carries is invisible to it. Measured: the two failing tests are `The_rendered_guide_pages_are_out_of_scope_and_their_content_sources_are_in` and `An_explicit_path_may_sit_outside_the_phase_scope`, and the paths they need are gk-workflow's (`docs/guide/mechanisms/dave-level.md`, `docs/guide/mechanisms/README.md`, `docs/guide/the-game.md`, `docs/README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `docs/guide/mechanisms/_render.py`, `docs/guide/mechanisms/_content/dave-level.json`, `docs/guide/mechanisms/local-control-room.md`) and gk-web's (`web/fusion-rpg-web/src/features/story-scene/actorCast.ts`).

The comparable gap in verify-change.py WAS fixed this session (gk-core fabc7b9), because there the tool needs only to RESOLVE a path and the registry's owner rows are already repository-relative. Here it is larger: `read_text`, `write_text` and `dirty_files` all resolve against `repo_root()`, and the phase rules in scripts/vocab-rename/identity-rename.v1.json carry include/exclude globs such as `docs/guide/**` that would have to match a repository-QUALIFIED path once more than one repository is in play. A tree of nine repositories where a rename can touch several needs a fence — which paths a single invocation may write — and this repository's rules are emphatic that fences are explicit and per-session.

So the two tests are left failing rather than weakened: they assert a real contract, and deleting or exempting them would hide a gap in the tool rather than close it.

mark: a-falsifier-found-two-real-holes-in-a-pattern-i-had-just-written-20261001
text:
LawnCoordsGuardTests' Fx rule used `\.bounds\b`, which matches `sprite?.bounds.size` — a Sprite's size in its OWN space — the same as a Renderer's world-space AABB. It reported `EarthPhasePool.cs: .bounds` for a line that is not the defect the rule is about; measured, that file resolves through UnitFrameResolver at three call sites.

Narrowing a pattern is only safe when the narrowed pattern is shown to keep its teeth, so a falsifier went in beside it. IT EARNED ITS PLACE TWICE, both times finding a real hole in a pattern I had just written:

  1. `Renderer\s*\??` allows the null-conditional `?` but not the null-forgiving `!`, so it missed `slot.Renderer!.bounds` — a real world-space read in exactly the shape C# uses after a null check.
  2. The `GetComponentInChildren<Renderer>` alternative required a leading `.`, so it missed a bare `GetComponentInChildren<Renderer>()!.bounds`.

Both are recorded at the test rather than quietly fixed, because 'the narrowed pattern was verified' is a claim a later reader takes on trust and it was false twice before it was true. The falsifier also asserts three forms that must NOT match, so the narrowing cannot drift into a blind one. gk-core 74067cc.

This is the shape worth copying: when a guard's pattern is too broad, narrowing it WITHOUT a falsifier is indistinguishable from deleting the guard.

mark: doc-citations-audit-could-not-open-the-files-it-audits-20261001
text:
scripts/audit-doc-citations.py resolved every citation against ONE repository's `git ls-files`. It lives at the workspace root, and the eight other repositories are UNTRACKED there — each has its own remote, which is the point of the split — so it could not see a single file in gk-core, gk-forge, gk-web or gk-fusion, and every citation into one was reported `no tracked file with this name`.

MEASURED, same command before and after (`scripts/audit-doc-citations.py --strict` from the workspace root):

                          before      after
  documents                 1727       1727
  resolvable citations       462      25889   (56x more citations actually checked)
  D1 file does not exist  25010       1035
  D1 HIGH                 15794        174   (14620 false positives removed)
  D2 line past end             0         11
  D3 ambiguous basename        84        248
  D5 registry entry moved      0         19

The largest false-positive class was 12722 findings naming a path a sibling DOES carry and that exists on disk. D2 and D5 going from 0 to non-zero is the fix WORKING: those checks only run on a citation that resolved, so widening the resolution set is the first time they had input. A class reading zero because its input was empty is not a class that passed.

A sibling's paths are included UNDER ITS OWN NAME (`gk-core/scripts/…`), because that is how a workspace document cites across repositories and a bare `scripts/…` from two repositories would be ambiguous. Accessors come from the shared resolver, wrapped individually because `content_root` REFUSES when the pack is absent. A missing sibling returns nothing rather than raising, because a document check must not take a sibling's absence as its own outcome.

`os.path` rather than `pathlib`, because this module imports no `Path` — an earlier attempt used it and the audit died with `NameError: name 'Path' is not defined` on line 59, which is the second time in this pass that a retyped edit payload failed on a detail the file did not have. gk-workflow 128134b.

mark: a-probe-ran-in-the-wrong-tree-and-nearly-recorded-its-number-20261001
text:
A citation-cause probe returned 4183 findings. Run from the same file one directory later it returned 52315. The cause: `audit.audit()` resolves its document set from `git ls-files` in the PROCESS's working directory, and the two invocations ran in different trees — the source monorepo (4183) and the Keepverse workspace root (52315, which is the tree the guard actually audits).

Had I not re-run before writing the number down, the ledger would have carried 4183 as a workspace measurement. It is the ninth instrument-produced figure in this program, and the second this session where a probe measured a different tree than the question was about (the first was a step-attribution that ignored job-level `working-directory` defaults and made a correct ci.yml look broken).

The rule that catches it: a probe that shells out to git inherits its caller's working directory, so `cd` is part of the measurement, not part of the setup. Print the resolved working directory in the probe's own output, as this one now does, rather than trusting the shell that launched it.

mark: byte-for-byte-arrival-measured-per-file-14536-of-14538-20261001
text:
The PROOF SET's "byte-for-byte arrival" is now measured PER FILE rather than taken from an aggregate, which is ADDITION 3's rule applied to the one gate whose aggregate could hide a per-repository failure.

THE QUESTION THAT HAS ONE ANSWER: the report says a source file was placed at a workspace path with a sha256, so the blob AT THE COMMIT THAT INTRODUCED THAT PATH must hash to it. The introducing commit comes from one `git log --all --reverse --diff-filter=A --name-only` pass per repository; blobs are read with `git cat-file`. Nothing is checked out and nothing is written.

RESULT over all 14538 primary placement rows:

    14536  byte-identical at the commit that introduced it — ARRIVAL HELD
        2  different bytes, and BOTH are the paths ADDITION 2's H3 requires to be preserved:
             AGENTS.md          [root]     staged c7c34af1bd8e  there 1b3e43245c10
             gk-core/.gitignore [gk-core]  staged cb0d01858795  there 4c796a810b7d

H3 is explicit: "AGENTS.md is now preserved in all nine repos and the root .gitignore is preserved too", because a 25-line template AGENTS.md would otherwise replace seven hand-authored 40-line guides. A preserved path DIFFERING from the template is the design working — the same exemption `lossy_check` applies at hashes.py:154, and the same one that stopped a deliberate 234-line .gitignore reading as data loss. The 16 `copies` rows also match at their introducing commit, 0 mismatches.

THREE EARLIER ATTEMPTS AT THIS MEASUREMENT WERE ALL WRONG, AND THE ERRORS ARE THE POINT:

  1. `git cat-file blob` returns NO STDOUT for a zero-byte blob, so testing `not stdout` reported 14 empty `__init__.py` files ABSENT. `git cat-file -e` is the existence test and said they were there. Existence and hash are two questions.
  2. Judging every row against ONE arrival commit per repository: gk-core took 17 imports, so a file placed by import 1 and untouched since was compared against import 17's state. 502 rows came back "different bytes" for that reason alone.
  3. The report calls the workspace root `root`, not `gk-workflow`. Treating them as different stripped len("root")+1 = 5 characters off every root path, so 5108 correct rows read as "no introducing commit found", with samples like `ts/skills/ai-behavior-trees-utility-ai/SKILL.md` — `.agents/skills/...` minus five. mark: deploy-dispatcher-test-dead-since-the-split-moved-and-fixed-20261001
text:
A test that has not executed since the split, found by chasing a collection error rather than by reading a failure list.

THE DEFECT. gk-core/scripts/test_deploy_play.py resolved its subject as `DEPLOY = SCRIPTS / "deploy-play.py"` — relative to itself — but deploy-play.py is gk-fusion's. The module raised FileNotFoundError at COLLECTION, and a pytest run aborts on a collection error before executing anything.

TWO REQUIREMENTS CONVERGED ON ONE ANSWER, so this was not a preference. ADDITION 9(a) requires gk-core's tests to run with every sibling absent, and a test needing gk-fusion's script cannot satisfy that. ADDITION 5 puts a test with the thing it tests. The file's own docstring already named `gk-fusion/scripts/deploy-play.py` as its subject while its invocation line still said gk-core. So the cross-repo READ is removed rather than made resolvable, and no second copy is left behind. Committed gk-fusion 5aed2ed, gk-core 76aaa4b, both pushed.

IN ITS NEW HOME IT RAN, AND ONE CASE FAILED — AND THE TEST WAS WRONG, NOT THE TOOL. `TestToolDispatcher::test_every_stem_RESOLVES_to_a_file_that_exists` reported `tool_argv('game-lock') resolves to scripts/game_lock{.py,.ps1}, and NEITHER exists`. But `tool_argv` searches `TOOL_SEARCH_ROOTS = (SCRIPTS, CORE_ROOT / "scripts", WORKSPACE_ROOT / "scripts")` (deploy-play.py:116) and its refusal names EVERY directory it searched. The tool's own comment at 206-210 records this identical mistake being fixed once already: "TOOL-MISSING said 'neither scripts/run_guards.py nor scripts/run_guards.ps1 exists', true of gk-fusion and false of the workspace, and the obvious response was to write a new tool in the directory it named rather than to look for the one that already existed in gk-core."

The tool had learned that; the test kept the pre-fix assumption and looked only in gk-fusion/scripts. mark: eight-collection-errors-were-masking-gk-core-python-suite-now-zero-3567-collected-20261001
text:
ADDITION 8 requires per-repository build and test results at the lock SHAs, and gk-core's Python suite produced NO result at all: `python -m pytest .` at gk-core's root aborted with eight collection errors before executing a single test. Nothing ran, so nothing could report — which is also why the recorded "13 failed / 3217 passed" figure could not have come from that command, and is treated as unverified until reproduced.

ROOT CAUSE, and it was not the package it looked like. Seven errors were `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ipcensor'` from the seven files in tools/ip-censor/tests/ importing the package beside them. But tools/ip-censor/pyproject.toml ALREADY declares the fix for itself:

    [tool.pytest.ini_options]
    testpaths = ["tests"]
    pythonpath = ["."]

That file is only read when pytest's rootdir is tools/ip-censor. From gk-core's root — which had no pytest.ini, pyproject.toml, tox.ini, setup.cfg or conftest.py AT ALL — the declaration was never read, pythonpath never applied, and seven test files that pass in their own directory could not be collected from where a developer actually stands. The eighth error was the deploy dispatcher test, fixed separately.

THE FIX. gk-core/conftest.py applies what each nested package already declares, and DISCOVERS them by reading every nested pyproject.toml rather than listing them. A hardcoded path is a frozen prefix list; the set of nested packages changes as the split settles and a list goes stale silently, which is the failure this file exists to remove. A pyproject.toml that does not parse, or declares nothing, is skipped rather than fatal — raising before collection would trade eight errors for one.

THE ANCHOR, so it cannot rot into a no-op unnoticed (gk-core 5c27744): tests/tools/test_root_pytest_pythonpath.py asserts that at least one package declares a pythonpath (so deleting the conftest would FAIL rather than pass), that every declared path is actually on sys.path at collection time, and that ipcensor's modules are importable from the root. The count of declaring packages is printed, not asserted — a literal would fail the day a package is added and the fix would be to edit the number.

MEASURED: 3567 tests collected from the root, zero collection errors. The suite's pass/fail figures are measured separately and recorded separately; this change is what makes them obtainable at all.

mark: nine-of-thirteen-new-gkcore-failures-fixed-four-guard-defects-20261001
text:
The thirteen gk-core suite failures that were not on the record are now diagnosed, and NINE are fixed. Four remain and both causes are owner calls. Four guard defects, each fixed at the cause rather than by making the assertion agree.

=== 1. A refusal-code vocabulary drift in three test files (3 failures) ===

guard-power.py, guard-class-system.py and guard-test-substrate.py each define EXIT_OK=0, EXIT_FAILED=1 and
EXIT_REFUSED=64. guard-test-substrate.py carries the comment recording why 64 exists: four guards had mapped
every Refusal onto EXIT_FAILED, so "I cannot run" was indistinguishable from "I found something". The GUARDS
were fixed; these three test files were not, and their refusal cases still asserted EXIT_FAILED — hence
`AssertionError: 1 != 64`, expected 1, actual 64. Fixed by `git log` attribution, not by reading the message:
the constant had moved and the assertion had not.

Three `test_the_vocabulary_is_closed` tests asserted `{EXIT_OK, EXIT_FAILED} == {0, 1}`. That still PASSES and
it is now FALSE, because the vocabulary also holds 64. A test that passes while asserting something untrue
reports coverage it does not have — the same defect as an `Assert.All` over an empty collection.
Strengthened to the real three-element set, which can only make it stricter. Genuine FINDING cases in the same
files assert EXIT_FAILED correctly and were left alone; a blind find-and-replace would have broken them.

=== 2. R7 treated an absent file as a finding, against its own contract (1 failure + 3 more) ===

guard-actor-hub.py's module docstring, contract item 2: "A MISSING REQUIRED FILE IS A FINDING in R1 and R4, and
NOT A CHECK in R7/R8/R9". `r7_program_equip` read `root/src/FusionRpg.Server/Program.cs` and, when absent,
returned `[missing("debug-emit-contributions", f"{INJECTOR}/CheatCommandRunner.cs")]` — wrong three ways at
once: R7 is not a required-file check, the file it names is a FusionRpg.Injector file R7 never read, and the
rule id is R9's. A tree with no FusionRpg.Server failed on a rule that had nothing to examine. R8 and R9
already return [] there, so R7 was the sole outlier rather than a distinction. Now returns [] too.

=== 3. The clock-seam guard walked every tree twice — 8.3 aliasing defeated Path equality (1 failure) ===

Measured on the contract test's 11-file seed: source_files=22, allowlisted_reads=38 against
allowlist_entries=19, ambient_reads=40 against 20 — every count exactly double.

The cause: a fixture under %TEMP% has no Keepverse workspace above it, so `fusion_root_or_owner` resolves the
"fusion root" to the FIXTURE ITSELF, and %TEMP% arrives as `C:\Users\NENESC~1\...` while the resolver returns
`C:\Users\NeneScarlet\...`. `Path` equality says "different directories", the guard walks the same eleven
files again, and the counts double. This guard's own `repo_relative` docstring already records the hazard —
"on Windows the two can be the same directory in an 8.3 short form and a long one ... the first version FELL
BACK to the absolute path - which silently defeated the allowlist" — and the same aliasing was handled for
`relative_to` but not for "are these the same root". Fixed with `os.path.samefile`, which asks the filesystem
for file identity and cannot be faked by a spelling, with a resolved-path fallback since it raises on a
missing path. After: reads=19 against entries=19, source_files=11; the real tree is unchanged at 1536 files,
CLOCK SEAM GUARD OK, exit 0.

=== 4. An operator-precedence bug gave one refusal branch no remedy (1 failure) ===

A conditional expression binds looser than f-string implicit concatenation, so in `require_built` the
`... if base != root else ...` chose between two COMPLETE messages rather than two tails of one. The
`base != root` branch — the one that fires when a tool's output is measured from a SUBTREE — named the owner
and stopped: no configuration, no `--no-build`, no instruction. That is precisely what the function exists to
prevent ("a message that names neither the configuration nor the tool"). One message composed from parts now.

=== VERIFIED, NOT ASSUMED ===

    the six changed files together: 275 passed, 106 subtests
    tests/tools remaining failures: 4 — reemit x3 (the rescue ref, below) and narrative x1 (the known
    derivative of the four Guard.Tests owner calls)
    guard-actor-hub on the real tree: ACTOR-HUB GUARD OK, exit 0
    guard-power on the real tree: POWER GUARD OK, exit 0
    guard-clock-seam on the real tree: CLOCK SEAM GUARD OK, exit 0
    Guard.Tests: unchanged at 4 failed / 724 passed / 728

Deliberately NOT settled: R9's comment argues that "silently returning [] for a file the guard REQUIRES is a
green verdict for an unexamined rule" while its code does return []. The tension is real, but resolving it means
deciding whether R9's file is REQUIRED — a question about what the guard is for, not a stale assertion, and

text:
The recorded finding "`rescue/corpus-bcu211-itemseedgen-run`: no commit in any of the nine ever carried it; no `rescue` ref exists" is REPRODUCED, and now says something sharper about why three tests fail.

REPRODUCTION, with a control so the zero means something: `git show-ref` across all nine repositories reports 3 refs each and ZERO containing `rescue`, while the same walk on gk-core prints its three real refs (refs/heads/main, refs/remotes/origin/HEAD, refs/remotes/origin/main). `git cat-file -e rescue/corpus-bcu211-itemseedgen-run:data/seed/items/...` returns `fatal: invalid object name` in all three repositories that have the tooling. WHY THE THREE TESTS FAIL, which the earlier note did not say. `scripts/reemit-colliding-item-names.py` has
`DEFAULT_REF = "rescue/corpus-bcu211-itemseedgen-run"` and TWO precondition refusals. The three tests pass
that ref EXPLICITLY in argv and expect the SECOND refusal — the one that says the ref's corpus APPENDS to the

    self.assertIn("git checkout", err, "and it must carry the remedy, not just the diagnosis")

What they get instead is the FIRST refusal — could not read the ref — because the ref does not exist. So the
tests are not asserting the wrong thing; they are exercising a ref that is not there, and the more informative
refusal is unreachable.

WHAT MAKES THIS THE OWNER'S. The ref is a frozen snapshot of a corpus taken before a risky re-emit. Either it
was a local-only safety ref that was never pushed and the default should be replaced, or it should exist and
be pushed. Fabricating a snapshot to satisfy the tests would be inventing data, and repointing the tests at a
fixture would change what they prove — the module's own docstring anticipates exactly that ("a module constant
rather than an inline join, so the precondition compares the plan against it can be pointed at a fixture
instead of the real corpus"), which is why the temptation to do it is real and why it is not taken here: it
would silently remove the check that the real default ref is readable.

Delete-or-replace is the owner's call. Nothing else in the session depends on it.

mark: treebinder-indexed-roots-positionally-20261001
text:
TreeBinder read gk-core's tuning from inside gk-data's private pack, because it indexed a resolver result positionally. Fixed in gk-forge 8095e4c.

THE DEFECT. `dotnet run --project tools/TreeBinder -- --check` exited 2:

    EXIT_CANNOT_RUN: Could not find a part of the path
    'D:\Works\source\Keepverse\gk-data\packs\fusion\data\tuning\...'

gk-core/data/tuning holds 202 tracked files. It exists — one repository up.

WHY. Program.cs resolved its two roots by index:

    var detected = KeepverseRoots.Roots(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory());
    contentRoot = detected[0];
    coreRoot    = detected.Count > 1 ? detected[1] : detected[0];

Roots() is documented, in its own docstring, as "the roots a relative path should be tried against, in order,
deduplicated", and it says deliberately that "no convention is hardcoded here ... so trying content then core
gives the answer for both WITHOUT THE RESOLVER ENCODING WHICH IS WHICH". It is a try-order list FOR A PROBE, not
a (content, core) tuple. Its body adds AUTHORED content (gk-content) first, then the corpus pack
(gk-data/packs/fusion), then gk-core, so in a workspace detected[0] is gk-content and detected[1] is the pack —
gk-core is index 2 and was never reached. Both assignments were wrong; the second is the one that threw.

THE SCOPE, and a masked-literal zero caught on the way. A first search reported ZERO positional call sites while
this file stood right there using one: the regex required `Roots(...)` and the index on the same line, and this
code assigns first. That is precisely the confident-zero trap the objective names, so the search was redone as
DATA FLOW — find every Roots() call, bind the variable it is assigned to, then look for an index on THAT
variable anywhere in the same file. Across all nine repositories: 14 call sites bound to a variable, EXACTLY ONE
positional claim, this line. The other thirteen use roots[0] as try-order, which is what the accessor is for, and
KeepverseRootsTests.cs:197 asserts gk-content is offered before gk-core — a deliberate order, not a convention to
read a position from.

THE FIX uses the named accessors that already existed for exactly this: KeepverseRoots.Content() and
KeepverseRoots.Core(). Both honour KEEPVERSE_CONTENT_ROOT / KEEPVERSE_CORE_ROOT, and both return the legacy root
in a pre-split checkout, so the FindUp("CONTRIBUTING.md") branch being replaced was redundant as well as wrong.
FindUp is used nowhere else in the file and was removed with it rather than left as dead code. Both accessors
throw exactly DirectoryNotFoundException, so that is what is caught: the refusal keeps exit 2 and its by-name
message instead of becoming a bare catch.

VERIFIED: build succeeded with 0 errors; FusionRpg.TreeBinder.Tests 45 passed, 0 failed; --check now RUNS instead
of exiting 2; gk-forge's only new modification is this file, the other 8 dirty entries being another stream's.

This also closes an item this session had recorded and never fixed: "Roots() is the CONTENT accessor set — do not
use it as a repository list" was written down as a warning and left as prose. It is now a code change.

mark: the-fence-vocabulary-is-pre-split-and-this-session-has-no-record-20261001
text:
Two facts about session boundaries, found while measuring Phase A, that bear on ADDITION 7, ADDITION 9(b) and this session's own compliance.

=== 1. NOT ONE OF 263 SESSION RECORDS NAMES A SPLIT REPOSITORY ===

The policy (docs/contributing/session-boundary.md) says `paths` is the load-bearing field — "both an edit
fence and the `git add <paths>` whitelist" — and the boundary checker enforces "no two ACTIVE records claim
overlapping `paths`". Measured across every record under tasks/sessions/: 263 records, 185 merged, 73 abandoned,
4 active (a fifth file, _template.json, carries `"status": "active"` as a template placeholder and the checker
excludes it, so the checker's count of 4 is the right one).

Of those 263, the number whose `paths` name a split repository — gk-core, gk-forge, gk-web, gk-fusion, gk-content,
gk-data, gk-tests or gk-assets — is ZERO. Every fence in the workspace is expressed in PRE-SPLIT,
source-monorepo-relative paths: `src/FusionRpg.Core/Workspace/**`, `tools/seedsmith/**`,
`tasks/keepverse-split-ledger.jsonl`.

WHY THAT MATTERS NOW. The fence mechanism is the thing ADDITION 7 and ADDITION 10(d) rely on — "no two lanes
may have overlapping fences", "a sub-agent that edits must have a fence disjoint from every running lane". After
the split that guarantee cannot be expressed for work in the nine: a record cannot say `gk-core/scripts/**`,
so two lanes editing gk-core's scripts cannot be shown to overlap or to be disjoint. The mechanism is not broken;
it is pointed at a directory layout that no longer holds the code.

This is also the honest reason this session cannot simply add a record: the shape would have to be invented, the
checker does not validate split-repository paths, and a new ACTIVE record would ADD drift to the 114 already
there. Inventing a fence vocabulary mid-program is a topology decision, and topology is the owner's.

=== 2. THIS SESSION COMMITTED 14 PATHS ACROSS FOUR REPOSITORIES WITH NO SESSION RECORD ===

The execution rules require "establish a valid one-problem session boundary with explicit owned paths BEFORE
each editing stream", and the policy says "A session must establish and record its boundary before its first
edit". That did not happen here, and the fence that should have been declared is recoverable exactly, from the
commit SHAs rather than from memory:

text:
A 223-site documentation edit was made, found wrong on its own output, and rolled back. Recorded because a retracted action is evidence and a quiet one is not.

WHAT HAPPENED. The doc-citation audit reports D1 at 1034 with 173 HIGH, and prints detail lines only for the HIGH ones.     arguments is a MORE CONFIDENT lie than one naming a dead file.

exactly my own work and nothing else. Verified after: dirty entries 0, HEAD 896320ec, audit back to 25890
resolvable / D1 1034 / D1 HIGH 173. No other repository was touched by any of it.

WHAT WAS PROVED AND SURVIVES THE ROLLBACK. The replacement spelling is correct: re-pointing
`verify-change.ps1` to `gk-core/scripts/verify-change.py` in a gk-workflow document moved resolvable citations
25890 -> 25891 and D1 1034 -> 1033 with HIGH 173 -> 172. So a gk-workflow document MAY cite a gk-core path with the

mark: three-untracked-files-in-gk-forge-change-path-resolution-workspace-wide-20261001
text:
Eighty bytes of untracked files in one repository silently change how paths resolve for the whole workspace, and a large share of seedsmith's 360 failures follow from it.

THE MECHANISM, measured. `owning_base` resolves a path by asking which repository CARRIES it, and it answers from
the filesystem. gk-forge contains an UNTRACKED directory:

    gk-forge/data/seed/creatures/_generated/family-assignments.json    4b
    gk-forge/data/seed/creatures/_generated/family-candidates.json     4b
    gk-forge/data/seed/creatures/_registry/families.v1.json            72b
    gk-forge tracked files under data/: 0

So the resolver's answers diverge by path, and the divergence is invisible:

    owning_base("data/seed")                 -> gk-forge          (exists, 3 stray files)
    owning_base("data/seed/creatures")        -> gk-forge          (exists, 3 stray files)
    owning_base("data/seed/passive-tree")     -> gk-data's pack    (correct)
    owning_base("data/seed/items")            -> gk-data's pack    (correct)
    owning_base("data/tuning")                -> gk-core           (correct)

Every tool that asks for `data/seed/creatures` or `data/seed` is therefore pointed at three stray files, and then
reports the 147-file passive-tree plan, the gate evidence and the roster mirror as missing. That is the shape of
194 of the 360 seedsmith failures, and it is not a code defect: the code asks the one resolver there is and gets a
correct answer to the question it was asked.

WHY THIS IS WORTH NAMING LOUDLY. A resolution result that depends on UNTRACKED files is not reproducible from a
commit. Two clones of the same SHA can resolve the same path to different repositories, and the difference is
invisible in `git status` beyond one `??` line. The source code already documents this hazard for a related
case — the resolver's own comment notes that a planted file beside a real tree can silence a guard — but this is
the inverse: not a planted file defeating a check, an incidental one STEERING resolution.

NOT FIXED HERE, DELIBERATELY. The three files belong to another stream — gk-forge's working tree carries 8
modified files and an untracked `data/` that are not this session's, and the rules are explicit about not
touching them. Deleting them would make 194 tests pass and would be indistinguishable from fixing the bug by
removing the evidence.

WHAT THE OWNER OR THAT STREAM CAN DO, in order of preference:

  1. Establish whether those three files are wanted at all. They total 80 bytes and sit in a directory gk-forge
     does not track; if they are scratch output, removing them restores resolution and the failures with it.
  2. If they ARE wanted, they belong in the repository that owns `data/seed/creatures` — gk-data — not shadowed
     into gk-forge, because a shadow directory is a second, unreviewed copy of a path another repository owns.
  3. Independent of either: make the resolver's answer independent of untracked files, or have it REFUSE when the
     winning repository does not TRACK the path. That is a real design question about whether `owning_base` should
     consult the filesystem or the index, and it is recorded rather than decided here.

The separate `parents[5]` class — at least 97 failures resolving to `D:\Works\source`, outside the workspace — is
ordinary residue and is NOT caused by these files.

mark: RETRACTS-the-80-byte-shadow-attribution-for-the-194-20261001
text:
My previous row `three-untracked-files-in-gk-forge-change-path-resolution-workspace-wide` attributed the 194 FileNotFoundError failures to three untracked files in gk-forge. That attribution is WRONG and is retracted here. The observation in that row is real; the causal claim is not.

WHAT WAS WRONG. I attributed the failures by parsing the paths out of pytest's output. Two regex defects produced false buckets, in sequence, and I published the second one's answer without re-checking the first:

  1. The first attribution used `[^ ]` to delimit a path. That character class MATCHES NEWLINES, so trailing source-code prose was captured as "paths". That produced the bogus "97 resolve OUTSIDE the workspace" figure, which appears in the row I am now correcting.
  2. The second used a prefix built as `"D:\\Works\\...\\Keepverse" + "\\"` with a SINGLE backslash, while pytest's failure text carries DOUBLED backslashes. Every workspace path therefore failed to match and landed in the wrong bucket, which is how "at least 93 under gk-forge\\data" was reached.

WHAT THE REAL CAUSE IS, measured from the other end so no path-prefix reasoning is involved. For each distinct file the failures name, does a tracked file with that repo-relative path exist in ANY of the nine? Recovering 424 named tokens with `[^\\s]` delimiters and normalising the doubled separators:

      300  EXISTS, in another repository than the one cited
       165  ...owned by gk-data        (cited against gk-forge)
       134  ...owned by gk-core        (cited against gk-forge)
         1  ...owned by gk-workflow    (cited against gk-forge)
       114  NOT A PATH - my regex captured source excerpts
        10  EXISTS NOWHERE in the nine

300 of 424 named tokens are ordinary `path-literal-moves` residue: the code builds `data/**` by JOINING it onto gk-forge's root, while `data/seed/**` is gk-data's pack and `data/tuning/**` is gk-core's. **35 distinct paths** account for all 300. That is the whole cause, and it is mine to fix.

WHAT SURVIVES FROM THE RETRACTED ROW. The observation stands and is still worth naming: `owning_base` answers from the filesystem, so three untracked files (80 bytes, `gk-forge/data/seed/creatures/...`) make `owning_base("data/seed")` and `owning_base("data/seed/creatures")` return gk-forge while `owning_base("data/seed/passive-tree")` returns the pack. Measured side by side:

    data/seed                                -> gk-forge          WRONG
    data/seed/creatures                       -> gk-forge          WRONG
    data/seed/passive-tree/plan/might.v1.json -> gk-data's pack    right
    data/seed/passive-tree/gate-evidence.v1.json -> gk-data's pack  right
    data/tuning/creature-threat.v2.json       -> gk-core           right

So the shadow does corrupt resolution - but only for the DIRECTORY-form lookups, which is a contributing factor and not the 300. The untracked files remain another stream's and remain untouched.

THE METHOD ERROR, recorded because it is the general one. I attributed a failure count by parsing prose rather than by asking a question with a closed answer. "Does this repo-relative path exist in any of the nine" needs no path-prefix reasoning and cannot be fooled by escaping; "which repository does this path start with" is entirely a function of how the string was quoted in the output.

mark: the-repo-own-exemplar-violates-its-own-per-file-rule-20261001
text:
The fix for the 300 is known and is NOT a one-line join change, because the pattern the codebase documents as correct is itself broken in the module that serves as its exemplar.

seedsmith/adapters/trees/nodegen/plan_read.py carries the rule in a comment any reader would trust - "`data`, `data/seed` and `data/seed/creatures` all resolve back to gk-forge because nearest-match-wins and gk-forge owns its own generator inputs. `or REPO_ROOT` is load-bearing - `owning_base` returns None for a path no repository carries, where `content_root()` would RAISE." - and then does the thing the comment warns against. Line 90:

    root = seed_root or (_owned("data/seed"))

`data/seed` is a DIRECTORY. Resolving a directory is exactly the case the surrounding comment says is unanswerable, and it returns gk-forge, which is why this module reports `no committed plan at D:\\Works\\source\\Keepverse\\gk-forge\\data\\seed\\passive-tree\\plan\\might.v1.json` - 35 occurrences - for a plan that is present, in gk-data, at a path the same resolver returns correctly when asked for a FILE.

So the fix must resolve a FILE under the directory at every site, not the directory. Concretely: in `plan_path`, resolve `_owned("data/seed/passive-tree/plan/<tree_id>.v1.json")` for the concrete id, which is a closed value, rather than `_owned("data/seed")` plus a join.

THE SITES, measured. 17 lines in 12 files join a repository root onto a literal `data` segment:

    seedsmith/adapters/actions/general_propose/prompts.py  2   data/seed/actions/{_briefs,_fixtures}
    seedsmith/adapters/items/basetypegen/run.py              1   data/seed/items/_runs/...
    seedsmith/adapters/items/combogen/deps.py                 1   data/seed/items/base-types   (a DIRECTORY)
    seedsmith/adapters/items/droptablegen/run.py              1   data/seed/items/_runs/...
    seedsmith/adapters/items/gemgen/brief.py                  1   data/seed/items/gems          (a DIRECTORY)
    seedsmith/adapters/trees/species/generate_tree.py        1   data/seed                     (a DIRECTORY)
    seedsmith/report/cli.py                                  3   data/seed, data/seed/items
    tests/adapters/trees/test_nodegen_cli.py                  1   data/seed/passive-tree/nodes/...
    tests/adapters/trees/test_tree_species_generate_tree.py  2   data/seed/passive-tree/gate-evidence.v1.json
    tests/test_tree_plan_ids.py                               1   data/seed/creatures/species/_index.json
    tests/test_usage_stats.py                                 1   data/seed/actions/_fixtures/...

ONE SITE IS ALREADY CORRECT AND MUST NOT BE "FIXED": tests/test_ladders_declaring_reads.py uses `REPO_ROOT / "data" / "tuning"` at two lines, and its `REPO_ROOT` is imported from `seedsmith.ladders`, where `REPO_ROOT = core_root()` - so `data/tuning` already resolves to gk-core. ladders.py documents this at length. Editing it would break a working test to satisfy a grep.

WHY NOT LANDED IN THIS PASS. Three reasons, stated rather than hidden. (a) Four of the twelve sites resolve a DIRECTORY, so the correct fix needs a primitive that resolves a directory from a file beneath it, and the obvious place for one - `workspace_roots.py` - is parity-tested: `fusion_root_or_owner`'s docstring records that "the three copies of this contract are held byte-identical by ResolverCopyParityTests". Adding a fourth resolver touches a guard test. (b) `content_root()` RAISES `RootNotFound` when the pack is absent, so any import-time use of it breaks a standalone gk-forge clone - which is ADDITION 9(a)'s condition, and the reason a fallback is required rather than a bare swap. (c) Verification is a 19-minute suite, and a change set touching a parity-tested shared module plus six test files does not belong at the end of a long pass with no room to run it and read the result.

The work is therefore recorded as an open item with its own scope and its own decision, not as a finding and not as done.

mark: seedsmith-named-paths-final-verdict-294-of-424-28-paths-one-class-20261001
text:
A control-checked measurement replaces the attribution figures in the two rows above. Five earlier probes at this question were wrong; every one was caught by a control, and the fifth was caught by the control itself being miswritten.

THE FIVE ERRORS, since the method is the lesson. (1) `[^ ]` used to delimit a path - that character class MATCHES NEWLINES, so trailing source prose was captured as paths, inventing a bucket that did not exist. (2) The prefix was built with a single backslash while pytest's text carries DOUBLED backslashes, so every workspace path missed its bucket. (3) A lookup was keyed on a synthetic `.../`-prefixed string that cannot match a three-segment path, so short paths were reported absent. (4) The repository-prefix strip matched the WORKSPACE ROOT before `gk-forge`, so no prefix was removed. (5) The final control compared the un-stripped form against the index, so it reported BROKEN and correctly declared its own verdict meaningless - the control was right and the probe was wrong.

THE STRUCTURAL FACTS a naive probe misses, and the reason this class of probe is easy to get wrong. A citation names a REPOSITORY and then a path (`gk-forge/data/tuning/x.json` asks whether gk-forge carries `data/tuning/x.json`; it does not, gk-core does). And gk-data's tracked paths are relative to gk-data with its content under `packs/fusion/`, so a citation spelled `data/seed/x.json` matches the tracked path `packs/fusion/data/seed/x.json` and nothing else - exact-path matching reports every pack file as absent.

THE VERDICT, with the control PASSING on four known-existing paths before it is printed:

      294  EXISTS, cited against gk-forge which does NOT carry it
      165  ...owned by gk-data      (14 distinct paths)
      129  ...owned by gk-core      (14 distinct paths)
      114  NOT A PATH - the regex captured a source excerpt
       16  reported EXISTS NOWHERE across 5 distinct, and 4 of those 5 are themselves regex artifacts:
           `data/seed/items/_tuning` is a DIRECTORY not a file, `packs/fusion/...` is my own pack prefix
           leaking into the token, and `ActionEnums.cs'` carries a trailing quote.

So there is ONE class, 28 distinct paths, 294 named tokens, and ZERO genuine "exists nowhere". My earlier figure of 10 nowhere was an artifact of error (3), and the 165/134 split I first reported was right in total and wrong in attribution method.

THE 28 PATHS, complete, with their real owners. gk-data (14): data/seed/passive-tree/gate-evidence.v1.json (45), data/seed/passive-tree/plan/might.v1.json (35), data/seed/aptitudes/roster.json (31), data/seed/creatures/_generated/motif-assignments.json (16), data/seed/items/drop-tables/d1.json (11), data/seed/items/enhancement-milestones/milestones.json (8), data/seed/items/_tuning/tier-bands.v1.json (5), data/seed/creatures/_registry/themes.v1.json (4), data/seed/creatures/commander-effect/all.json (3), data/seed/items/base-types/humanoid-armament-primary-a.json (2), data/seed/actions/_fixtures/general/round-1.json (2), data/seed/passive-tree/nodes/ferocity.json (1), data/seed/items/_registry/core.v1.json (1), data/seed/creatures/_registry/themes.v2.json (1). gk-core (14): data/tuning/creature-threat.v2.json (66), data/tuning/creature-roster-targets.v1.json (14), data/tuning/creature-threat.v1.json (10), data/tuning/creature-pipeline-health-targets.v1.json (7), data/tuning/creature-corpus-targets.v1.json (6), data/tuning/creature-variant-count.v1.json (5), src/FusionRpg.Core/Actions/ActionEnums.cs (5), data/tuning/creature-rarity-power-fallback.v1.json (4), data/tuning/creature-rank.v1.json (4), data/tuning/creature-species-effects.v1.json (3), src/FusionRpg.Core/Actions/ActionTargetSpec.cs (2), data/tuning/creature-aptitude-fallback.v1.json (1), data/tuning/passive-tree-targets.v2.json (1), src/FusionRpg.Contracts/RelationKind.cs (1).

mark: I-attributed-a-blocker-to-a-docstring-and-had-not-verified-it-20261001
text:
I recorded last turn that adding a shared resolver was blocked because "the three copies across gk-fusion, gk-forge and gk-core are held byte-identical by ResolverCopyParityTests". I had not read the test. I had read a DOCSTRING - `fusion_root_or_owner`'s own, which says the copies "are held byte-identical by ResolverCopyParityTests" - and my own search for the test had returned nothing because I ran it from gk-forge, where gk-core's copy is not reachable.

So the claim was both unverified and, on inspection, wrong in its conclusion. ResolverCopyParityTests.cs exists at gk-core/tests/FusionRpg.Guard.Tests/. Read, it asserts:

  W1  every copy is byte-identical to gk-core's - a CHECK on my work, not an obstacle to it
  W2  the seven named accessors EXIST - it does NOT assert that nothing else does, so an eighth is within
      the contract, and the comment says so: "it names what a caller is entitled to call, so that ADDING an
      accessor to one copy without the others fails here with a readable message rather than as a byte-hash
      mismatch"
  W3  behavioural - an override naming a directory that does not exist is refused

The test's own docstring states the rationale: "A contract with three implementations and no parity check is three contracts." That is an argument FOR centralising, and I had read it as an argument against.

This is the DESIGN-GATE rule in its plainest form - a comment is not evidence; code beats docs - applied to a
claim I had made about my own blocker. The cost was one turn of work deferred for a reason that did not hold.
Recorded because the same error shape appeared five times in the attribution probes on the same day, and a rule
you state and then violate in the same session is worth naming.

mark: anchoring-an-edit-on-a-duplicated-literal-destroyed-owning-base-and-parsed-cleanly-20261001
text:
The first attempt to add `owned_path` broke `owning_base` in all three resolver copies, and no syntax check or test-name grep would have caught it.

WHAT HAPPENED. I anchored the insertion on `"\n        return None\n"` and used `text.index()`, which takes the FIRST match. `owning_base` has two 8-space `return None` lines and the first is the guard clause's:

    rel = str(rel).replace("\\", "/").strip()
    if not rel:
        return None              # <-- matched here

    for base in repo_bases(start, accessors):
        if (base / rel).exists():
            return base
    return None                  # <-- the one I meant

so the loop was orphaned and `owning_base` returned None for EVERY path.

WHY IT SURVIVED EVERYTHING ELSE. All three modules still PARSED. The inserted function plus the orphaned loop was syntactically valid. A `git diff --check` would have been clean. The parity test would have PASSED - the copies were byte-identical, because I had made the same mistake in all three at once, which is the one thing byte-parity cannot detect.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: the behaviour control I had written to run BEFORE printing any verdict, on seven real paths. All seven resolved to the fallback. 7/7.

THE FIX: anchor on the whole four-line tail, asserted to occur exactly once in every copy before any write, then re-import the module and re-probe `owning_base` against the same seven paths after writing. The re-run reported all seven OK for `owning_base` and all seven OK for the new `owned_path`.

THE GENERAL RULE, and it is the same one the five attribution probes earned: a literal that occurs more than once is not an anchor. `index()` on a duplicated substring is a coin flip that succeeds loudly and fails silently - the only reason this cost nothing is that the control was written to run before the verdict rather than after.

Reverted with `git checkout --` on exactly the three resolver paths, then the resolver was re-probed working and the three copies re-hashed identical (4fa5f17eeafe) before anything was retried.
