RATIONALE I AGREE WITH AND RECORD: the path has been wrong twice - the anchor has moved unclassified -> undead -> plant - and the runner's own comment says family is model-decided, not stable across runs. A literal 'zombie/plant.json' would satisfy today's suite and re-arm the identical trap on the next reclassification, which is the definition of a test that cannot fail for the right reason. This is a criterion change BY RULING, before the change that satisfies it, which is what A2 requires. (2) ONE LADDER, ONE FLOOR. registries.py stops slicing THREAT_BAND[6:] and reads encounter.v1.json's threatWindow.bossFloorRung, the same source DomainPreflight.cs:73-77 uses. The ladder was always correct and matches creature-threat.v1.json's ten thresholds exactly; it was the FLOOR that was guessed, and the file's comment claimed otherwise. CONSEQUENCE TO CARRY: eligibility widens from rung 7 to rung 4, so 'boss-eligible' becomes a much weaker filter - I measured the rung >= 7 sets as air 6, dark 6, earth 43, fire 13, ice 9, light 10, and the wider sets are substantially larger. The six shipped bosses were all verified at rung 10 or 8, so the data does not move; but any future domain will face a wider candidate set than the corpus has ever been checked against. BOTH ARE gk-forge CHANGES, QUEUED BEHIND THE IN-FLIGHT AGENT on that repository.

mark: A11's clause 'gk-core builds and tests with every private sibling absent' is HALF FALSE, and the false half is correct behaviour rather than a defect. The CRITERION is what is wrong, not the code.
text: Measured in a bare gk-core clone with zero sibling repositories present. BUILD: SUCCEEDS. dotnet build of tests/FusionRpg.Core.Status.Tests -c Release gave Build succeeded, 2 Warning(s), 0 Error(s), exit 0, with no gk-data, gk-forge, gk-web or gk-fusion anywhere on disk. So half of A11 holds and I can assert it. TEST: DOES NOT RUN, and cannot. Two distinct reasons, both measured rather than inferred. (1) ROOT RESOLUTION. A bare gk-core has FusionRpg.slnx and data/tuning but NOT data/seed, and it is not inside a workspace holding gk-core/ beside gk-data/, so NEITHER probe in KeepverseRoots._layout succeeds and it raises - 'no legacy repository or Keepverse workspace above ... A root is never guessed'. That is the same refusal that produced my 254-failure harness error earlier this session, so the lesson is now confirmed from a second direction. (2) EVEN WITH THE OVERRIDE, IT STILL FAILS - and this is the part that matters. Setting KEEPVERSE_CORE_ROOT, KEEPVERSE_WORKSPACE_ROOT and KEEPVERSE_CONTENT_ROOT resolves the root and moves the failure from a RootNotFound to a FileNotFoundException at ContractTuningTestBootstrap.cs:132. The bootstrap every one of the 254 tests funnels through reads the REAL shipped files: data/seed/commanders/_registry/default-commanders.v1.json at :134, data/seed/narrative/_registry/names.en.v1.json at :140, and the save-identity registry after that. Those files live in gk-data. Its own comments say why - 'read the real shipped file, like production does: the value is authored data (a measured calibration), not an inline working set' and 'read from the real authored registry exactly like production does (Core never touches a path)'. SO THE HONEST STATEMENT IS: gk-core BUILDS with every private sibling absent, and its test suite REQUIRES the content pack - deterministically, through documented KEEPVERSE_*_ROOT overrides - because the tests are built to read shipped content rather than inline fixtures. Substituting fixtures would destroy exactly the property the bootstrap exists to provide, which is the same argument that justified F1's one skip. WHY IT MATTERS FOR CLOSURE: A11 as written cannot be ticked by any implementation, and an audit agent reading it literally would either report a false gap or, worse, 'fix' it by stubbing the bootstrap and weaken 254 tests. The criterion should say what is true - gk-core builds alone, and its tests run against a configured content root - or the clause should be dropped as already-satisfied by the override mechanism. Either way it is a wording decision and it belongs to the owner.

mark: OWNER RULING 2026-10-04: A11 is REWORDED to what is true. gk-core builds with every sibling absent; its tests run against a configured content root. The clause as written cannot be ticked by anyone.
text: The ruling is to reword rather than drop, which is the better of the two because it keeps a real gate. THE CORRECTED CLAUSE: gk-core BUILDS with every private sibling absent - verified, Build succeeded, 2 warnings, 0 errors, exit 0, in a bare clone with no sibling on disk - and its test suite runs against a content root supplied through the documented KEEPVERSE_*_ROOT overrides. WHAT I FOUND WHILE ASKING, which strengthens the ruling and is the part worth keeping. A11's wording compresses a MIGRATION-TIME GATE, not a permanent property. tasks/keepverse-split-plan.md:268 lists the risk 'a core test depends on gk-data/gk-fusion through a path nothing caught' and handles it with 'Checkpoint A builds and tests gk-core staging with every sibling absent (public-CI condition); failures become residue'. The purpose was to SURFACE sibling dependencies during the split so the transform could fix them as residue. That purpose is served: the split happened, the Resolver contract landed, and the remaining dependency is explicit, documented and overridable rather than accidental. And the Resolver contract itself already says why the tests read real content - line 209 exempts runtime code under src/FusionRpg.{Core,Data,Server} because 'it resolves content against its build output, whose layout the <Content Link="data\..."> items preserve'. SO THE CLAUSE DID ITS JOB, and restating it as a standing requirement asks for the job to be done forever. Any audit agent reading it literally would either report a false gap or stub the bootstrap - and stubbing it would replace the real shipped registries that all 254 status tests depend on with inline fixtures, which is the exact substitution that would destroy what the tests exist to prove.

mark: Landed by owner ruling: data/SUPERSEDED.md plus one AGENTS.md line. The stale 227-family corpus is now marked, with authority and the reason for keeping the tree both stated. Monorepo e5da0b9, pushed.
text: The owner chose to MARK the tree superseded and KEEP the data, over deleting the copy. Measured and stated in the notice: 904 species and 227 distinct family labels here against 509 in gk-data, and the three registry keys academic, afflicted and alchemical exist only in gk-data. Two things the notice records that a deletion would have destroyed, which is why keeping was the right call rather than merely the cautious one. First, this repository still holds deploy-play.py, tools/debug-mcp/cli.py, verify-change.py and live_slot.py - the live-probe tooling exists in NO split repository, and F4's proof chain depends on it. Second, the pack mirrors the legacy repo root on purpose so repo-relative content literals stay valid and only the root they resolve from changes; deleting this tree's data/ would break the reference the migration's own plan is written against. AGENTS.md gained ONE line, because the rule it carries at that point - that data/tuning, data/seed and data/generated are tracked and belong in commits - is precisely what makes this tree look authoritative to a reader in a hurry. VALIDATED BEFORE COMMITTING, in a step that could fail, which is the rule after a dropped brace and a smashed import reached the integration branch in this programme. The repository's own audit-doc-citations.py --strict reports 134 D1 findings, all pre-existing, all in docs/** naming .ps1 files that no longer exist. I did not take that on trust: the audit's finding set was grouped by file and NEITHER AGENTS.md NOR data/SUPERSEDED.md appears in it, and the document carrying the largest cluster was last touched 2026-10-02, two days before this change. Zero findings introduced.

mark: RETRACTING the eligible-set figures I put in the boss-floor ruling row: 87 total was wrong. It is 239 under the current slice and 476 under the owner-ruled floor. An agent refuted my number and was exactly right.
text: My boss-floor ruling row told the owner 'rung >= 7 sets are air 6, dark 6, earth 43, fire 13, ice 9, light 10', total 87, and offered it as the consequence of their ruling. Those figures are WRONG and they were wrong before I wrote them down. The cause is the same shape as the other glob and search errors on this record, one level worse: I computed them with a GUESSED band ladder - I had written BAND = [fodder, minion, scourge, marauder, raider, elite, champion, tyrant, boss, apex] because I assumed those were the rung names. Three of the four names in that list's [6:] slice do not exist in the corpus, so the slice collapsed to the one band that does, 'tyrant'. 87 is EXACTLY the tyrant population. A number that equals a single band's population is what gave it away. The real figures, which I have now reproduced with the ladder read from gk-core/data/tuning/creature-threat.v1.json's ten thresholds: rung >= 7 gives air 10, dark 20, earth 125, fire 37, ice 24, light 23, TOTAL 239; rung >= 4, the owner-ruled floor, gives air 27, dark 31, earth 223, fire 103, ice 48, light 44, TOTAL 476. The wider figure cross-checks arithmetically: raider 76 + warden 61 + scourge 100 + tyrant 87 + harbinger 61 + cataclysm 47 + calamity 44 = 476. The agent that refuted me produced these same numbers unprompted, and independently noted that my 87 was 'exactly the count of tyrant species, which suggests a one-band read'. That is what a refutation is for: it changed a figure the owner was asked to rule on, and it was right. THE CONSEQUENCE I TOLD THE OWNER IS ALSO LARGER THAN I SAID, which matters because they ruled on it: eligibility nearly DOUBLES, 239 to 476, and earth alone goes 125 to 223. 'Boss-eligible' becomes a much weaker filter than either of us described at the time of the ruling. The ruling itself still stands - one ladder and one floor is right, and reading the tuning beats a frozen slice - but it carries a larger side effect than the brief I put to the owner said.

mark: I read gk-forge as having LOST a commit and nearly escalated a recovery. Nothing was lost - I had sampled a transient state between two checkouts.
text: The un-declared-dead agent's work appeared to vanish: HEAD was aedc3a4, the tree was clean, and the reflog showed 'checkout: moving from main to aedc3a4'. Its commit 0e0d7fc, 1,008 insertions across ten files, was not on the branch I was reading, and my merge-base check told me it was an ancestor of main while HEAD sat at its parent. I was one step from reporting lost work and deploying a recovery agent. Re-measured two minutes later: HEAD, main and 0e0d7fc are the SAME commit, the branch is 'main', and the single commit is unpushed rather than lost. The agent had committed, checked out aedc3a4 to inspect the state my redeployment left behind, and checked back out to main. What I caught was the middle of a two-step inspection. THE LESSON, and it is the mirror image of the one I recorded an hour ago about declaring a live agent dead. Both errors come from the same place: treating ONE sample of a moving system as its state. I declared an agent dead from one mtime reading, and I declared its work lost from one rev-parse. The correct discipline is to sample TWICE and compare - which is the rule I wrote into the ledger after the first error and then broke on the second, in the same session, about the same fence. Stating a rule once does not install it; the second violation is the evidence that it needed to be a habit rather than a sentence.

mark: REFUTED: 'nothing runs pytest in CI' is false. gk-core's ci.yml carries NINE steps with working-directory gk-forge/tools/seedsmith. The seedsmith suite IS gated.
text: An agent reported, as its lead finding, that 'nothing runs pytest at all - gk-forge/.github/workflows/ci.yml:67 is dotnet test FusionRpg.slnx only' and that therefore no gate would ever run its new test. I checked every workflow in the workspace before acting on it, and the claim is wrong. gk-core/.github/workflows/ci.yml has working-directory 'gk-forge/tools/seedsmith' on NINE separate steps, alongside gk-core/tools/tuning, gk-core (tests/tools), gk-workflow/.claude/cmdc-agents/scripts, gk-core/tools/ip-censor and gk-web/web/fusion-rpg-web. gk-forge's own ci.yml has no pytest because gk-forge is not where the workspace gate lives - gk-core's CI is the one that can reach a private sibling, which is exactly why the seedsmith suite is wired from there and not from gk-forge. There is also a gate that enforces this and the agent did not find it: gk-core/tests/FusionRpg.Guard.Tests/CiPytestWiringTests.cs, whose Every_pytest_project_has_a_ci_step_running_pytest_in_its_own_root asserts that every pytest project has a 'python -m pytest' CI step at that exact working-directory. Its own comment records the previous instance of this failure class - a project 'landed with its tests but with no CI step, so CiPytestWiringTests was red'. WHY THE ERROR IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN JUST CORRECTING. The conclusion - this test is ungated, placement is contested, nothing runs pytest - was built on a real observation about ONE repository's workflow, generalised to the workspace. A narrow true fact became a broad false one, and the shape is identical to the masked-search errors: a search bounded to the wrong root returns a confident answer. The agent was otherwise careful, and it did correctly identify that gk-data has no CI workflow of its own and that its ownership rules route gk-data validators to gk-forge - both true, and both still open. The false part is specifically the claim that no CI runs pytest anywhere.

mark: gk-forge 0e0d7fc (pushed): the source-side refusals and the deterministic family fallback are WIRED into derive_live_family_assignments, and the has-no-family raise is deliberately KEPT.
text: The reconciliation I was braced to run by hand happened by the agents' own hand, and better: 0e0d7fc's parent IS aedc3a4, so the two designs are STACKED rather than competing. aedc3a4's label_rules.py classifies; 0e0d7fc adds the source-side refusals in schema.py and theme_enrich.py, the corroboration-gated head-noun merge in consolidate.py, and creatures/family/fallback.py; and 1,008 insertions across ten files including two test modules and a 173-line mutation-control harness. THE WIRING, which is the criterion aedc3a4 failed on its own: catalog.py's derive_live_family_assignments now imports resolve_unresolved_family from creatures.family.fallback and routes a species whose labels are ALL refused as artefacts into it. AND THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST, because it is the restraint: a species carrying NO live family label at all still raises 'has no family'. Its own comment says the raise 'is the contract which made 338 family-less species visible in the first place; relaxing it is not this change's job and a silent default would hide the next one'. That is exactly right - a fallback that also swallowed the genuinely empty case would have converted the loudest defect signal in the corpus into silence, and it would have done so while every test went green. Its commit message also records a REJECTED alternative with the measurement that rejected it: refusing every uncorroborated head-noun was built first and broke four pre-existing test_family_consolidate cases by splitting wall-nut/defensive-nut/nut-type three ways, and did not even fix 'botanical'. The remainder is recorded rather than papered over - deciding fragile-body -> body needs to know what a word means, and nothing in the repository does. That is the same refusal to invent a taxonomy that the committed predicate's own class-D exception is built on.

mark: Three judgement calls on the new boss-contract test: relocate it to gk-forge where CI runs it, STRIKE its distinctness assertion, and leave the older, redundant gate completely alone.
text: (1) RELOCATE gk-data/tests/test_dungeon_domain_boss_contract.py to gk-forge/tools/seedsmith/tests. The agent that wrote it flagged the placement as contested and recommended the move without making it; the decision is mine and the evidence is threefold. gk-data held 3,185 tracked files and ZERO Python before this test, with no .github, no pyproject and no conftest - it would be the first executable code in a repository that has none. kvsplit/rules/ownership.v1.json routes validators of gk-data to gk-forge with the reason 'validates private content', and five sibling rules repeat 'input is private content (data/seed); public gk-core CI cannot read gk-data' - the convention is content in gk-data, every reader and gate in gk-forge. And CiPytestWiringTests asserts that every pytest project has a CI step at its own working-directory, with a recorded prior instance of exactly this failure. The post-condition is gk-data back to ZERO tracked Python files, which is the shape the repository was in before this programme added a gate to it. (2) STRIKE test_two_domains_never_name_the_same_boss_species. The contract is three parts - the boss names a real species, its threatBand is at or above the floor, its elementPrimary equals the domain's climate - and distinctness is not derivable from any of them. It is a claim about authored content that will grow, and an assertion with no stated contract behind it eventually blocks legitimate content, at which point removing it looks like weakening a test. Better not to have it than to remove it under pressure. This is NOT a defect being silenced: it was never a defect, and the agent had already isolated it in its own method and documented it as strikeable rather than quietly keeping it. (3) LEAVE tests/test_dungeon_domain_content.py byte-identical, including the now-redundant lines 101-105. The agent recommended striking them and I declined. Redundancy is cheap and costs nothing at runtime; deleting an existing assertion is the riskier move, and that test's loop-reporting behaviour - asserting inside a loop is what under-reported five dungeon defects as one - is a separate question from its coverage and deserves its own decision rather than riding along with a file move.

mark: OPEN: gk-data had zero tracked Python until 55c34a1, and no CI workflow of its own. Resolved by relocation, but the underlying question - where a gate over private content lives - deserves an ADR row.
text: The rule that decided it is not written down anywhere I could find: a gate that READS private content must live in the repository whose CI can reach it, because gk-core's public CI cannot read gk-data. That is the same per-consumer shape recorded as ADR row 1 in content-gen - one contract predicate per consumer, never a merged one - applied to where the gate runs rather than to what it asserts. A gate placed next to the data it validates, in a repository with no CI, is a gate that reads well and runs never; that is the failure mode, and it is invisible until someone counts workflows instead of assuming the one next door is the one that matters. Owner: agent work, done by relocation. Also worth an ADR row rather than only a ledger row, since a future lane adding a second gate over private content will hit the same question and the answer should not require rediscovering it. The theme/retinueFamily coupling stays open separately and is an authored-content call, not a gate question: each domain's theme and retinueFamily were chosen to fit the OLD boss and may now read oddly - ice-001's theme is creature.iceshroom and UltimateSeaShroom (ice, cataclysm) would fit it better than the chosen BedRockSnowZombie, and creature.ultimateseashroom already exists in themes.v2.json. No test couples either field to the boss, so nothing will catch the drift. Left alone deliberately.

mark: F1 MEASURED, third time, isolated workspace-rooted clone: 10 failed / 5104 passed / 1 skipped / 6501 subtests, exit 1, 538s. Up from 5 - and the increase is diagnosed, not mysterious.
text: At gk-forge 0e0d7fc, gk-data 55c34a1, gk-workflow 20a2dca, gk-core 20fd859. Harness shape verified BEFORE the run - gk-core beside gk-data beside gk-forge, gk-workflow as the workspace root, CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/ and gate-evidence all present - because an incomplete fixture produced 46 phantom failures earlier in this same session. That check is now part of launching a measurement, not an afterthought. THE COUNT WENT UP, 5 to 10, and the reason is the most important thing in this row. Six of the ten are caused by 0e0d7fc, which changed the family derivation: the corroboration-gated head-noun merge now emits compound ids such as undead-warlord and fire-source where the committed vocabulary holds the bare head nouns warlord and fire, moving the derived namespace from 509 keys to 612. Every artifact derived from that vocabulary is now stale by construction - the brief count moves 8,065 to 8,580 and a no-report no-top-up round-trip moves 7,645 to 8,065. That is precisely the stale-generated-artifact cascade recorded as an ADR row in content-gen earlier today, arriving in the shape the ADR predicted: the cascade is not a bug, it is the price of changing a derivation, and the only correct response is regeneration in dependency order. ATTRIBUTION IS THE OTHER AGENT'S, and it matches my own numbers independently. It ran the suite at the parent commit 3caad71 with a verified restore and split the ten into SIX caused by its commit - test_type_weights (3) and test_distribution_planner (3) - and FOUR already failing at aedc3a4. My own targeted re-run of eight suspect files found seven of the ten; the missing three are exactly its test_type_weights, which I had not included. Two independent measurements, same total, same split. WHAT IS FIXED: the dungeon boss contract failure is gone, and test_dungeon_domain_content is 15 passed. So the count rose by six while one closed - the fixes are landing, and the derivation change is larger than the fixes.

mark: DECISION NEEDED: main now carries TWO implementations of one family-label predicate in one package - aedc3a4's label_rules.py, which is NOT wired, and 0e0d7fc's, which is. Duplicate authority over whether a label is refused.
text: Neither agent deleted anything, and both flagged it rather than resolving it, which is correct. aedc3a4 shipped creatures/family/label_rules.py: a 481-line five-class classifier (A placeholder, B identity echo, C head-noun walk-back, D under-populated singleton, E legitimate) with census() per-class counts and 33 tests asserting invariants rather than counts, plus eight mutation controls each verified installed by sha256. Its own commit message states it is NOT wired into catalog.derive_live_family_assignments. 0e0d7fc shipped the wired half: anchor/schema.py refuses placeholder and no-identity labels inside seed_consumer_violations, family/consolidate.py adds merge_corroborated, and family/fallback.py resolves deterministically - with a three-refusal, seven-gate mutation-control harness whose R3 control found a bug IN ITSELF, because the first mutation disabled an early-return guard so the function fell through rather than blocked and all eleven cases stayed green on a mutant that did nothing. THE INVARIANT I AM STATED, so the agent implementing it has a testable target: EXACTLY ONE module may decide whether a family label is refused. The other must either be deleted, or reduced to non-deciding reporting that the decider itself calls. Two deciders in one package is duplicate authority, and it is the shape that lets a later change tighten one and leave the other asserting the opposite. An unwired predicate is not a safety net; it is drift with good test coverage, which is worse than no coverage because it looks maintained. THE CHOICE OF DECIDER IS NOT MINE TO MAKE BY ASSERTION and the agent should make it on evidence: the wired one is the only one currently enforced, so it is the presumptive authority, and label_rules.py earns its place only if its classification is something the wired path genuinely calls. If the wired refusals already cover classes A, B and C, label_rules is redundant and goes; if census() is wanted for monitoring, census is reporting, not decision, and belongs behind the decider.

mark: RECORDED, NOT FIXED: icecorn and nuclearsquash are named artefacts whose key groups TWO species, so the structural test passes them. Two agents' 11-species list and the structural test disagree on exactly these two.
text: Neither agent manufactured a fix, and that restraint is the finding. The rule everyone agreed on is structural - a family label must group something, because it becomes a namespace key - and by that rule icecorn and nuclearsquash are FINE: both share 'botanical', which groups two species. But both are named artefacts by inspection, and both appear on the 11-species list the earlier work assembled. So the list and the rule disagree, on exactly these two. The fallback resolves nine of the eleven with stated sources - boatimp to imp from a corroborated CamelCase name, bucketplant to bucket from the curated registry, nutblover and nuttorch to nut rather than the heads blover and torch, peablover/peamine/peapuff to pea rather than the attested-but-wrong 'mine', penguinzombie to penguin because 'zombie' is a side word. Two do not resolve, and the reason is the rule, not a gap in the implementation. This is a CONTENT decision wearing a technical costume: either the rule gains a second clause - a label may not be the whole of a species name even when it groups - which is a real and checkable property, or the two species are accepted as legitimately grouped and the artefact list is corrected. Inventing a fix to make a count reach zero would be the exact failure this programme has recorded repeatedly, so it is left open and named rather than closed. One further measured fact for whoever rules: a frequency rule that resolved all eleven was built, measured and CUT, because it yields 'ultimate' for four Ultimate-prefixed species plus 'super', 'doom' and 'b' - nine new artefacts to fix eleven.

mark: OWNER RULING 2026-10-04: add a SECOND clause to the family-label rule - a label may not be the whole of a species' name even when it groups more than one. NOT 'accept the two and fix the list'.
text: The owner chose to extend the rule rather than correct the artefact list, so the eleven-species list stands as written and the structural test gains a clause. That is the better answer on the merits: the list was assembled from inspection and the rule from structure, and when they disagree the honest move is to find the property the inspection saw and make it decidable, not to delete the observation. IT MUST BE IMPLEMENTED AS A DECIDABLE SECOND CLAUSE, NOT A LEXICON. The species' own name is already in the data, so a clause about names needs no invented vocabulary - which is the constraint both agents independently hit and recorded: a wider refusal built first broke four pre-existing test_family_consolidate cases by splitting wall-nut/defensive-nut/nut-type three ways and did not even fix botanical, and a frequency rule built to resolve all eleven was cut because it yields 'ultimate' for four Ultimate-prefixed species plus super, doom and b - nine new artefacts to fix eleven. Both were the same mistake in different clothes: substituting a heuristic for a property. A CONCERN I AM RECORDING RATHER THAN DISSOLVING, because it may change the implementation. I phrased the clause as 'a label may not be the whole of a species' name even when it groups', but the two species in question are not labelled with their own names - icecorn carries 'botanical', which it shares with nuclearsquash. On its own reading the clause would therefore not fire on either of them, and a clause that does not achieve the stated goal is worse than no clause because it reads as coverage. The instruction to the implementing agent is explicit as a result: implement the clause as ruled, MEASURE whether it actually resolves icecorn and nuclearsquash, and if it does not, report that with the measurement and propose the minimal amendment rather than quietly substituting a different rule. The distinction between a category descriptor that happens to group two species and a real taxon that does is probably the property the inspection saw - bamboo and cattail were deliberately spared as real taxa with one species each, and botanical is the same shape with two - but naming that distinction may need the lexicon both agents said they would not invent. That is a finding to report, not a licence to guess.

mark: F3 RE-PROVED BY CONTROL IN THIS SESSION (not inherited). The forbidden silent fallback to delegated mode makes the suite RED; restoring the pre-read bytes returns a byte-identical hash and GREEN.
text: This closes the second of the two criteria I had been carrying as inherited-and-unverified. Earlier this session I recorded that I had been ticking F3 and F4 off a previous session's claim, which A1 forbids, and that F3 required proof BY CONTROL rather than inspection. Now it has one, produced here, against gk-forge 3caad71. THE MECHANISM UNDER TEST, read from the source first. pipeline/llm_caller.py:409 dispatches on mode; line 410 takes delegated deliberately; and lines 413-420 REFUSE an unrecognised mode by name with AUTHORING-UNKNOWN-MODE, its comment stating 'There is no else branch that could fall into delegated: an unrecognised mode is a NAMED refusal, never a silent default. That is the whole of ruling C6.' THE MUTANT is exactly the forbidden thing: the refusal replaced by a silent delegation, so a wrong mode quietly selects the transport that may edit the corpus. THE CONTROL, in full. Baseline over the five files that exercise the seam - test_authorer_seam, test_mode_plumbing, test_llm_caller, test_item_gen_live_endpoint, test_items_fill_ux - was 167 passed, 17 subtests, exit 0. The mutant installed and was VERIFIED INSTALLED twice over: its sha256 fa8b90b6a3657067a0493afeda80968eecab394bbd30a3afd1831b940e6e67c3 differs from the base 6fa31225face68f2ceba3eecad747edd30d0482a69a6e49bf22a2605fd89ee0b, and the silent-fallback block is present in the bytes on disk. The suite then went RED with exit 1 and exactly one failure: test_mode_plumbing.py::CallModelDispatchTests::test_an_unknown_mode_is_refused_and_reaches_neither_transport. That name IS the invariant - the test does not merely check that an error is raised, it checks the unknown mode reaches NEITHER transport, which is the property a silent fallback destroys and a weaker assertion would not notice. THE RESTORE used the bytes read BEFORE the mutation, written back directly, so no git checkout was involved and nothing that was not mine was at risk. The restored sha256 is byte-identical to the base, and the suite returned to 167 passed, exit 0. IT RAN IN AN ISOLATED CLONE, so the live repository was never modified and no agent's fence was crossed - which is the reason this was possible at all while three agents held repositories. That is the third time a control run against a clone has been the right instrument, and it is worth knowing that F3 is now genuinely closed rather than merely asserted: a suite that stays green when the seam is broken would have failed this control, and it did not.

mark: boss-contract-relocation: the boss gate now lives where CI runs it

A token search for label_rules across both repositories and all file types returns exactly ONE hit, its own test; the same search returns FOURTEEN for merge_corroborated, so the zero is a demonstrated zero and not a masked one. mark: The dead module's tests were not merely dead - two of them asserted the OPPOSITE of the owner's ruling, and the live raise had NO test at all
text: The 33 tests attached to label_rules.py were judged one by one rather than deleted wholesale. 22 were DEAD - they guarded a five-class taxonomy that nothing consulted. Two of those 22 were worse than dead, and this is the part worth remembering: test_a_name_echo_that_groups_several_species_is_legitimate asserted that 'squash' is NEVER refused, which is the exact opposite of what the owner subsequently ruled; and test_a_species_with_no_family_field_at_all_resolves_instead_of_raising asserted that an empty family set RESOLVES, while the live loader RAISES. A dead test is inert; a dead test encoding the losing side of a policy decision is a trap for whoever reinstates the module. 11 were LIVE - invariants of the shipped pipeline, restated against fallback/catalog rather than deleted. 1 was DROPPED rather than restated, with the reason recorded: the deleted module guaranteed that no artefact id survives, and that guarantee is FALSE of the shipped pipeline, because the fallback fires only when EVERY label is an artefact - so a species holding one real grouping keeps its singletons, deliberately. Measured, 398 of 612 ids are singletons. Asserting the old invariant would have demanded a behaviour change nobody asked for. It was replaced by something stronger and behavioural: shipped output equals resolve_unresolved_family(consolidate(...)) for all 904 species. AND A REAL HOLE, which my brief asserted did not exist: I told the agent that a test named test_a_species_with_no_family_has_no_family guards the kept 'has no family' raise. THAT TEST DOES NOT EXIST in any file - test_actions_description_completeness.py has 12 tests, none family-related. The raise at catalog.py:329 was live and completely uncovered. It is still present and now tested over FOUR unusable-label shapes, with a mutation control proving the test can actually fail. The generalisable lesson: I briefed a test name from memory and nearly had it reported as coverage that existed. A named test in a brief is a hypothesis, exactly like a number.

mark: The owner's second clause DOES fire - on 6 species - and my brief predicted it would not
text: I briefed this agent expecting the clause might never fire, on the reasoning that icecorn carries the label 'botanical' rather than 'icecorn'. I WAS WRONG, and the owner is to be credited: the clause fires on 6 species. Measured A/B in one process, clause disabled versus live: species assigned 904 -> 904; distinct family ids 612 -> 608; deterministic fallback surface unchanged at 25, so no provenance was faked; species whose family changed 6; emptied/lost/added all 0. cactus and squash are precisely the case the ruling is about - they group 8 and 7 other species, so the grouping test passes them outright - and both survive intact for the species not named after them. THE FORM MATTERS and the agent chose deliberately rather than by widening until it worked. A token-MULTISET comparison was implemented, not string equality: ice-bean versus IceBean and pumpkin-lantern versus LanternPumpkin are the same name written as a label. The exact-slug reading fires on 3; the token-multiset reading fires on 6. Crucially the agent recorded that the exact-slug reading ALREADY FIRED on 3, so the wider form is not the forbidden widen-until-it-passes - the narrower form was never a no-op, and the token-multiset form is simply the correct predicate. Fragments are deliberately NOT caught: CactusBlover carrying 'cactus' still resolves, because a fragment is not a name echo. THE STRUCTURAL TRAP, which is the reusable finding here: the clause had to be a FILTER, not a fourth artefact clause. family_label_is_artefact is only consulted when EVERY label on a species is an artefact, and each of the six species holds real labels - so the naive placement was UNREACHABLE for all six. It would have read as correct, measured as correct, and never once executed. Dead code that a coverage check cannot see is the most expensive kind to ship.

mark: R6 IS WRONG IN KIND AND DANGEROUS TO ACT ON - six of its nine figures were already zero, and one predicate was applied across three shape classes
text: This is the most operationally urgent finding in the program, because R6 looked open, was briefed as open, and acting on it would DAMAGE a corpus that currently has zero violations. I briefed R6 with nine per-field figures: acquisition, resourceProfile and gameTypeId missing-or-non-string on all 904 entries, attackTempo on 102, aptitudeSecondary on 84, reach and targetPreference on 54 each, aptitudePrimary on 41, deployMode on 14. An independent audit re-measured them against the authoritative predicate csharp_anchor_consumer_violations and found ZERO violations across all 904 entries. WHY THE BRIEF WAS WRONG, and the mechanism matters more than the numbers. The C# contract splits nine fields across THREE SHAPE CLASSES: eleven StrFields that are strings, gameTypeId which is an INTEGER, and acquisition which is a FLAG LIST of three. My brief applied ONE predicate - missing-or-non-string - to all nine. So acquisition was never non-string at all; it is a flag list on 904 of 904 entries. gameTypeId was never non-string either; it is an int on 904 of 904, and the contract's own message says 'missing or non-integer'. And resourceProfile is absent on 314 - and is NOT IN THE C# CONTRACT AT ALL, because its own docstring says it is deliberately unparsed because nothing downstream reads it yet. The other six fields measure zero because they were backfilled. THE FAILURE MODE THIS MAKES POSSIBLE, which is why it is urgent rather than merely interesting: a session that trusted those figures would generate or hand-edit 904 integer gameTypeIds into strings, or 'backfill' attackTempo, reach and deployMode that already stand at 904 of 904 - forking the corpus from its generator to satisfy a test that encodes the wrong type. That is precisely what this repository's hardest rule forbids, and it would have been done in the exact shape the rule exists to prevent: an agent acting faithfully on a brief that was wrong. THE LESSON IS ABOUT ME, not about the agent. I re-measured every other carried figure this session and still passed nine numbers forward unverified into a brief, labelling them 'hypotheses to verify' in the hope the agent would check. Labelling a number a hypothesis does not make it one. Four of the six named obligations turned out to be already done or already stale, and the sixth is dangerous - which is the shape of a brief that was written once and never revisited, the same decay documented four times over today.

mark: F4's LIVE-LAWN CLAUSE IS SATISFIED - a legitimate focus-free entry path exists, and it is the game's own vanilla API
text: The question I set this agent was whether a match can be entered WITHOUT stealing the operator's keyboard, because a Unity title polls real device state and ignores posted messages. The answer is yes, and the mechanism is better than I expected. FOUR PATHS RULED OUT WITH EVIDENCE, not by guessing. There is no command-line argument to start a level - no command-line parsing anywhere in the injector. There is no server-driven run start the client joins - runs are created FROM INGESTED EVENTS, so the server records a board that already happened rather than causing one. There is no server-to-injector command channel that enters a level: the entire command vocabulary was enumerated and the only level entry is a debug one. And the launcher has no match path at all. THE PATH THAT WORKS is a config key driving the game's OWN API: FUSIONRPG_LEVEL_ENTRY reaches UIMgr.EnterGame, which the repository's own research notes record as the identical vanilla call the real Adventure button makes, executed on Unity's main thread. The same notes state that setting the board's level and type does NOT spawn a Board - which is precisely why the board-creating debug endpoint cannot work and why that endpoint is banned in those notes. The design is coherent; the ban was on the right thing. THE SEQUENCE USED ONLY REAL IN-PROCESS CALLS AND ZERO OS INPUT: a real click on the boot modal's confirm button through the game's own control-click path, then the level entry, then the game's own start-game button. Result: hasBoard true, hasInitBoard true, board type Advanture, matchPhase InMatch, phaseMismatch false, liveState InMatch. Confirmed visually as Adventure level 1 with mowers, seed bank, sun rising 725 to 775, and a real peashooter with a health bar on the lawn. Server-side corroboration: level name, five mower placements, and repeating economy events. Injector connected with an advancing heartbeat, twelve established connections into the slot port, three of them owned by the slot's own executable. THE OWNER'S INSTALL IS BYTE-IDENTICAL: 2381 files, sha256 171603fd054347d04927132bd5b7e8754616e7c303fc065fcb58a454bfec1e7e6, zero errors, identical mtimes, and the agent REPRODUCED the baseline itself rather than inheriting mine. The owner's directory was only ever read from, as the clone source. THE HONEST QUALIFIER, which the agent volunteered and which is the reason this row is written at length: the board is genuinely the game's own, but the TRIGGER arrived through the debug channel's gated wrapper rather than a human clicking Adventure. No fabrication, no focus taken, no cursor moved - but a reader should know which of those two things happened. AND THE RESEARCH NOTE THAT MADE THIS POSSIBLE IS WORTH KEEPING: docs/research/level-entry.md records which entry is vanilla and which are fabrication, and bans board creation explicitly. The knowledge existed; nobody had connected it to the criterion. That is a documentation asset doing exactly its job.

mark: F4's THIRD LEG IS NOT CLOSABLE AS WRITTEN - a lawn zombie resolves a different pool than the allocation the criterion names
text: This is a criterion defect, not a probe failure, and it is the reason F4 is not claimed satisfied in full. WHAT WORKS. The allocation itself is real and proven through the normal path end to end on the server: the player id obtained from the normal read endpoint and never invented, a real allocation that ran the reallocation gate and spent 42 within budget at a priced amount of 50, leaving a stated balance, and a read-back showing the two named aptitudes at 21 each with the rest at zero. mark: MY OWN RECOMMENDATION WAS WRONG: rewording F4 to name the per-empire actor cannot close it, because that pool has ZERO normal write paths - by design
text: I recommended the owner reword F4's third leg to name the actor a lawn zombie actually reads, on the reasoning that a live zombie whose stats demonstrably change is a stronger proof than a persistence row. The owner accepted. THE RECOMMENDATION WAS WRONG, and it was wrong because I checked WHICH actor the lawn reads without checking whether that actor is WRITABLE. THE POOL A LAWN ZOMBIE CONSUMES HAS NO NORMAL SERVER WRITE PATH. The chain, verified end to end: a zombie context takes its empire from its side, which is always the Zomboss, and resolves its commander allocation from the per-empire pool for a non-human empire - never the human's. That pool is fed by a key of the form zomboss:{save}, and if the key is absent the assign-ladder default is COMPUTED AT READ TIME, which is why six points appear to be allocated when no row exists. EVERY commander write route keys the human's player:{id}: the allocate endpoint, the preset-activation endpoint which hardcodes it, the passive-tree endpoint, and the debug audit endpoint. Every species write route hardcodes the human empire id. This is deliberate and documented, not an oversight. A non-human empire request is refused with 409 empire_scope_not_widened precisely so that such a route never reaches SQL with an empire it cannot serve, and the repository's own progression map states that nothing writes the Zomboss key and only the allocation is dark. Another file says the Zomboss reads the human's pool because reading its own would be circular. So the entity a lawn consumes is deliberately unwritable, by construction, in the normal path. AND THE EFFECT SIZE IS THEREFORE STRUCTURALLY ZERO. A before/after on a real lawn zombie cannot exist today, not because a probe was missing but because there is no write that could move it. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT is product work, not proof work: widen the commander write surface past the human key - and the agent notes the Tier-A seam for exactly that already exists - or move the Zomboss pool off compute-at-read and onto a written row. Both change what the game means, which is why neither is an agent's call. Owner: the owner. Until one lands, any demonstration that an allocation affects a lawn zombie has to be a debug call, which is precisely the fabrication the reworded criterion was written to exclude. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS AND IT IS ABOUT MY OWN PROCESS. I verified the premise's first half - which actor the lawn reads - and skipped the second - whether that actor can be written. A criterion cannot be closed by observing an entity nothing writes to. I checked a fact, found it correct, and recommended a rewording on the strength of it without asking whether the fact made the criterion achievable. That is the same shape as the R6 booby trap: a verified fact used as if it established more than it did.

mark: TWO DATABASES WERE BEING CONFLATED - the earlier allocation read-back was against a NON-LIVE database whose row came from a fabricating debug call
text: This is the most important correction of the session, and it was found by an agent that read the prior agent's raw log rather than its summary. THE EARLIER READ-BACK WAS AGAINST THE WRONG DATABASE. The previous agent's read-back script opened the server's data directory under gk-core's dist tree. The live server's log says its data directory is the slot's own directory. Those are two different databases, and they do not agree: the dist copy holds twelve uniform rows of one hundred and twenty, while the slot copy holds the two rows at twenty-one that the allocation actually wrote. AND THE UNIFORM ROWS ARE A DEBUG ARTEFACT. Twelve equal allocations of one hundred and twenty is the signature of the debug broad-allocation endpoint, not of anything a player or the normal path did. So the earlier claim that the server half of the allocation was proven end to end was resting on a row that a fabricating debug call created, read out of a database the live server was not using. This is the exact failure the rules name: a successful response from the same scope that created the state is not proof, and here the scope was not merely the same but the WRONG DIRECTORY. It also means the earlier agent's honest refusals were right for the wrong reason - it declined to present a client-side trace as proof, while its server-side leg was itself built on a debug row in a stale database. The fix is procedural and cheap and should be routine: read the data directory out of the server's own startup log rather than inferring it from the executable's location, and confirm the path exists before querying it. An agent should have to look that up rather than be able to get it wrong by construction. Owner: agent.

mark: The allocate endpoint SILENTLY IGNORES an explicit per-empire intent - the request type has no empire property, so System.Text.Json drops it
text: Found by the same agent, and it is a real interface defect independent of F4. A caller that sends an explicit per-empire intent in the allocate request body has that field SILENTLY DROPPED: the request type declares no such property, so deserialisation discards it without error. The write then lands on the human's key. The observable symptom is exactly the failure mode this programme keeps meeting: the call returns success, with a priced result and a real balance change, and the caller has no way to know their intent was discarded. The agent proved it by executing the write with an explicit intent and observing the per-empire pool stay byte-for-byte unchanged while the human's shares changed. Two things are worth separating. The SILENT IGNORE is a defect and should be fixed - either the request type accepts the field and honours it, or it rejects an unknown field rather than dropping it, because a dropped field that changes where a write lands is worse than a rejected one. The fact that the write LANDED ON THE HUMAN KEY is arguably correct behaviour under the current design, since the non-human empire is deliberately refused elsewhere; the defect is that the caller was not told. Owner: agent. Not fixed here - the allocating endpoints are in a repository another agent holds.

mark: VERIFIED BY ME: the two green-while-blind guards now REFUSE with a named reason instead of reporting clean
text: An independent check of the fix that landed in gk-core, run by me rather than taken from the agent's report. Both guards previously reported success while inspecting nothing; both now refuse. generated-seed, run with an explicit range against a repository that carries none of its subject, exits 1 with a message naming all eight declared generated trees as absent from that repository, and then states the reason in the terms that matter: this guard's subject is the generated corpus, the split moved it into another repository, so a standalone clone has nothing for it to inspect, and reporting clean here would be a coverage claim about nothing. That sentence is the whole defect class made explicit in the tool itself. population-pin likewise now exits 1 where it previously exited 0 after catching its own missing root and warning on a stream the runner discarded. So the class this programme has been fighting - a gate converting an unknown into an answer - is now closed for these two instances, and the refusal carries a reason a reader can act on rather than a bare non-zero exit. The deeper fix, surfacing child standard-error so a degraded pass cannot look like a real one, is separate and should be verified when that agent reports.

mark: OWNER RULES F4's third leg is PRODUCT WORK: build the empire write path, using the Tier-A seam that already exists
text: F4's third leg cannot be closed by proof work, because the entity a lawn consumes has no normal write path. The owner has ruled that the answer is to BUILD that path rather than to narrow the criterion again. THE RULING, and why it is the right kind of answer. Two narrower options were on the table: drop the leg and record that the entity is deliberately unwritable, or reword the criterion to persistence plus a clean refusal. Both would have left F4 green on the two legs that are real while quietly retiring the third - which is the outcome this programme has been correcting all session, in the other direction. Building the path keeps the criterion intact and makes it true. THE WORK IS NOT ROUTE PLUMBING, and it should not be mistaken for it. It touches at least four places, each of which the investigation located by reading rather than guessing: the allocate endpoint, where the request type currently declares no empire property at all and therefore SILENTLY DROPS an explicit per-empire intent; the empire-scope seam, which already has a Tier-A and a Tier-B shape and whose whole purpose is to stop a route reaching the database with an empire it cannot serve; the store's commander-pool read, which today computes a default at read time when no row exists, so a written row would change what that read returns and every consumer of it; and the species write side, which hardcodes the human empire and so has the same defect in a second place. THE DESIGN QUESTION THE WORK MUST ANSWER, which is the owner's and not an agent's: what does it MEAN for a Zomboss pool to be written? The current design has the Zomboss read the human's pool deliberately, because reading its own would be circular - one file says so in as many words. Writing its own pool changes the game's progression semantics, not just its plumbing. An agent may implement the seam, but it must not decide that question, and any proposal that quietly picks a reading is a defect even if the code compiles and the tests pass. THE BAR FOR THE PROOF IS ALREADY SET AND SHOULD NOT BE LOWERED. When the path exists, the leg closes on exactly what was specified: a real allocation through the normal server path, observed taking effect on a real lawn zombie in a live match, reached through the focus-free vanilla entry so the operator's keyboard is never touched, and with nothing that creates state called to make it observable. The evidence base gathered so far - the server route enumerated, the executed write landing on the wrong key, the read-only database showing no row before and none after, and the repository's own statements that the key is never written - is what makes the eventual proof worth having: it is falsifiable against a known absence. SEQUENCING, because the fence is held: this work is in gk-core, where the standalone-remediation agent is finishing. It is queued rather than launched, and the fence clears before it starts. Owner: agent, queued behind the standalone lane.

mark: THE DOCS FORK IS RESOLVED, AND THE ARTEFACT ITSELF SAYS SO - gk-workflow is authoritative, proven from a ruling row the monorepo's copy predates
text: The two lock-file trees are reconciled, and the deciding evidence was inside the lock file rather than in anyone's preference. gk-workflow's decisions/world.md carries an owner ruling of 2026-09-30 naming gk-workflow the single source of truth for architecture decisions, principles, plans, task records and development documentation. The ruling states its own reason, and that sentence names this exact defect: a second copy of a boundary map or a guard definition inside a sub-repository is a competing copy, and two copies diverge silently with no test failing at the moment they do. THE DIRECTION OF THE FORK IS THEREFORE PROVEN FROM INSIDE THE ARTEFACT: the monorepo's copy of that very row is the PRE-RULING text, omitting the clause. Corroborated by measurement - all fourteen lock files are newer in gk-workflow, with thirty-two substantive documentation commits across two hundred and fifty-four files since the import, against a last-touched date two weeks earlier for the monorepo's. And the citation guard, pointed at the monorepo instead, reports seventy-six drift findings and ten orphaned baseline entries; pointed in place, zero. THE DIVERGENCE IS ONE-WAY AND CLASSIFIED, not merely measured: twenty-seven net lines, all of them in gk-workflow, none anywhere else. Three documented transformation classes account for it - substantive rows only the live tree has, including the status-tracks decision row and an eighteen-line appendix stating that a cited line must still MEAN what the sentence says; post-split path repointing; and positional citation renumbering. One file differs substantively by a single repaired table delimiter. Exactly one differs in content at all. A FINDING THAT CONTRADICTED THE BRIEF AND SAVED A WRONG FIX: both repositories' BLOBS are LF. The carriage returns are a working-tree artefact of one checkout only. A naive byte-comparison guard would have manufactured a fork that exists in neither repository and then 'fixed' it by rewriting committed content. The guard reads normalised content for exactly this reason. WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO: chase the other eleven files. A stale copy that tracked the live one exactly would still be a second source of truth - that is the defect, not its cure. Reconciliation was confined to the two indexes, with the authority block appended at the END so no cited line moved: the citation guard still reports one hundred and ninety-seven citations and zero drift. TWO OF ITS OWN DESIGNS WERE FALSIFIED AND FIXED RATHER THAN SHIPPED, and both are worth recording. First: a blob-only reading was GREEN through all three planted mutations, because it cannot see an uncommitted edit - it was blind at precisely the moment the guard exists for, and CI would have been its only working mode. It now reads the working tree, with an explicit flag restoring blob mode. Second: the first marker design failed its own parity check on its own text, because the two blocks say opposite things - one asserts authority, the other declares itself a superseded snapshot, so comparing them is comparing opposites. That is now fenced out of band for the comparison, and an unterminated fence is itself a finding rather than a silent pass. AND A GATE THAT FAILS ON THE DECLARED STATE GETS BYPASSED, which the design accounts for: equality or containment satisfies the one-sided check, and 'behind' is the declared state, so a revision prints as a note every run rather than a failure. ABSENCE is the failure - a row present on one side only. The guard also refuses, with exit 3, when the other tree is absent or when it is pointed at itself, because a guard aimed at a single tree is green by construction. All three mutants were caught and all three restores were byte-identical.

mark: MY BRIEF WAS WRONG ABOUT THE DEAD LOCATORS: §2 was never restructured, §2.N is a house convention, and repointing 16 locators would be the wrong fix
text: I briefed that the design gate had been restructured while its citations kept the old numbering, which is why fourteen cited sections resolve to nothing. The agent checked the history and that is false: the section has NEVER had subsection headings in any commit in either tree. It is a flat numbered list of sixteen items, and the locator form is a HOUSE CONVENTION meaning item N of that section - the gate uses it against itself. So the real count is sixteen of seventeen locators resolving to no anchor, not fourteen, but the cause is a missing anchor rather than stale numbering. AND THE RECOMMENDATION IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE ONE MY BRIEF IMPLIED. Do NOT repoint the sixteen. Make the section addressable - heading anchors, or a per-item anchor - instead. Rewriting sixteen locators into line citations would convert a deliberate house convention into sixteen one-off positional citations, which the citation guard would then have to hold forever, and would break again the next time a line moved. The agent supplied, for each of the sixteen, the invariant's identifier, its rule quoted verbatim, and the line where that rule lives today - so the mapping work is done and the choice of mechanism is the only thing left. Every one of them names a rule that genuinely exists; the citations are unreachable, not wrong. TWO CORROBORATING MEASUREMENTS worth keeping: of the forty invariants carrying no recorded reason for being unguardable, every one names a guard that is registered and enabled, with zero orphans across thirty-four registered guards. And the two remaining gate-line citations resolve to the audit checklist row and are baselined identically in both trees. So the invariant survives everywhere; only the address does not. That is a much smaller defect than the one I described, and the fix is one mechanism rather than sixteen edits.

mark: A CITATION REPOINT CAMPAIGN RAN TWICE - once per tree - so any post-2026-10-02 audit figure may be double-counted
text: The most consequential thing this agent found that nobody had asked about. The bulk citation repointing landed on 2026-10-02 IN BOTH TREES - one hundred and seventy-nine files in one, six hundred and twenty-seven references in the other. The same work was done twice, because each session's root resolver picked whichever tree it happened to be standing in. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THIS LEDGER SPECIFICALLY: F6 asks that no figure in the final report was inherited rather than reproduced, and every citation-count, drift-count and documentation-audit figure measured after 2026-10-02 may be counting the same work twice across two trees. Any such figure needs its provenance stated before it is quoted, or the count is meaningless. This is the double-counting hazard in its purest form: two correct measurements of two different trees, added together by a reader who assumed they were one thing. IT ALSO CORRECTS MY CHARACTERISATION OF THE MONOREPO. I had been treating its documentation as a stale snapshot. It is not frozen: agents ARE editing it, which is why its last documentation commit is 10-02 rather than the 09-27 I inferred from file dates. Two live trees, one authoritative - which is exactly the condition the guard now exists to keep from diverging again.

mark: THE LEDGER IS AUTHORITATIVE IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION, and the ruling's own clause is not honoured - 719 entries vs 82, frozen
text: The ruling that settles the documentation fork names gk-workflow as the single source of truth for architecture decisions, principles, plans, TASK RECORDS and development documentation. The documentation half is now honoured. The TASK RECORDS half is not. MEASURED: the ledger holds 719 entries in the monorepo and 82 in gk-workflow, and gk-workflow's 82 are an exact semantic PREFIX of the monorepo's 719 - frozen since 2026-09-30 while the other has been appended to every day since, including today. So the authoritative record and the ruled source of truth point at different repositories, and the ruled one holds a prefix. THIS IS A GENUINE CONTRADICTION AND NOT A DEFECT ANY AGENT SHOULD RESOLVE. The ruling was written about a split that had not yet fully happened; the ledger has since become the place everything is actually recorded. Reconciling means choosing which of the two claims wins - the ruling's clause, or the practice that has overtaken it - and then either moving the ledger or amending the ruling. Both are owner decisions. The agent correctly escalated rather than touching it, and correctly did NOT encode the ledger half into its parity guard, which covers the documentation half deliberately and ignores the task tree entirely. Owner: the owner. There is a practical urgency: the monorepo is the pre-split repository, and a document of record living in the repository the split was meant to dissolve is the same class of problem as two copies of a lock file. Recorded here so the next session inherits the contradiction rather than rediscovering it as a mystery.

mark: A DOCUMENTATION-AUDIT TOOL IS ALSO FORKED - the same defect class, one layer down, and the parity guard is not yet in CI
text: Two follow-ons from the fork work, both named by the agent and neither fixed, because both sit behind a fence or need a home. FIRST: the documentation-audit tool itself is forked - thirty-nine thousand two hundred and ten bytes in gk-workflow against thirty-three thousand eight hundred and seventy-six in the monorepo. That is the identical defect one layer down: the checker that exists to catch drift between two copies of a document is itself two copies, and the one in the wrong place would report on the wrong tree. Its root resolver is shared with thirty-three other guards, and those two copies are byte-identical, so the resolver is sound and only this tool forked. SECOND, and the more important: the new parity guard lives in the monorepo and therefore runs only when someone remembers to run it. Its durable home is the repository where the other thirty-three guards live, with a row in the enforcement registry so CI enforces it - because a parity guard that is not wired is not a guard, it is a script. That repository is currently fenced by another agent, so this is queued rather than done. Owner: agent, queued behind the fence. Both are the same lesson the fork itself teaches, applied to the things that were supposed to prevent it.

mark: RETRACTION - I called the corpus-dump test's relocation an OWNER DECISION. It is not. The dependency direction settles it, and I had the scope wrong by three.
text: I recorded that relocating tests/FusionRpg.Core.Tests/Creatures/CorpusDumpTests.cs needs an owner decision, because it imports a gk-forge type from a gk-core test project. That framing was wrong on both counts, and I withdrew it without waiting for a ruling. THE DEPENDENCY DIRECTION IS NOT AMBIGUOUS, and I could have measured it in one command instead of escalating it. Twenty gk-forge tool projects reference gk-core projects - AffixMetricsGate, AtomImporter, CreatureBuildPlanGen, CreatureCatalogGen, CreatureCorpusDump, CreatureCorpusEmit, CreatureQualityReport, CreatureRecipeDistributionIndex, CreatureRecipeReconcileInput, CreatureSpeciesGen, CreatureSpeciesImport, DominanceBaseline, ElementEnumGen, FamilyExpandGen, ItemSeedValidator, PassiveTreeRosterGen, ProveHubCombat, TreeBinder and others. The edge therefore runs forge to core, so core must not depend on forge, and the standalone requirement already asserts that. There is exactly ONE architecturally correct home for a test of a gk-forge tool: gk-forge's own tests directory, which already carries five sibling test projects as precedent. Nobody had to choose. AND THE SCOPE WAS THREE SITES SMALLER THAN I THOUGHT. I named ONE unconditional forge reference. There are FOUR, across three of gk-core's test projects: FusionRpg.Core.Balance.Tests line 23 pointing at DominanceBaseline, FusionRpg.Core.Tests line 57 at CreatureCorpusDump, FusionRpg.Data.Tests line 35 at CreatureSpeciesImport, and FusionRpg.Guard.Tests line 35 at DominanceBaseline. While any of the four stands, the standalone condition - gk-core builds and tests with every private sibling absent - is FALSE, whatever any agent's report says. A TRAP WORTH WRITING DOWN, because the obvious fix is wrong in two different ways. The repository already conditions three other forge references on a GkForgeAvailable boolean. That pattern is CORRECT for those three, which invoke forge tools as processes, and WRONG for these four. A ProjectReference cannot be conditioned away while a source file in the project still imports its types: the moment the sibling is present, the project fails to compile. So adding the same condition to a compile-time reference converts a build break into a compile break - a strictly worse failure, and one that only appears in the developer environment that has the sibling. And the alternative, a conditional Compile Remove, is a SKIP, which the no-weakening rule forbids substituting for a real fix. The genuine fix is relocation, which needs no condition because after it the dependency is simply gone.

mark: THE NINE REPOSITORIES ARE ALL FRESHLY GREEN AND FOUR AGENTS ARE LIVE, so the program's constraint is integration bandwidth, not correctness
text: A state observation recorded because it changes how the next session should act. At the time of writing, every one of the nine Keepverse repositories plus the pre-split monorepo reports a clean or near-clean tree with no failing gate known anywhere. The measurable deficits are concentrated in a handful of named items, not spread as a failing suite. Four agents were live simultaneously, each holding a disjoint fence: gk-core, gk-forge, the documentation trees, and one read-only auditor holding no fence at all. The consequence is structural, and it is worth naming rather than working around: with every writable fence held, no further implementation can be launched without colliding, so the only lanes that remain are read-only ones. The read-only auditor is therefore not a luxury - it is the correct way to keep making progress when the writable repositories are all occupied. A NOTE ON WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE READ-ONLY LANE'S TRUSTWORTHINESS: an audit that runs while three other agents are mid-edit is auditing a moving target, and a finding of 'not established' can mean either a real gap or a read that happened to land on a half-applied edit. Those are opposite verdicts with the same evidence. Every such finding must be re-checked once the fences clear before it is treated as a defect, and the re-check is part of the finding rather than a separate courtesy. A snapshot is not a verdict.

mark: THE STANDALONE-CLONE TEST CANNOT DISTINGUISH A CORRECT ROOT RESOLVER FROM ONE THAT IS UNCONDITIONALLY STANDALONE - and that is why a real bug passed it
text: The gk-core agent refuted its own earlier commit, and the reason matters far beyond that one commit. A probe it had added to the root resolver inside Detect() matched gk-core AT ITS OWN ROOT, so a walk upward from anywhere inside gk-core stopped there and reported STANDALONE before it ever reached the directory one level up that actually holds gk-core beside gk-data. Every content path then resolved against gk-core instead of the gk-data pack, and eighty-six narrative tests threw. Its own words: running the workspace suite is the only thing that showed it. THE GENERAL FORM, AND IT IS A HOLE IN THE STANDARD TEST RATHER THAN A BUG IN ONE IMPLEMENTATION: a resolver that is unconditionally standalone and a resolver that is correctly standalone produce IDENTICAL behaviour in an isolated clone, because in a clone the sibling is genuinely absent and 'standalone' is the right answer. So the standalone-clone test passes exactly when the resolver is wrong. It is necessary and nowhere near sufficient, and treating its green as proof of correctness is a category error - the test cannot see the class of failure it is most often cited for. THE FIX SHAPE, WHICH FOLLOWS DIRECTLY: every standalone claim needs a PAIRED assertion in the full workspace. The clone proves 'works with the siblings absent'; only a workspace run can prove 'and correctly does not treat them as absent when they are present'. Neither half implies the other, and a program that records only the first half has verified something strictly weaker than it believes. This also retires a specific piece of folklore: 'run it in an isolated clone' is the standard, and this incident is the case where following the standard faithfully would have shipped the bug with a green gate beside it.

mark: A GUARD THAT REFUSES OVER WHAT IT CAN SEE IS THE SAME DEFECT AS ONE THAT RUNS OVER NOTHING - both are a green row over no work
text: From the same agent, and it generalises the rule the program already knows in one direction. The generated-seed guard refused when ALL declared generated trees were absent from a root. But that guard also has a test that builds a fixture root holding only data/seed/items/ and the items adapter directory and nothing else - and that test was failing with 'generated seed edited without its generator' instead of the row it planted. The fixture is partial by construction, and an all-or-nothing rule made the guard refuse to look at the corpus it could perfectly well see. THE RULE, STATED SO IT CAN BE APPLIED: the real question a guard must answer is whether it INSPECTED NOTHING - not whether its population was complete. Zero trees present is a refusal, because nothing was examined. Some present means the scan ran and its own verdict stands, with the trees it did not inspect named on stdout rather than converted into a refusal over the ones it did. THE DEEPER POINT, AND IT IS THE ONE WORTH KEEPING: the verbosity failure has two directions, and the programme only had a name for one. A guard that scans nothing is the obvious defect - a green row over an empty population. A guard that refuses over a partial population is the SAME defect wearing a different hat, and it is strictly harder to notice, because the refusal is loud and looks like diligence. A guard that announces 'nothing here' and a guard that announces 'I will not look at this' produce the same reader experience and the same absence of coverage. Note this was found by a TEST, not by inspection - the fixture failed, and the agent read the failure as a statement about the guard rather than about the fixture. That is the correct reading and it is worth remembering that the fixture was right and the rule was wrong.

mark: MY OWN F2 GREEN IS REFUTED - the guard suite is RED in CI's own invocation, and the cause is a missing field in the registry SCHEMA, not one row's omission
text: I have been reporting F2 as thirty of thirty green. That claim is wrong and I withdraw it. An independent auditor ran the guard suite in the exact shape gk-core/.github/workflows/ci.yml uses and got thirty run, one red, exit one - and I then confirmed the cause myself from disk, structurally, without depending on its run. The generated-seed guard row is tier ci, status gating, script scripts/guard-generated-seed.py, living in gk-core. Its subject - eight declared generated trees - exists NOWHERE under gk-core, because the split moved the corpus to gk-data. And the row declares no repository, so the runner dispatches it into a tree where it can only ever refuse. All eight trees absent is a refusal by design, and ci.yml line 505 throws on a non-zero exit. The boundary-guards step therefore FAILS AT HEAD. THE ROOT CAUSE IS BIGGER THAN THE ROW, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS: not one of the thirty-four registry rows declares a repository. Zero of thirty-four. So the runner has no mechanism at all by which a guard can say 'my subject moved to another repository'. This is a missing field in the schema, not a value somebody forgot to fill in - which means every guard whose subject the split relocated is silently unrunnable, and a relocation is exactly what this migration did to hundreds of paths. The refusal text itself is exemplary, and it even says that reporting clean there would be a coverage claim about nothing. The refusal is honest; the wiring that makes it unavoidable is the defect. A SECOND FINDING IN THE SAME RUN, UNEXPLAINED AND DECLARED AS SUCH: the narrative guard was red in one legal batch shape and green in two others, and its own message says a trait that selected zero tests enforces nothing. A gating guard whose verdict depends on batch composition is not a gate. The auditor could not isolate the cause because two variables moved together, and it declined to invent one. I am not inventing one either. One caveat that cuts AGAINST the refutation and is therefore part of the record: the run executed two guard files that were uncommitted in-progress edits at the time. I verified the structural cause independently - the absent trees and the absent schema field - so the finding does not rest on those files, but the batch figure does and should be re-measured once the fence clears.

mark: A11's WEB CLAUSE WAS NEVER EVIDENCED - four ledger rows assert it on evidence that cannot establish it, and it is now closed properly
text: The standing condition requires that the real server starts and SERVES THE REAL WEB UI. Four rows assert this clause. Their evidence was identical each time: a two hundred on the index document, a two hundred on a script bundle, and the substring createRoot found inside that bundle. That is a node, not a wire. It cannot distinguish an application that mounts and renders from a shell that serves files and then throws on load. A migrating agent reading that row would reasonably believe the clause closed. It had not. Nor did the test suite cover it: the web end-to-end configuration points its base URL at the preview and dev servers on ports four-one-seven-three and five-one-seven-three, so all two hundred and sixty-seven of those tests never touch the dotnet server at all. A search of every repository's tasks and docs trees for a browser driven against the real server returned zero hits. The gap was structural, not accidental. IT IS NOW CLOSED, by the only evidence that can close it. A real server on a real port was driven by a real browser: navigation two hundred, the root element rendered twelve thousand characters and held stable across a second sample six seconds later, zero console errors, zero page errors, zero failed requests, and nineteen API calls all returning two hundred - players, souls with a balance and a revision, the creature catalog returning the real corpus, the roster, the run history matching the game log's own start minute, commanders, relics, expeditions, contracts, onboarding, delve, notifications, catalogues. A screenshot read directly shows the full navigation rail, a creature card, and the lawn-defence panel. Not a probe. A wire. AND THE PORT AND THE DATABASE WERE BOTH READ FROM THE SERVER'S OWN STARTUP LOG, never inferred from the executable path - which matters, because the executable also has a data directory beside it holding a DIFFERENT database. Both exist. The running server used the one its log named. That trap is live, not hypothetical. THREE THINGS THE RENDER EXPOSED THAT NOBODY HAD LOOKED AT. First, and worst for trust: the live roster is showing a user an actor whose identifier is literally derived-audit, created by a debug audit endpoint, and it is the only actor the roster has. The repository's own rule is that a debug API may trigger a real operation but its result must never be mistaken for gameplay; here the row survives into the shipped product surface. Second, six shipped panels render placeholder copy admitting they are not implemented. Third, creature names in the catalog are generator placeholders - the first species is named Creature 300. None of the three is a wiring defect. All three are the product looking like a finished thing while it is not.

mark: TWO OF THE NINE REPOSITORIES ARE ORPHANS, AND ONE OF THEM CONTAINS NO TESTS - the failure most likely to survive this program unnoticed
text: A repository split is measured by whether the code moved. It is not measured by whether anything consumes what moved, and the difference is where this migration's quietest failure lives. Measured across all nine: seven repositories are genuinely consumed. Two are not. GK-TESTS IS THE HEADLINE. Its entire tracked content is four files - a gitignore, a licence, a readme and an agents document. It contains no tests. No build, no test project, no CI workflow, no consumer. The one property that references it is declared in three build files and read by nothing. So a nine-repository migration counts gk-tests among its nine, the repository exists, it is on the remote, it is clean and pushed - and the class of artefact its name promises does not exist anywhere inside it. This is the finding most likely to pass every review, because each individual fact is true and only the conjunction is damning. GK-ASSETS is the softer case and should not be over-called. It holds a hundred and twenty-four blend files, texture sets, Blender tooling and skills. Nothing in the workspace reads it - and a human-facing authoring repository that ships visual packs and needs no programmatic consumer is perfectly legitimate. What is NOT legitimate is that no artefact says so, while the split's own readme lists it as a peer destination, which reads as an integration claim. Silence and a claim are different things. GK-CONTENT is the interesting middle and the one with a live consequence. Its accessor IS wired - into a ci-tier guard and two resolver copies - but its only payload is a single display string table, and the one web-side reference to it is a comment recording that the file has no rows for four key families the interface already renders. So the root resolves, the guard checks that the root exists, and the content is substantively incomplete for exactly the surfaces that want it. A guard that verifies the existence of an empty payload is the same class of green-over-nothing this ledger keeps recording, wearing a different hat.

mark: MY HEADLINE FINDING IS REFUTED BY A SECOND AUDITOR - gk-tests containing no tests is NOT a defect, it is a specified end state, and I inferred a requirement from a repository's NAME
text: I recorded, in this ledger and in the new open-items register, that the most severe finding of the whole programme was that gk-tests holds no tests - a nine-repository migration counting a repository for tests that contains none, so the artefact its name promises does not exist. A second independent auditor, briefed with a different lens, refuted it. And it was right. THE EVIDENCE. gk-tests' own AGENTS document and readme quote a seal reason recorded in the split tool's own rules file - gk-workflow's tools/kvsplit/rules/layout.v1.json - and emptiness is the SPECIFIED END STATE there, not an unfinished migration.
