Its most recent commit is titled 'docs: say what this repository is, which is not what it claimed to be' - that is, a previous session already corrected the very claim I treated as a discovery. And there is independent structural confirmation: the rules' template list contains gk-assets, gk-content, gk-core, gk-data, gk-forge, gk-fusion, gk-web and root - and no gk-tests - which corroborates the repository's own corrected claim that its 'change the template' pointer was bogus. The claim I published as my worst finding was already known, already fixed, and already documented by the session that owned it. WHAT I ACTUALLY DID WRONG, because the method matters more than the item. I inferred a requirement from a NAME. 'A repository named for tests that contains no tests' felt self-evidently damning, and I never asked the one question that decides it: is there a rule that says this repository must contain tests? That is the same failure this ledger records repeatedly under another name - a masked-literal search reporting a confident zero, a parser compared only with itself, a stale premise carried forward unexamined. Reading a requirement into a name is a pattern match on a string. The corrective is cheap and I did not do it: before reporting what a repository should contain, read the rule that governs what it should contain. THE LIMIT OF THE REFUTATION, stated so a third auditor does not treat this as settled beyond what it is: the second auditor could not read the seal text itself, because that file is inside a repository another agent held. So the refutation rests on gk-tests' own documentation quoting the rule plus the corroborating template list - strong, and not the same as having read it. Reading that one file settles it. ALSO RECONCILED, because two auditors disagreed and a reader deserves the reconciliation rather than both versions: on gk-content, one reported it consumed because its accessor is wired into a ci-tier guard, the other reported nothing consumes it because there is no alias for it in the web tier and the build properties naming its root are declared and never read. BOTH ARE TRUE AND THEY ARE THE SAME FACT. The guard verifies that the root EXISTS. Nothing reads what is inside it. A guard that checks the existence of a payload nothing consumes is not evidence of consumption, and this is the green-over-nothing defect wearing yet another hat - already recorded elsewhere in this ledger, and now confirmed from a second direction.

mark: THE AUDIT-TOOL FORK IS CLOSED, AND ITS CAUSE WAS NOT WHAT ANY OF US ASSUMED - the two copies never shared a blob
text: The forked documentation-audit tool is now ONE copy, in the repository the registry and CI identify as authoritative, carrying both feature sets, and its parity mode is wired into a CI workflow. That part is routine. The cause is the finding. I briefed that the two copies were 39,210 bytes against 33,876 and that a previous agent's diff pass was wrong because replaced blocks hide deletions. BOTH FIGURES WERE STALE AND THE CAUSE WAS WRONG. Measured now: 39,210 does not exist in the current state at all - 33,876 is the blob at the import commit the snapshot names as its source, and the superseded working tree is 54,921 bytes while the reconciled copy is 64,432. And the copies NEVER SHARED A BLOB. The divergence is four lines, all inside COMMENTS, each the same rewrite - scripts pointing at gk-core/scripts, tuning at gk-core/data/tuning, tools at gk-core/tools - applied by the split's own declared transform, whose rule file names that exact pattern class. So BOTH SPELLINGS WERE CORRECT FOR THE TREE EACH COPY LIVES IN, and a byte comparison of these two files manufactures a fork that exists in neither repository. That is now the programme's third recorded instance of the same shape: a comparison that cannot distinguish 'these drifted' from 'each is right here'. It is the reason the reconciled parity check reads NORMALISED content, and it should be the reason any future comparison of two split-related files does the same. WHICH REPOSITORY, settled from the registry and CI rather than from size: the runner's own docstring records where guards live - twenty-three in gk-core, four in gk-fusion, and two here - and an existing workflow is the exact precedent. Resolution was verified live, both guards green. THE MERGE WAS REAL AND CONFLICTED ONCE: both sides had added at the same import site and neither subsumed the other. The parity mode also needed adaptation, because it had been written for a copy sitting in the SUPERSEDED tree and therefore read the other side as its own tree; in its new home that argument now names the superseded side, and a missing one is a NAMED REFUSAL rather than a silent fallback - which is the property that makes a refusal safe to leave in place. THE HONEST PART OF ITS REPORT: it declined to add the parity mode to the guard registry as a row, and gave a structural reason rather than a preference - the runner executes every child with gk-core as the working directory, while the legacy-root argument must name a tree that is not a workspace sibling, so a registry row would compare lock files from the wrong directory and refuse - producing a red build that says nothing about any document. That reasoning is sound and I accept it. It also has a consequence worth recording: the registry lacks the ability to say which repository a guard runs against, which is the same missing schema field being fixed on the other side of this split right now. The two pieces are complementary - once a row can declare its repository, this argument stops applying. Worth revisiting then, and not before. Every planted mutation went red on its own check and every restore was byte-identical by sha256, and the previous agent's three mutants were re-run independently against its own copy and still went red three of three - so the parity mode survived the reconciliation rather than being quietly dropped by it. It also asserted a zero CR count, which matters here: the repository's attributes declare LF, and a CRLF blob committed into it would be invisible to a diff and would read as a real change to any byte comparison.

mark: TWO FIGURES I CARRIED ARE WRONG, AND TWO APPARENTLY CONTRADICTORY CLAIMS WERE BOTH TRUE OF DIFFERENT PAIRS
text: Recorded because each of these would have produced a wrong action, and because the pattern - a carried figure decaying, and a reconciliation mistaken for a contradiction - has now recurred enough times to be worth naming as a class rather than an incident. FIRST, the forked tool's size. I have been carrying thirty-nine thousand two hundred and ten bytes against thirty-three thousand eight hundred and seventy-six. Measured now: the reconciled copy is sixty-four thousand four hundred and thirty-two, the superseded working tree is fifty-four thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, and thirty-three thousand eight hundred and seventy-six is the pre-parity blob at the import commit. Neither number I carried describes any current state, and one of them describes a historical state that no longer exists on either side. A carried size is not a size; it is a rumour with a unit. SECOND, an apparent contradiction that was not one. One audit reported the root-resolver copies byte-identical; another reported them not byte-identical. Measured: gk-core's and gk-fusion's are both exactly twenty-three thousand seven hundred and fifty-three bytes, so the first claim is true of that pair; the monorepo's is two thousand six hundred and six bytes and lacks five of the accessors the sibling-index feature needs, so the second claim is true of that pair. Both auditors were right and I was about to record a contradiction. THE GENERAL RULE, which is the part worth keeping: a contradiction between two findings is a hypothesis about the pair they measured, not a defect - until the pair is named and measured. Two auditors reporting the same artefact differently usually means they measured different pairs, not that one of them is wrong. And it is the same shape as the stale-premise pattern this ledger records repeatedly: a figure or a claim carried forward without re-derivation, acting on something that was true of a configuration nobody has looked at since. Cheapest corrective there is, and it keeps being skipped: measure the pair before recording a conflict, and re-measure a carried figure before quoting it.

mark: R7 is closed and I verified it myself because its author is dead - 61 files scanned, and the guard is NOT WIRED
text: The seedsmith writers that wrote carriage returns into trees whose blobs are line-feed only are fixed, and the agent that fixed them died on a transport error immediately afterwards. So the claim was verified by someone else rather than inherited: the guard exists, runs, and exits zero over sixty-one scanned files with nine exempt hazards and zero unexempted findings. The population is real, which is the entire point - a green row over nothing is worse than a failing one, and this is the first sweep in this programme whose green I can see the denominator of. THE SCOPE WAS WIDER THAN THE BRIEF, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. I briefed seedsmith writers. The agent swept past Python and found the same defect in five C# GENERATORS, then found that the guard it had just written could not see two drivers, and fixed that blind spot rather than shipping a guard with a known hole. Three commits, and the middle one is the discipline: a detector's own blind spot treated as a reason to stop looking. That is a defect CLASS closed rather than a task list ticked. BUT IT IS NOT WIRED, and only the integration layer can fix that. The enforcement registry carries thirty-four guards and the only newline-related identifier in it is a different, pre-existing guard. So this one runs when someone remembers - which is the same defect the documentation parity guard carried until this morning, when another agent wired it and wrote the reason into a commit subject: a guard CI never invokes is a script. The registry lives in a repository another agent currently holds, so the row is queued rather than reached for. A durable fix that is not registered is a fix that regresses quietly, and the regression would look like the defect never having been found.

mark: THREE agent death notifications arrived for sessions I had ALREADY replaced or completed - a death notice is not lost work, and not a reason to distrust work that landed
text: Three upstream transport errors arrived in a row after a server restart, and the useful thing was reading their session identifiers rather than reacting to the word error. Two named sessions I had already replaced at the restart. The third named a session whose work had already landed - three commits, a clean tree, zero unpushed, and pushed. Not one of the three was a new failure, and reacting as though they were would have cost three more launches and very likely destroyed committed work. BOTH DIRECTIONS MATTER AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE PEOPLE GET WRONG. A death notification is not lost work: the author of a landed change can die on the transport the instant after committing, and the commit is still a commit. Equally, a death notification is not a reason to distrust work that landed - so the correct response to one is to verify the artefact, not to relaunch the task. I verified the finished agent's guard by running it, and the run is what made its value knowable rather than its author's survival. THE GENERAL RULE, which this programme has now paid for repeatedly: an agent that produces nothing is redeployed, and an agent that dies mid-flight may have already landed its work. Those are different situations demanding opposite responses, and the discriminator is the ARTEFACT - what is on disk and what is committed - never the notification. Nine agents have now died on this transport error across the programme; the reliable question is not whether a session reported an error but what the tree says it left behind.

mark: I REPORTED A CONFIDENT ZERO FROM A COMMAND THAT ERRORED ON EVERY FILE - the masked-search failure, committed to my own record this time
text: Landing the gk-assets work I reported its line-ending count as zero carriage-return bytes across every file it touched. **That was false, and the way it was false is the exact failure this ledger records repeatedly.** The shell probe used an encoding parameter this PowerShell version rejects, so it raised an error for every single file - and I read the empty result as a measurement rather than as a failed command. The real figure is three thousand one hundred and twenty-six. What makes it worth recording rather than quietly correcting is that the corrected number would have been misread in the opposite direction too. Three thousand carriage returns across a dirty tree looks alarming until you check which side of the checkout you measured: this repository declares no attributes file and has autocrlf on, so the working tree carries carriage returns while **every committed blob measures zero**. The content that ships is line-feed. The same two numbers mean opposite things depending on where you read them, which is the whole reason the line-ending work in this programme was necessary - and the reason a figure without its measurement site attached is not a figure. The rule, now written down because I broke it myself: **a command that errored is not a command that returned nothing.** In a pipeline that error can vanish entirely and leave a plausible empty result, and an empty result is exactly what a correct search returns when there is nothing to find. Those two are indistinguishable unless you check the exit status - which is why every measurement in this record carries a site and a method, and why this one did not.

mark: A DEV TOOL THAT WORKED ONLY BECAUSE THE DISSOLVED REPOSITORY WAS STILL ON DISK IS FIXED - and its check MODELS the absence instead of asserting a list
text: The gk-assets preview server resolved the web tier through a candidate list of three absolute paths whose only resolvable entry was the pre-split monorepo, one level above the workspace, while the candidate naming the real web tier was absent entirely. It degraded to a warning and a not-found, so nothing looked broken - which is why it survived, and why the day that monorepo is deleted the tool would have failed presenting as a missing asset rather than as the stale path it was. The fix removes the dependency rather than reordering the list: candidates derive from the file's own location and resolve a SIBLING, and the pre-split monorepo is not a sibling, so **no candidate built from this repository's root can reach it whether or not it is deleted.** That is the difference between a fix and a reordering that happens to work today. THE PART THAT EARNS THE COMMIT is the check, and it is the shape this programme keeps arriving at. A check asserting the candidate LIST would have passed against the broken version - the broken version did contain sibling-shaped paths; it merely also depended on a repository that is going away. So the check MODELS that repository being absent and then asserts resolution still finds the real web tier. Verified in both directions: the pre-fix server exits one naming both symptoms, reaching outside the workspace and resolving to nothing once the monorepo is gone; the fixed one exits zero resolving to the web tier with one candidate, all inside the workspace. TWO MORE CLASSES CLOSED IN THE SAME CHANGE. A tool wrote its own pre-split invocation into a committed file, so correcting that file by hand would be undone by the next run - the invocation is now derived from the file's location, and regeneration is byte-stable, so the fix survives the next run instead of being reverted by it. And thirteen tool docstrings named a path that does not exist here; an audit had classified all seventeen such references as executed, which was wrong, and that correction is recorded rather than quietly applied. The agent that did this DIED WITHOUT REPORTING and left the work uncommitted. I read it line by line and verified it before landing, because an agent that reports nothing attaches no evidence to what it leaves behind - and in both cases where I have taken over rather than relaunched, the stranded work was better than what I would have written. That is the argument for reading the artefact before redeploying, and it has now happened twice.

mark: AN AGENT THAT PRODUCES NOTHING AND AN AGENT THAT DIES ARE DIFFERENT SITUATIONS, AND THE ARTEFACT IS THE ONLY DISCRIMINATOR
text: Nine agents have now died on the same transport error in this programme, and the recovery differs completely depending on what they left behind. One died holding finished work: three commits, a clean tree, nothing unpushed. One died holding thirteen modified files of uncommitted work that I had to review before landing. One died holding a hundred-and-nineteen-line test file with six tests, unattested. And one produced nothing at all across three separate launches in the same task. Treating all four identically - which is what reacting to the word error invites - would have destroyed committed work, discarded unreviewed work that turned out to be good, and relaunched a task whose problem was never the agent. The reliable question is not whether a session reported an error or produced output, but **what the tree says it left behind**: is there a commit, is there uncommitted work, and is that work attested by anything. The practical rule that follows, and it is the one worth carrying: **read the artefact before deciding whether to redeploy.** Twice this session the stranded work was better than what I would have written had I simply restarted the task - one agent modelled the absence of a repository instead of asserting a path list, which is precisely the trap that let the defect survive. A restart discards that. A read keeps it.

mark: THE INHERITED E1 FIGURE IS WRONG IN BOTH THE NUMBER AND THE SHAPE - 62 production and 59 test call sites, not 58 across 30 files
text: A ledger row claimed fifty-eight transport call sites across thirty files bypassing the two-mode seam. Measured this session by scanning every Python file under the package, excluding comments and definition lines: **one hundred and twenty-one call sites across thirty-nine files** - sixty-two in production across twenty-one files, and fifty-nine in tests across five. So the row is wrong in the count AND wrong in the shape, and the shape is what changes the job. It is not 'sixty-two sites to migrate'. It is sixty-two production sites, plus a separate question of whether five test files reaching the transport directly is legitimate or is itself a bypass. Forty-nine of the calls are in the test suite, which is a finding worth naming rather than a number to migrate. Broken down in production: the live-transport resolver thirty-eight, the answer caller twelve, the model caller six, the self-healing caller six. Only three files import the seam at all - the transport module itself and two tests - so the mode decision is genuinely distributed rather than centralised, which is exactly what the owner's ruling requires it not to be. THE FIGURE ALSO DEMONSTRATES THE STALE-PATTERN ONE MORE TIME, and the detail that makes it worth recording: an audit had reported this row's number as read-from-the-ledger rather than re-derived, and said so honestly, and I briefed the next agent with the inherited number before checking it myself. The honest label on the row did not stop the number propagating - it only made the propagation visible to anyone who read the caveat. Re-measuring before briefing is cheap and I skipped it, which is the part worth correcting.

mark: A PATH NAMED IN THE RECORD HAS NEVER EXISTED, and my own briefing repeated the error - the seam is two files, not one
text: The ledger names the seam as a single file at the plumbing layer. **That file does not exist.** The seam is split across the plumbing authorer module and the pipeline model-caller module. I wrote the same wrong path into an agent brief before discovering it by asking for the file and being refused. This is the third time this record has named a path that is not there, and the failure mode is identical each time: a path is written down because it reads correctly, and nothing checks that it resolves. A ledger health check of 'every row parses' would never catch it, because the row is perfectly well formed - it is a sentence about a file that was never built. The existing note that the row describes a four-hundred-and-thirty-nine-line module at a path with no such file should have stopped the number propagating; instead it travelled with it. THE GENERAL FORM, which is worth having in one place: **a path in prose is a claim, not a reference.** Nothing in a narrative record dereferences it, so it degrades silently and can be wrong indefinitely without any test going red. The cheap discipline is to resolve every path a row names when the row is written or quoted, and the honest consequence is that a figure carried without its path checked is a figure carried on trust. Read from a fresh interpreter rather than by eye, the seam's default mode is the API mode - which is the owner's ruling holding, and is worth stating as measured rather than as remembered.

mark: THE MISSING REGISTRY FIELD WAS AN EXISTING CONVENTION APPLIED IN THE WRONG PLACE, not a new idea - the same field and the same resolver already exist elsewhere
text: Work in flight on the red criterion has established something that changes how the fix should be judged. The enforcement registry could not say which repository a guard inspects, so a guard whose subject the split relocated could only ever refuse. The obvious fix is a new field with new plumbing. **It is not new.** The verification-boundaries registry already carries a repository field with a closed vocabulary, and the same resolver answers both. So the correct change is an existing convention applied where it was missing - which is a materially different act from adding a mechanism, because it removes the possibility of the two drifting apart and of a third convention appearing later. The vocabulary is spelled out rather than inferred, and this repository is included in it explicitly so that a row can declare its own root and the wiring check can then REQUIRE that explicitness. That is the right shape: the check does not merely permit the field, it makes silence a finding. This also retro-explains a decision another agent made earlier and I accepted at the time. That agent declined to register a parity check, giving a structural reason - the runner executes every child with this repository as its working directory, while that check needs a path naming a tree outside the workspace, so registering it would compare the wrong thing and refuse. That argument assumed the runner could not vary a guard's root. If this field lands, the argument stops applying and the parity check becomes registrable - so the two pieces are complementary and the earlier decision should be revisited once the field is in. Recorded now so that 'it was decided against' is not mistaken for 'it was settled'.

mark: THE ROOT CAUSE OF THE RED CRITERION IS CLOSED AND VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS - the corpus guard now inspects 17 files, and STILL refuses when its subject is absent
text: The one red success criterion in this programme was the guard suite failing in the exact invocation CI uses. The cause was that no registry row could say which repository a guard inspects, so a guard whose subject the split relocated could only ever refuse. That is now fixed, and the fix is verified rather than reported. THE POSITIVE DIRECTION: the corpus guard now resolves to the repository that carries the corpus and inspects a real population - seventeen changed files - exiting zero. Before, it found all eight of its declared trees absent under the wrong root and refused. It is green in the suite's own summary table as a gating row with exit zero. THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS MORE, because a guard that passes over nothing is worse than one that fails: given a root where its subject does not exist, it STILL refuses, and names both why and where to run instead. It says that reporting clean there would be a coverage claim about nothing, and it identifies which repository carries the corpus and which tools moved to the forge. So the property that makes it safe to register survived the change that made it green. ALL THIRTY-FOUR ROWS now declare their repository, and the vocabulary is being USED rather than merely present: twenty-five name this repository, four name the fusion repository, three the workflow repository, one the forge repository and one the data repository. The field is spelled out rather than inferred, this repository is included in it explicitly, and the wiring check makes silence a finding - so a future row that forgets the field is refused rather than quietly defaulting to the wrong root. AND THE FIELD PAID FOR ITSELF IMMEDIATELY, in a way I had not anticipated. It created a requirement that did not exist before: a commit range names ONE repository's history, so a guard inspecting another repository needs that repository's range. The runner refuses with a named message when one is missing, and refuses again when the supplied range does not resolve in that repository - which is correct, because the base I first supplied was a commit in this repository's history and named nothing in the other. It walked me through four refusals, each naming the next repository it needed. Every refusal was right, and every one would have been a silent wrong comparison under the old schema. THE SUITE IS NOT GREEN YET - two rows remain red, and this is reported rather than smoothed over. Both are VALUE errors the new field exposed rather than schema errors: two guards declare this repository while their subject, an index file and a citation registry, lives in the workflow repository. Two other citation guards already declare that repository correctly, so the correction is two field values and no new plumbing. Until they are corrected the criterion stays red, and a suite forced green by editing the values to match what the guards happen to find would be worse than the red.

mark: A NEW GUARD'S SUCCESS MESSAGE CLAIMS A CHECK IT DOES NOT PERFORM - the same defect class as the false 'checksum-mirrored' comment, in a guard
text: A guard was added to assert that every registry row is wired: that its repository resolves, that its script exists, and - it says - that its subject is found. Its success line reads that every row names a present repository, an existing script, AND A FINDABLE SUBJECT. **It cannot check that, and its own documentation says so.** It explains that a runner cannot know what any given guard scans, that inventing a per-guard subject list inside the checker would be a second source of truth that drifts from the guards themselves, and that this third shape is therefore left to each guard to answer for itself. That is a defensible design decision and I would not argue against it. The defect is the MESSAGE, which claims the check it deliberately does not perform. I verified this by control rather than by reading: I planted the exact value error the suite is currently red on - a row whose subject lives in one repository while the row names another - confirmed the mutant was installed by reading the file back, and the guard still exited zero with its all-clear. The file was then restored byte-identically. So a reader who trusts the success line believes a check is running that is not. That is the identical failure shape as a comment claiming a mirroring mechanism that does not exist, and it is worth naming twice in one programme because the shape does not care whether the false claim is in prose or in a tool's own output. THE PART THAT MAKES THIS TOLERABLE, and it is the reason I am recording it as a finding rather than an alarm: the guards themselves catch the mislocation, loudly and by name. The suite still exits non-zero, and the failing guard prints the exact path it looked for and did not find. So nothing is hidden by the weaker checker - the safety comes from the guards refusing rather than from the wiring check detecting. That is the right dependency direction, and it is worth stating explicitly, because a reader could otherwise conclude the wiring guard was load-bearing when in fact it is a convenience. THE CORRECTION IS TO THE MESSAGE, not the mechanism: say what it checks. A tool that says less than it does is safe; a tool that says more is not, because the overstatement is what someone downstream will rely on.

mark: TWO GUARDS REMAIN RED ON A VALUE ERROR, NOT A SCHEMA DEFECT - and the suite is red until two field values are corrected
text: The registry schema work is landed and the root cause is closed, but the success criterion is still red and that is stated rather than smoothed over. Two rows remain failing, and the diagnosis is precise: both declare this repository while their subject - an index file and a citation registry - lives in the workflow repository. Measured: the index file is absent under this repository and present in the other; the second guard refuses with zero citations found, which is what a guard looking in the wrong place reports. **Two other citation guards in the same registry already declare the workflow repository correctly**, so the correction is two field values and no new plumbing. The schema is not the problem and must not be adjusted to accommodate the wrong values - a schema change here would hide the error rather than fix it. The criterion stays red until those two values are corrected. Recording the reasoning because the tempting shortcut is to edit the VALUES so the guards find what they expect, which would make the suite green by pointing two checks at a different repository than the one whose content they are supposed to be checking - a green that certifies nothing. The red is more informative than the green would be, which is the whole argument this programme keeps having to relearn about gates.

mark: THE RELEASE WORKFLOW NOW RUNS - and two of its failures were worse than a broken path, because they reported SUCCESS having done nothing
text: The release job named seven distinct paths and resolved none of them: six live in the core repository and one exists in no repository at all. The job died at its first reference, so the release could not run - in a file that already documented removing exactly this defect class from a sibling block, with the reason: a gate which cannot pass is worse than no gate because it looks like coverage. TWO OF THESE WERE WORSE THAN A BROKEN PATH, and that is why a red build would never have caught either. The scan output redirect pointed at a directory that does not exist; per a measurement already recorded in another repository's workflow, a redirect to a missing parent raises before the command runs and leaves the exit code at zero - so **the release's only blocking intellectual-property gate reported success having run no scan at all.** And the injector-refs step sat inside a handler that could never fire, because under that shell a native non-zero exit does not raise; the fallback was unreachable, and the tool refuses by design on a runner with no interop assemblies - precisely the case the fallback existed for. Both are the same class as the whole programme's favourite failure: not a red that says no, but a green that certifies nothing. The job now checks out the five repositories its paths were written against and sets the workspace root explicitly, because the root resolver walks upward for a directory holding documentation and a five-sibling runner workspace has no such directory. That last point was not in the original finding and is easy to miss: of thirty-five registered guards, thirty-one resolve in two repositories, three in a third and one in a fourth, so a two-checkout runner would have refused outright. Verified by me: all seven paths, including the one that exists in no repository, now resolve inside a checkout the declaring job creates. AND THE DURABLE PART IS A GUARD, because repointing lines without one means the next half-finished migration is invisible again. It **reports its own vocabulary and its own blind spots on every run** - the forms it recognises, the outputs it does not examine, and the named inputs it skips. That is the property that makes it trustworthy: a checker that does not say what it cannot see is the very defect this programme just spent a day removing from a comment. It found four bugs in itself, including one where a comment as the first line of a step silently discarded the whole step, so it **reported green having examined nothing** - the exact failure it exists to prevent, found in itself. Mutation-tested with six rules disabled one at a time: **three were green on the first attempt**, and the cases closing those gaps were added because the run found them rather than because they were predicted. That is a mutation control that earned its result.

mark: AN AGENT HANDED BACK THREE ITEMS RATHER THAN REACHING ACROSS FOUR FENCES - and one of them says the release still will not publish
text: The agent that repaired the release finished by naming three things outside its fence and NOT touching them. That restraint is the finding worth recording, because in a programme where several streams share a tree, reaching across is the default failure and produces merge conflicts that look like merge conflicts. THE MOST IMPORTANT OF THE THREE IS A DEFECT NOBODY KNEW EXISTED: the publisher cannot run from any split repository at all. Its layout builder needs one root holding the server, the launcher and injector hosts, and the web tier - three repositories that no single root contains since the split. The specification is to give it explicit server-root and web-root arguments, and the telling detail is that the Server's own content items **already read their roots by configuration**, so the publisher is the last component still assuming the pre-split monorepo existed. **The release will not publish until this lands**, and that was true before the repair and invisible because the workflow could not run far enough to fail on it. The second is two registry rows, specified precisely and deliberately not applied, because the registry belongs to a repository another agent was working in. It also flagged a real decision inside its own specification rather than picking silently: the four existing guards in that repository pair their tests under a tests directory, while its new one sits beside the tool the way that repository's own test does - which nothing bounds. It named the choice and left it to me. The third it discovered was **already done**: the actor-HUD manifest over-claimed tiers it does not carry, and I had corrected that in the other repository before the report arrived. Worth recording as a coordination fact rather than a fix - two agents reached the same defect from opposite ends, and the second one checked the current state instead of acting on its own brief. That is the correct behaviour when two fences describe one artefact. It also corrected three figures I had given it, all in the direction of my brief overstating: the machine-local path count was ten distinct paths rather than twenty-two lines, because three overlapping patterns were counting the same lines; the glyph-ownership direction was the opposite of how I framed it; and one path I had listed as broken is a redirect target rather than a reference. An agent that corrects its brief is doing its job; one that quietly complies with a wrong number is not.

mark: THE EMPIRE WRITE PATH EXISTS AND THE SILENT INTENT DROP IS CLOSED AT THREE LEVELS - including making the SERVER refuse any field it does not understand
text: The third leg of the live-lawn proof was red by owner ruling because the per-empire pool a lawn zombie consumes had no normal server write path, and because an allocate route **silently discarded** an explicit per-empire intent: the request type had no such member, the deserializer dropped it without complaint, and the route still answered success - having written the human pool for a caller that had asked for an empire's. A discarded field that reports success is worse than a rejection, because the caller cannot know it was ignored. It is now closed at three levels, and the third is the one worth keeping. One: the request type carries the field, and its absence is documented on the property itself as a defect that was fixed rather than a default that was chosen. Two: the route resolves the named empire through the existing seam, treats absence as the save's human empire so every pre-existing caller is unchanged, and answers a named empire that is not an empire of THIS save with a not-found - never another save's pool - then takes the per-empire arm, computes that empire's own budget, and writes through a dedicated store call that can refuse with a reason. Three, and this is the part that generalises: **the deserializing type now refuses any field it does not recognise.** So any FUTURE unrecognised field becomes a loud bad request rather than a second instance of the identical defect. That converts one specific bug into a class that cannot recur silently, and the stated principle is the right one - a request the server did not fully understand must never report success. The property comment names the defect it replaced, which is what stops the next reader from 'simplifying' the handling back out on the grounds that absence was always the default. It was never a neutral default; it was a silent drop wearing one. Note what was deliberately NOT decided here: what a written pool MEANS - how a per-empire pool differs from a player roster, what happens on transfer or disband - remains the owner's reserved question. The implementation persists the value and refuses loudly where it must, and stops there. That boundary held.

mark: A REPOSITORY README TOLD THE TRUTH ABOUT ITS OWN EMPTINESS FOR DAYS - the first document a migrating agent reads was false
text: The core repository's readme carried a Status section saying the repository was empty and that the migration tool had not staged into it yet. Measured, the repository held three thousand eight hundred and ninety-two tracked files. **Every repository readme had been last touched on the day of the import**, which is the likely cause: the sentence was true when written and was never revisited, and nothing in the build, the tests or the guards reads a readme. This is worth recording as a category rather than an incident, because the failure mode is distinctive and it is not the one this programme usually suffers. The usual failure is a gate that passes over nothing. This is a **document that asserts a state nothing verifies** - a claim with no checker behind it, in the one file every new agent is guaranteed to read before forming a model of the repository. An agent that believed it would conclude the work had not started, which is the exact inverse of the truth and would have stopped this programme's largest effort from being attempted at all. The general rule, and it pairs with the one already recorded about paths in prose: **a prose claim about machine state is a claim with no test behind it.** Paths at least fail to resolve when something dereferences them; a sentence about how many files exist resolves forever. The cheap guard is not a guard at all - it is to have the count in the sentence and a check that the count still holds, or to delete the number. A readme that says 'large' cannot rot; one that says 'empty' can, and this one did, in the most expensive direction available.

mark: F2 IS GREEN - 30 guards run, 0 red, every row gating, and the three that were red or refusing hours ago are all among them
text: The one success criterion that was red for most of this programme is now green, and I reproduced it rather than accepting it. Thirty guards ran, zero red, every row marked gating, exit zero - and the population is real, which is the only thing that makes a green meaningful. The clock-seam row reports scanning one thousand five hundred and thirty-eight source files; the corpus guard reports inspecting changed files under the repository that actually carries the corpus; the two citation guards each took twenty seconds of real work. This is the first green in this programme where I can see the denominator for every row rather than a passing line. THE THREE THAT WERE NOT GREEN ARE THE PROOF. The corpus guard had been refusing because it could not be told which repository to inspect. The index-marker guard had been refusing because its subject file was looked for in the wrong repository. The registry-append guard had been refusing because it found zero citations where it was standing. All three are now green, and all three were fixed by making the wiring say which repository owns what - never by narrowing a table, adjusting a schema to accommodate a wrong value, or relaxing a check. That distinction is the whole difference between a criterion closed and a criterion silenced. THE STALE FIGURE IS CORRECTED HERE, because it has been quoted repeatedly in this record and is now wrong. Several rows state the suite as twenty-nine or thirty guards with one red. The current reading is thirty run, zero red, exit zero. The criterion's own wording still says 'all twenty-five green', which is stale by five; the count has been re-measured rather than adjusted, and the discrepancy is recorded instead of quietly reconciled. One honest limit on this closure: the runner requires a per-repository range for every repository a guard inspects, so the green above was obtained by supplying four of them alongside the criterion's own invocation. That is the new field working as designed rather than a workaround - a commit range names one repository's history, and a guard inspecting another needs that repository's range - but it does mean the bare invocation in the criterion's wording alone refuses, and says so by name. The criterion's text should be updated to state the required invocations, and that is a wording change to be made deliberately rather than a gate to be relaxed.

mark: AN AGENT REPORTED FOUR REGRESSIONS IT CAUSED ITSELF, AND THE STANDARD TEST WAS THE ONE THAT WAS BLIND
text: An agent finished the standalone work and listed four regressions it had introduced and caught. Recording them is worth more than the fixes, because each names a way a correct-looking change can break a tree. First: a resolver probe added inside the detection function matched the repository at its OWN root, so a walk upward from anywhere inside it stopped there and reported standalone before reaching the directory one level up that actually holds it beside its siblings - eighty-six narrative tests failed. **That is the same root-resolver trap already recorded in this ledger, and it recurred in a different agent's hands, which is the strongest evidence available that the pattern is a property of the codebase rather than a mistake any individual makes once.** Second: marking a project reference as not producing a reference assembly breaks an application host, because the host is copied but its library is not - so the tool died on launch with an unreadable error and no output at all. Third: treating an unrecognised owner as 'reachable' silently disabled the very test that was supposed to catch it. Fourth: deciding ownership from hardcoded prefix tables made the real tree report eighty-two correct boundary rows as stale, because a table cannot answer 'which repository actually holds this path'. Each was caught, and each is a category rather than a one-off. The load-bearing part of the account is what it could NOT make standalone, stated plainly rather than minimised. One test file still compiles against a sibling's namespace, and closing it properly needs a two-repository move that its fence could not reach - and it explicitly refused the shortcut of copying instead of moving, on the grounds that a copy would leave two renderers and a test validating a copy production never runs. That judgement is right and it is worth naming as the standard: coverage was kept rather than deleted, and the honest cost was recorded. It also converted a large number of clone failures from assembly-wide wipeouts into individually named refusals, and reported the before-and-after counts for both directions - failures and passes - rather than only the flattering one. A report that gives you one number is asking to be believed; one that gives you both is asking to be checked.

mark: MY BRIEF'S CENTRAL PREMISE WAS WRONG - the seam was ALREADY universal; 36 of 57 sites never reach a model, and a 21-file rewrite would have been pure risk for zero routing benefit
text: I briefed the seam task with the premise that almost nothing walks through the seam, that twenty-one production files each reach the transport themselves, and that the mode decision is therefore distributed. **All three were wrong**, and the agent said so rather than complying - which is the correct response to a wrong brief and the reason this row exists. Measured by parsing the source rather than matching text: of fifty-seven production call sites, **thirty-six are configuration resolution that reaches no model at all** - they are inputs to the seam, not calls through it - and the remaining twenty-one that genuinely reach a model each terminate in the two functions that dispatch through the seam. **No production module imports an HTTP client, constructs an authorer, or branches on a mode literal.** The seam was already universal. So the rewrite I asked for would have touched twenty-one already-correct files for no routing benefit, in a task whose stated risk was quietly changing a default. It is the second time in this programme that an agent has refused a brief's premise and been right, and the pattern is worth naming: **a plausible-sounding architectural claim is not a measurement, and a refactor premised on one is a refactor premised on nothing.** The cheap check - parse and classify before scoping - costs an hour and prevents the largest kind of wasted change. IT ALSO CORRECTED MY COUNTS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, and showed the work rather than asserting it. My per-symbol figures could not have come from one method: I had summed across methods, so the total was an artefact. Its figures, counted as call nodes so that a definition is a binding, a comment is not code, and a name passed as a value is a reference rather than a call site, differ from mine on every symbol and match on none for two of them. The corrected reading is fifty-seven production sites across thirty files, and fifty-seven test sites across four. A second agent working the same task independently arrived at the same total, which is corroboration rather than coincidence. What was genuinely missing turned out to be narrower and more mechanical than my premise: nothing stopped the NEXT adapter from routing around the seam. So the fix is a guard with each rule proven to fire on a synthetic offender, because a scanner matching nothing is indistinguishable from a clean tree. That last clause is the one worth keeping - it is the difference between a scanner and a green row over nothing, which is the failure this ledger keeps recording from new directions.

mark: AN IMPORT-TIME CONFIG FREEZE WAS A REAL DEFECT NEITHER OF US KNEW ABOUT - and two agents built overlapping guards for it before either knew the other existed
text: The most substantive thing the seam work surfaced is a defect that was invisible to both briefs, including mine. Four production call sites defaulted a parameter to a configuration object **constructed at import time**. The transport module's own comment had already named this as the single known exception to the seam - so the codebase knew, in a comment, and nothing acted on it. The consequence is not stylistic. An import-time configuration is frozen **before the operator's environment file is read**, so the mode, the endpoint and the model identifier could never reach that pipeline. On a configured machine a run answered from the built-in model identifier instead of the configured one; on a machine with no endpoint it raised rather than reporting a missing configuration. Both are the worst shape: a run that looks like it honoured your settings and did not. What makes this worth recording beyond the fix is **how it was discovered and what happened next.** Two agents were briefed on overlapping tasks in the same fence, neither told about the other, and each independently found this defect and built a guard for it. One agent noticed mid-session that the other had modified files during its work, checked what the changes were, found them good and corroborating, **and did not touch, stage or commit any of them** - then escalated the collision and the uncommitted work rather than absorbing it. That is the behaviour the fence rules are meant to produce under pressure, and it worked. It also reported honestly that the other agent's guard was **strictly stronger on one axis** - it scans top-level drivers, which the first guard does not, and covers the configuration-freeze rules by name - while its own was stronger on seam-entry and mode-literal decisions. Two overlapping guards for one invariant is a real cost: they will drift, and one will eventually be the stale copy. But consolidating them is a decision with a cost either way, so it is escalated rather than resolved by whichever agent finished first. The general lesson, and it is the fourth distinct mechanism this programme has produced for the same underlying failure: **two things that must agree need one definition, and a comment is not a definition.** The codebase knew about this freeze in a comment; the comment named the exception correctly; and the defect survived anyway, because nothing read the comment and nothing enforced it.

mark: F1 IS GREEN - 5130 passed, 1 skipped, 7038 subtests, 0 failed, 0 errors - and the single skip is justified in the exact way the criterion demands
text: The seedsmith suite, measured this session on a quiescent tree with every repository clean and fully pushed, which is the first time in this programme that measurement has been possible: **five thousand one hundred and thirty passed, one skipped, seven thousand and thirty-eight subtests passed, zero failed, zero errors**, in eight minutes and forty-one seconds. Launched as a background process so it could not be reaped with a caller's process tree - a failure mode this programme has already hit once, where a run died at seventy-seven percent with empty stderr and no summary. THE CRITERION HAS A SECOND CLAUSE and this run satisfies it rather than merely satisfying the count. Every skip is enumerated by name and reason: there is exactly one, it is a real-content test, and its reason states that the smoke-batch round-one candidates are generation intermediates that have never been tracked, so they exist only in a session that just produced them. **It therefore asserts no property of shipped content** - which is precisely the distinction the clause asks for. Making it hermetic by planting fixtures would leave a permanently green test proving nothing, and the committed comment says so in those terms. That is the correct answer to this criterion and it is now evidenced rather than asserted. The figure is a reading, not a constant: it was taken at a specific commit with a specific tree state, and the record states both. Earlier figures in this ledger - twelve failures, then five thousand one hundred and eleven passing - are historical readings at older commits and are not superseded as claims about those commits. A NOTE ON WHAT THE NUMBER DOES NOT COVER, recorded because the honest limit is easy to lose: this is the Python suite. The .NET test suites are a separate measurement and are not included in this figure, and a reader should not treat five thousand one hundred and thirty as a whole-programme total.

mark: A COMMITTED CHANGE HAD MADE THE CORPUS GUARD GREEN OVER NOTHING - and my own earlier report accepted that commit's success without testing what it inspected
text: An earlier commit in this programme - landed by an agent fixing the corpus guard's refusal - turned the suite GREEN while inspecting nothing at all, and **I accepted its success at face value.** The cause is subtle and worth recording precisely: a file-listing command prints paths relative to the REPOSITORY root, not the directory the command ran in. Rooted at the corpus pack, the guard asked for one directory and received another - the pack prefix included - and because every one of its patterns is anchored to the start of the line, **not one pattern could ever match**. So on a range that genuinely changed the corpus it reported clean over forty-three changed files, and **zero of those forty-three reached a single declared tree.** That is the same defect this ledger has recorded repeatedly - a coverage claim about nothing - reached from the opposite direction to every previous instance. Every previous one was a guard scanning an empty population; this one was a guard scanning a full population of the wrong shape. Verified by me: that commit's guard contains no path-relativity handling at all, and the current one does. THE LESSON IS ABOUT ME, not about the guard. I recorded that commit as closing the root cause and I verified the REFUSAL was gone - which was true, and was not the property that mattered. The property that mattered is whether the guard **inspected a real population**, and the only way to know that is to ask what it actually matched. Verifying a guard stopped complaining is not verifying it started looking. Every green in this programme now has to carry its denominator, and the denominator is the number of items the guard actually examined - not the number it reported examining. That is now proven rather than asserted, by planting thirteen hand-edited corpus files with no generator change: the guard missed them entirely before the fix and reported thirteen violations after it. So the guard's green is load-bearing, which is the only kind of green worth having.

mark: NINE MUTATIONS CONFIRM THE EMPIRE WRITE PATH IS LOAD-BEARING - and the two tests I suspected were vacuous are not
text: An agent was asked to verify work an earlier agent had left uncommitted and to land it if sound. It spent most of its session trying to break it, and nine mutations - each installed and read back from disk before the run, because two controls in this programme previously 'passed' because the mutant was never installed - produced reds in every case. The pre-change behaviour, ignoring the empire field, goes red on four tests. Removing the unmapped-field refusal goes red on exactly the unmapped-field test. Dropping the human-empire refusal goes red on exactly that test. Writing to the human key instead of the empire's goes red on four including the one that says it does not touch the human pool. Accepting an empire the save does not carry goes red **because the code reported success** - the assertion flips from false to true, which is precisely the silent-drop failure the change exists to remove. Ignoring the save id in the key goes red with two saves clobbering each other. The two tests I had flagged as possibly vacuous both carry weight, and the agent established why by reading the shipped registry rather than trusting a comment: the human pool is keyed by the player and the non-human pool by the empire, so a test asserting one does not touch the other is meaningful only because those keys differ in the shipped data - and the fourth mutation proves it fails the moment they are confused. **A test can be vacuous against the wrong world, not only against the wrong code**, which is a distinction worth carrying. It also preserved something deliberately rather than tidying it away: the store refuses the human empire through this path while the route still serves the human through the priced gate. That is not a rewording of a criterion - the player-facing behaviour is unchanged and what it prevents is a second unpriced writer for one key - and a ninth mutation confirms that naming the human empire is byte-equivalent to omitting it. The read-time default was preserved deliberately rather than by accident: not one line of it changed, and the write is an override the read already preferred. The schema needs no migration for the pool, and the one marker that does need one is additive with a default - proven by a test that seeds a pre-marker table and asserts the old rows stay visible.

mark: A COMMIT MESSAGE WAS WRITTEN THROUGH A SHELL QUOTED STRING, EATING A WORD - and the rule that forbids it exists because the failure is invisible
text: A commit message in this repository contains two literal escape bytes, where the word 'empire' lost its middle character. I measured it rather than taking the report: that message carries two escape bytes and the word is still findable elsewhere, while three sibling messages from the same period carry none. The cause is identifiable - the message was written through a shell double-quoted string in which an escape was consumed, rather than written to a file and passed to a commit command that reads it. This is the rule this programme has been bitten by before, and the failure mode is what makes it worth recording rather than merely correcting. The message is not truncated, not empty, and not obviously wrong to a reader skimming it: it renders as a plausible word with a missing letter, in a commit that changed exactly the right things. **A silently damaged commit message is indistinguishable from a deliberate stylistic choice**, and since the message is the artefact a future session reads to understand *why* a change was made, that is a real cost rather than a cosmetic one. The standing rule exists for exactly this: write the message to a file, then commit reading that file. It costs one extra step and it removes an entire class of silent corruption from the record. **A commit message is the only part of a change that no test will ever check**, which is precisely why it needs a mechanical guarantee rather than care.

mark: LEDGER DEFECT, third kind, and this one my own two-counters check found: rows 609-616 carry no timestamp.
text: Found by insisting on a SHAPE check rather than a parse check. Every row parses and every row is a JSON object, so the standing 'every row parses' assertion is satisfied - and it is satisfied while 8 rows have no 'ts' field at all, found at contiguous lines 609-616. The cause is identifiable and it is a repair scar, not a random omission: those 8 lines are precisely the 8 double-encoded rows recorded two rows earlier as repaired, so the repair rebuilt each one as an object carrying 'kind', 'mark' and 'text' and dropped the timestamp it did not have a field name for. Their content is intact - I read all eight. Their ORDER is intact, which is what makes the defect recoverable: position in the file plus the neighbouring timestamps bracket each one's true time to the enclosing rows. I did NOT backfill the eight timestamps. Writing plausible values would be fabricating provenance in the one artefact whose whole purpose is provenance, and an invented timestamp is worse than an absent one because it is indistinguishable from a real one to every future reader, including a script. The honest state is 'timestamp lost', and it is recorded as such. This is the third distinct shape of ledger defect this programme has hit, and they are worth separating because each one defeats a different check: a row that is a JSON string instead of an object defeats 'every row is a dict'; a row missing its body defeats 'every row is a dict'; and this one - a well-formed object missing one field - defeats BOTH, because it passes every assertion the programme had been running for five turns. The generalisable rule, and the reason it is worth a row rather than a fix: 'it parses' was never the property being cared about, and a checker that confirms syntax cannot detect a lost field. Any future health check over this file must assert the SHAPE PER FIELD - not that every line loads, but that every line carries the fields the record claims it carries.

mark: OPEN ITEM 0 IS NOT A PRECEDENCE QUESTION - the code already chose, and the divergence is DEAD TEXT, not a player-facing choice.
text: Register item 0 asks the owner to decide 'which side wins' between authored display text and generated corpus descriptions, on the belief that 25 of 25 shared keys diverge and a player might see the wrong one. Reproduced every figure first: gk-data carries 181 keys with inline description text, gk-content's display catalog carries 304 keys, the intersection is exactly 25, and of those 25 **none** matches - 0 verbatim, not 25 divergent paraphrases. 156 gk-data keys have no gk-content entry, which reproduces the register's figure exactly. So the count was right and the framing is wrong. The framing is wrong because the two sides are not competing for one slot. `ActionRow` has no `Description` field at all - it carries `DescriptionKey` and nothing else, and its own doc comment says the key is 'never the sentence itself' and that display text 'lives in a _key column and resolves through the string catalog'. `ActionCorpusBriefJson` parses `descriptionKey` and never reads a `description` element. `ActionCorpusComposer` forwards only `DescriptionKey`. And `ItemCard.cs:690` resolves it: `LookupString(a.DescriptionKey)` into `__rendered`. **So gk-content wins by construction, and the gk-data inline sentence has no reader anywhere in the import path.** It is not shown to a player and it cannot be shown. There is no precedence to choose. This is worth more than the decision it replaces, because it reclassifies the item. The 25 divergent pairs are not a live ambiguity a player can hit; they are 25 corpus rows carrying a sentence that contradicts the one the player actually reads, and a reader comparing the two files later would reasonably conclude the shipped game has the wrong text in it. The generator emitted a field with no consumer - the UNWIRED failure class - and the register filed it as a content dispute. Two consequences, and only the first is agent work. First, the generator should stop emitting a field nothing reads, or the field should be removed; either way the corpus stops contradicting the display catalog, and the fix is a generator fix because these rows are generated. Second, whether 156 keys with text but no display entry are correct or missing content is a real question, and it is a DIFFERENT question - it is about absent display entries, not about which of two live texts wins. The existing test `GrantedActionTextTests` already pins the correct behaviour and does it through the real catalog: it resolves each brief's key against the real display file, asserts the resolution is non-empty, and asserts prose rather than a stat line. So the shipped answer was right all along and there is no player-facing bug here at all - only a corpus that lies about itself.

mark: TWO OWNER DECISIONS TAKEN. The ledger moves to gk-workflow. The dead description field is removed at the GENERATOR and the tree regenerated - but only after a near-miss that would have deleted an input.
text: DECISION ONE, the ledger's home. Consolidate into gk-workflow, the repository that is not being dissolved. Executed with a precondition rather than on trust: the destination's 82 rows had to be a strict prefix of the source's 766, compared AS OBJECTS, and the move asserts that property or aborts. A byte-level prefix check would have been the wrong test and reported a false conflict, because 16 of the 82 differ in bytes while parsing to identical objects. After the move: 766 rows, every row a dict, every source row present in the same order, no CR bytes, and the eight timestamp-less rows still at the same positions - the property that makes that defect recoverable. The monorepo keeps a pointer stub plus the pre-move copy, so a reader who greps the old path finds the record instead of silently reading a stale prefix. Nothing in any split repo read either file by name, so the move relocates no consumer. DECISION TWO, the 181 unread descriptions: stop emitting them and regenerate. Before briefing the removal I looked for the pipeline that consumes them, because deleting an INPUT is a different act from deleting an orphan - and I nearly got this wrong. `DisplayTemplates.cs` says 'gk-content/content/display/en.json (N2) is generated from these', which reads at first glance like the action descriptions are an input to the display catalog. They are not: that comment is about AFFIX display templates, a different file and a different key space. The sentence that actually governs these rows is in the actions generator itself: 'The key is structural (<id>.desc); the SENTENCE behind it is authored content that lands in gk-content/content/display/en.json.' The generator mints the key and explicitly assigns the prose to gk-content. So the corpus sentence is genuinely unread, and removing it does not starve the catalog. The near-miss is the point worth keeping. Had I briefed the removal on the first comment I read, I would have instructed an agent to delete the input to a live generator, and the regeneration would have emptied a display catalog. **A doc comment naming a file is not evidence of what feeds it** - the same rule as 'a comment is not evidence' in this programme's design gate, arriving in a new costume. The two candidate comments differ by one word ('from these' vs 'the SENTENCE behind it is authored content that lands in'), and that word is the whole decision. Both statements are true of different files.

mark: A11 IS NOT SATISFIED, and my own earlier claim of it was a build result wearing a test result's clothes.
text: I reported A11 - 'gk-core builds and tests with every sibling absent' - as met. It is not, and the distinction I drew was wrong in a way worth recording. What I actually had was a BUILD: `dotnet build tests/FusionRpg.Core.Tests` in a fresh standalone clone returned exit 0, 0 errors, 15 seconds. What A11 asks for is that the repository **tests**. Running the suite in that same clone gives **Failed: 4757, Passed: 5043, Skipped: 0, Total: 9800** in 2m43s. The cause is not subtle and not a code defect: `DirectoryNotFoundException: No legacy repository (FusionRpg.slnx next to data/seed/) or Keepverse workspace (gk-core/ n...)`. Most of gk-core's test tree resolves its corpus by walking up to a sibling repository, so with every sibling absent there is no corpus to read and roughly half the suite cannot start. **A green build and a green test run are different claims, and I presented the first while naming it as the second.** This programme has an instrument for exactly that error class - a stale binary producing a crash report four minutes out of date - and this is the same failure wearing different clothes: a cheaper measurement standing in for an expensive one. Second correction to the same criterion, found the same way. `CorpusDumpTests.cs` - which my carried state called the last cross-repo compile dependency needing a two-repo move - **compiles and builds fine standalone**, because the gk-forge reference is CONDITIONAL (`$(GkForgeAvailable)`). It is therefore **not** a compile blocker and the planned relocation is unnecessary. But `dotnet test --filter CorpusDump` in the clone returns **exit 0 with 'No test matches the given testcase filter'** - the file declares 17 test attributes and contributes **zero** tests, because the csproj removes it when the sibling is absent. That exclusion is deliberate and documented, and the comment gives the reason honestly: an unhandled CS0234 once turned one sibling's absence into 9,615 failing tests whose names said nothing about the cause. So coverage is not lost, but **the cost is a silently shrinking suite that reports success**. The generalisable finding is the shape, and it is the same shape as the audit's finding about a guard that passed for five turns while eight rows were broken: **exit 0 is not a result.** It is the absence of a complaint. Both the corpus-dump filter and the half-empty suite would have been recorded as passes by anything checking the exit code, and the count of tests that ran is the only thing that distinguishes them. Any future A11 check must assert a test COUNT against the sibling-present run, not an exit code.

mark: VERIFIED independently: an owner ruling's unique-deploy cap has ZERO production callers, while the sibling cap one line away is called from six places.
text: An audit reported this; I reproduced it rather than accepting it. `LawnUniqueDeployCap.TryAdmit` (`gk-core/src/FusionRpg.Core/Match/LawnUniqueDeployCap.cs:34`) appears in exactly two places in the whole workspace: its own definition, and `tests/FusionRpg.Core.Tests/Match/LawnUniqueDeployCapTests.cs`. The seven tests around it pass, which is exactly what makes the gap invisible - a policy with a full test suite and no caller looks maximally finished. The contrast is what makes it serious rather than pedantic. One line away in the same directory, `CapPolicy.TryAdmit` is reached from `MatchRuntime.TryAdmitSpawn`, which is in turn called from the Injector's `Match.SpawnAdmit.TryAdmit` at six separate call sites in `gk-fusion` - `CheatActions.cs:323,351,404,481`, `DebugActions.cs:23,73,140,612`. **The plumbing for 'a cap blocks a spawn' exists, is built, is wired through the host, and this cap simply is not on it.** So the ruling the cap quotes - at most 5 unique creatures per side, 10 on the board - is not enforced anywhere in a running game, and the frame-budget protection it exists for is not in force. Classified UNWIRED, not UNBUILT: the code is written, tested and reachable by an import. What is missing is the one line that puts it on a path a player can take. That is the cheapest possible kind of gap to close and the most expensive kind to leave, because a passing test suite and a passing guard both certify this cap as done. The audited report's proposed next step - call it from the unique-deploy admission gate in `RpgStore.UniqueActors.cs` - is the right seam, on the evidence of where its sibling lives.

mark: INDEPENDENT PIPELINE AUDIT: the damage pipeline is wired end to end; the stamina gate it runs on is theatre below one power point, and the player is never told.
text: A read-only audit applied the nine completeness criteria to the lawn-to-combat pipeline, in a different lens from my own standing checks. It corrected four of my figures and I am recording the corrections along with the findings rather than the summary. REACHABLE, OBTAINABLE, PERSISTS and FAILURE-IS-REACHABLE all hold, with the pipeline traced stage by stage across four repositories and every stage named to a file. The rider's damage magnitude was proven load-bearing by mutation: zeroing the packet builder went red on four tests, so the arithmetic is real and the defect is not in the damage maths. The substantive finding is criterion 6, and it is the better half of the criterion - the half that says a gate must be NON-TRIVIAL, not merely satisfiable. The stamina pool is seeded as a share of the power-ladder HP curve, which is quadratic in the ladder's argument, so the pool grows with progression while the per-swing cost is a flat 25. Solving that against the shipped tuning file gives sustainable fire at **exactly one** power point and a failure at **every** point from 1 to 19: at the low end a player regenerates 2 stamina per second against a cost of 25, so the rider can fire on 12% of swings. The shipped CI guard evaluates `Pin = 20` and nothing else. That single number is the whole problem, and the audit proved it by mutation rather than argument: moving the guard's pin from 20 to 1 turns the shipped gate RED with a message naming the real inequality. So the gate is not lying, it is checking one point of a band - and the derivation that produced the cost was honest about being derived at that point, which is exactly why nothing ever caught it. Player-visible consequence: the rider's effect is **silently dropped** on most swings below that point, with no UI and no signal, while the vanilla shot still lands. The plant looks identical and simply stops contributing. Classified VACUOUS rather than UNBUILT - the code runs, the wiring exists, but the condition that lets it act is false most of the time - and it is worse than a tuning nit because the player cannot tell a nerf from a bug. Two related gaps make it worse: the exhaustion events the pipeline emits have **zero consumers** anywhere in the codebase, so the one signal that could explain the drop is emitted into nothing; and the repair chain is blocked, because the tuning file the scale work depends on does not exist. Corrections I accept: the guard suite is **31** guards, not the 30 I have been quoting, and dispatch needs a per-repository range for **gk-data** specifically or one row fails closed on that repository's SHAs. My F2 figure was measured with ranges supplied for gk-workflow, gk-fusion, gk-forge and gk-data, so it stands - but it was one range away from being wrong, and I had been quoting the count as though it were stable. A count that moves when a registry row is added was never a constant. The audit also refused a figure rather than laundering one: it could not obtain a trustworthy seedsmith number because another stream mutated the tree mid-run, and it said so instead of reporting the number it had. That is the behaviour this programme is trying to buy.

mark: PUBLISHER, PARTIAL: the server and web roots are now explicit and fail closed with named stages - and the release is still blocked, by three MORE roots in other repositories and one spawn bug that predates this work.
text: The publisher could not be made to run from a split repository by doing what I asked, and saying so was worth more than a green result would have been. What landed, verified as exactly two files: the server output root and the web root are explicit inputs, each refused by name when absent, wrong or not a package, with `--json` carrying the verdict, the failing stage and the resolved roots, and stdout asserted empty on a refusal. The pre-change failure named a lockfile requirement; the post-change failure names the absent directory that actually caused it, which is the difference between a message that misleads and one that diagnoses. The control was run properly: baseline hash, mutant installed, **hash confirmed to differ before running**, red, byte-identical restore, green. It also handled a real hazard I would not have thought of - CPython validates a cached bytecode file against mtime AND size, so a restored source can still execute the mutant. That is this programme's 'a stale binary producing a report four minutes out of date' in a new form, and it would have produced a false PASS rather than a false failure, which is the more dangerous direction. It also strengthened an existing check rather than leaving it: the closed-vocabulary regex required a string literal for the stage argument, so every refusal built from a constant was invisible to it. Measured, the old pattern read 9 of 16 reasons and the new one reads all 16 - one refusal had never once been checked. **A guard that cannot see half the refusals is not a weaker guard, it is a different guard**, and it was passing. Why release is still blocked, each part reproduced by me rather than accepted: `FusionRpg.Launcher`, both Injector hosts and `game-profiles.json` are all in **gk-fusion**, and `PLAYERS.txt` is at the **workspace root** - neither gk-fusion nor gk-core, confirmed by existence check on all eight paths. So a publish needs FIVE roots across three repositories, not two. And a fourth blocker, pre-existing and inside the file: the npm invocation passes a bare program name, which Win32 cannot CreateProcess when the shim is a `.CMD`. I reproduced the resolution myself - `shutil.which('npm')` returns `C:/nvm4w/nodejs/npm.CMD` - so preflight passes and the spawn then fails. Every nvm-windows install on this machine is affected. It fails closed, so nothing ships broken, which is why it survived: **a tool that refuses correctly still blocks, and correctness is not availability.** The agent also reported that the enforcement registry was already dirty when it started and belonged to another stream, and did not stage it. I confirmed the tree state directly rather than trusting that report.

mark: MY QUOTED GUARD COUNT WAS WRONG: 31, not 30 - and I learned it from an audit that was trying to refute me.
text: I have been quoting '30 guards, 0 red' as F2's figure for several turns. The independent audit measured 31 and named the number as a correction, which is precisely the behaviour I asked it for. I re-measured rather than adopting either figure: `run_guards.py --tier ci` on the current tree returns **GUARDS OK - 31 guard(s) run, 0 red, exit 0**. The count moved from 30 to 31 because a seedsmith guard row was added to the registry during the migration - which is the whole point of the registry, and means the number was never a property of the codebase, only of the moment I happened to measure. Counting the registry directly gives the same answer and a better one: 35 rows, 33 in the `ci` tier, 2 in `local`, and **0 rows missing a `repository` field** - the F2 root cause stays fixed as rows are added, which is the property that matters and the one a count would never show. 33 registered minus 31 run is two rows the ci tier selects but the dispatcher resolves elsewhere; I am not going to explain that difference away, and it is the right thing to measure next rather than round to a comfortable number. Also worth recording because it is the same failure twice: passing `--root gk-data` made the runner refuse with `REGISTRY-MISSING`, and my first instinct was that a sibling root was the correct argument. Reading the code showed `--root` means **the gk-core root**, and the registry path is derived from it. I had taken the flag's name for its meaning - the audit's report had said a row 'also needs --root gk-data', which was a misreading on its part that I nearly converted into a second wrong claim by repeating it. **A flag name is not a definition, and a reported instruction is not a specification** - the same rule as 'a path in prose is a claim, not a reference', arriving for the second time in this programme.

mark: SEAM GUARDS MERGED, and the two guards disagreed in a way that made them worse than either alone.
text: Two overlapping guards are now one, and the evidence for merging was not tidiness - it was a **live disagreement between them about the same property**. Both asserted 'only the seam may open an HTTP client', and they disagreed on the spellings: one caught `import openai` and the other did not; the other caught bare `import urllib`, `urllib.parse`, `from urllib import parse` and `import http`, and the first did not. Both were green at the same time, on the same tree, each silently blind to a quarter of the bypasses the other saw. **Two guards covering one property with two definitions is not redundancy; it is a coin flip on which bypass survives.** The merged file asserts the UNION, and the agent measured it as a strict superset - 26 tests where the two had 19 between them. Two mutations make this falsifiable rather than asserted, and they were run as **differentials**, which is the right shape for this claim: each mutant violates exactly one guard's private axis, and each is checked against all three versions.
