A direct authorer construction is caught by the merged guard and by the old A and **missed by the old B**; a frozen config in a top-level driver outside A's scan root is caught by the merged guard and by the old B and **missed by the old A**. Every mutant was hash-verified on disk before the run and restored byte-identically after, because two mutation controls in this programme passed without the mutant ever being installed. Three exemptions the old code granted were DROPPED as measured dead weight, and the exemption set had to become per-rule rather than per-module - one module legitimately trips the HTTP rule and none of the mode rules, and a single set would have handed it exemptions it never had. **Exemptions granted in bulk are permissions nobody chose**, and the fix is to make each one say which rule it is escaping. The agent also corrected two of its own overstated comments and one inherited one: three of seven allowlisted injection sites do not bind the transport the way the list's name claimed. It reported that its brief's alternative (keeping two files) was not taken, and that it edited a gk-core registry file the brief had scoped out - naming the contradiction rather than quietly widening its fence.

mark: THE GATE THAT PROMISES CITATIONS CANNOT BE SHIFTED INVISIBLY IS INVISIBLY BLIND ON 13 LINES - and it says so, in its own output, while reporting OK.
text: Reproduced by me, not accepted from the report. The append-safety gate exists to prove that adding a registry row cannot silently repoint a document's citation. It cannot prove that here, and its own output says so while still reporting OK. The mechanism: the gate compares a cited line's TEXT to decide whether it moved. In `scripts/enforcement-registry.v1.json` there are **13 lines byte-identical to `      "paths": [`**, and one of them is a cited line. A shift onto a byte-identical line is invisible by construction - the text matches, so the gate concludes nothing moved, and it is right about the text and wrong about the meaning. The guard prints '2/7 cited line(s) hold text that is not unique in the file, so a shift onto an identical line is invisible to S1 by content' and then prints OK. **A gate that names its own blind spot and then passes anyway is worse than one that cannot see it**, because a reader has been told the property holds. Worse, and already realised: the same output carries an UNVERIFIED banner stating that all 7 citations of this registry **already resolve to different content than they cited** - caused by a 7-line row inserted at line 74 of a file whose highest cited line is 392. The guard's green therefore means 'no FURTHER drift since the baseline', never 'these citations are right'. The citing documents all live in the workspace root, so the repair is not gk-core's to make alone. The agent faced a real dilemma and chose correctly: there is no insertion point for a guard row that moves nothing, because `guards` is the only container and the append container the gate derives is an unrelated design-gate list. It did not re-baseline - which would have destroyed the evidence - and did not edit a citing document outside its fence. **The honest output here is a blocked item with a named cause, not a green run.** The generalisable point, and it is the third time this shape has appeared in this programme: a detector needs a denominator and a uniqueness property, not a comparison. Content-equality detects a shift only when the target differs; a registry of 35 structurally identical rows will always contain a byte-identical candidate, so the check is structurally incapable of the thing it promises. Every green from a content-comparison gate over a repetitive structure needs to be read as 'no detectable drift', never as the property.

mark: F5 VERIFIED AGAINST LIVE REMOTES, not stale refs - 9/9 IN-SYNC. The audit was right that the two checks are not the same check.
text: I have been reporting 'every repository clean and fully pushed' using `git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD`, which compares the working branch against a **cached** upstream ref. That ref is whatever was last fetched, so the check can be green while the remote has moved on - it proves nothing was committed locally, not that the remote has it. The independent audit made exactly this point and I had been treating the weaker check as the stronger one. Re-measured with `git ls-remote origin HEAD`, which asks the server: **all nine repositories IN-SYNC, 0 dirty, 0 unpushed** - gk-assets e56c960, gk-content d2337d8, gk-core 6a27e30, gk-data 3832675, gk-forge 26e4608, gk-fusion a033fad, gk-tests ad8636c, gk-web 888d427, gk-workflow bb8a102. The three agents' landings (58ad3d8 publisher, 26e4608 seam merge, 6a27e30 registry row) are on the remote, not merely committed. The distinction is cheap to observe and easy to skip, and it is the same family as every other instrument defect in this programme: a check that confirms a local belief instead of querying the thing. **Green over a cached ref is green over a memory.** The live-remote query is now the check of record, because a F5 report that cannot distinguish 'pushed' from 'committed' is not a report about the remote.

mark: THE SUSTAINABLE-FIRE GAP IS NOW A RED TEST: the rider fires on 12% of swings at the bottom of the band, and a test says so on every run until it is retuned.
text:
An agent was asked to make a balance gap visible without pretending the gap was not there. It delivered a RED test as the artefact, and that is the correct shape for this finding.
What landed is one new file, 409 lines, and nothing else. Verified by me directly: exactly one file in the commit, `data/tuning/**` untouched, the working tree clean, and the tuning file's bytes equal to its committed blob. The agent's mutation was to the regen share in `battle-resources.v2.json`, and the file's hash after its restore (`aa3452e1`, 4118 bytes) is the same value it reported as the pre-mutation baseline - so the byte-identical restore is confirmed independently rather than taken on trust.
The result, reproduced by me on the current tree: **7 failed, 9 passed, 0 skipped**. Seven is the finding: the sub-pin band, asserted point by point, with each failure message carrying the duty-cycle percentage so a reader sees the number rather than a bare red. The shipped one-point guard stays GREEN throughout, which is the whole point - it was never wrong about the pin, it was silent about everything else.
The reasoning is the part worth keeping. I told the agent to choose between two options and justify it from the specs; it found the specs are NOT silent - the pin-scoped claim is explicit in three places in `spec-lawn-combat-calibration.md` and in the `_meta` block of BOTH tuning files, each saying 'derived at the pin (theta=20)'. So the contract genuinely is pin-scoped, and below the pin nothing authorises a lower bar either. It implemented the pin-scoped contract over the whole region above the pin (strictly stronger than the shipped single-point check, which would stay green with everything above the pin broken) and, below the pin, asserted the duty cycle against a floor of **1.0**.
That floor is the decision I want recorded, because it is the one place an agent could have quietly bought a green run. A floor of 1.0 means 'the rider must fire on every swing'. Any value below 1.0 would have been a tolerance invented by the test author to make a known balance gap report as a pass - and the agent said so in its own comment. **A test that sets its own tolerance is a test that cannot fail usefully**, and the temptation is strongest exactly where the finding is most inconvenient.
It also checked the claim the specs make *unconditionally*, and those are what the tuning violates: exhaustion is 'a burst-fire consequence and not a permanent stop'; 'a cost far over [sustainable] makes every plant inert'; and 'an action cost is authored against the pool's REGEN, never against its MAX'. The shipped tuning breaks an unconditional spec sentence below the pin, and now there is a test that says so out loud.
Three supporting gates were added so the measurement is honest rather than merely red: regen must be non-decreasing across the band (which is what makes a finite sample a proof rather than a spot check), the host-configured ladder must BE the shipped curve at every point (so the test cannot pass against an ambient fixture), and the production functions must still reproduce the file's own arithmetic at every point.
One correction it made to my own figures, which I accept: I had reported `swings@start` of 12 at theta=1; the correct value is **2** (poolMax 53 divided by cost 25). Every other cell reproduced exactly. That is the stale-premise pattern again - a table I carried into a brief rather than re-measuring - and the agent reproduced the whole thing from production functions against the shipped files anyway, which is how it was caught.
It reported two out-of-fence findings rather than fixing them: a stale comment in a shared test bootstrap that names the v1 power curve where the fixture actually configures v2 (harmless here, misleading to anyone reasoning about the fixture), and a spec document whose testing-strategy table does not yet list the new band file.
Net position: the rider's elemental effect is silently dropped on 88% of swings at the bottom of the progression band, that was invisible, and there is now a test that fails every time until someone retunes the pool or the cost. The retune is the owner's - the values are balance, and no agent changed them.

mark: THE REGISTER DID NOT CONTAIN THE TWO WORST FINDINGS, AND IT HAD TWO STRUCTURAL DEFECTS - both found by parsing it rather than by reading my own edit.
text: The register exists so that 'what is left' is answerable from a file. Reconciling it against the session's later findings found it was not answering that. **The two most serious defects this programme found had no row at all** - an owner ruling's unique-deploy cap with zero production callers, and a rider effect silently dropped on 88% of swings. Neither had a row because both were found after the register was written and **nothing reconciled the register against later findings**. A derived index with no reconciliation step is a snapshot, and a snapshot is exactly what it claimed not to be. Five rows added, each with owner, reason, evidence and status. Then two structural defects, both invisible to an edit-and-trust workflow: item id **5 was used twice**, pre-existing, by the release-workflow row and the A11 row, so a register keyed on ids silently carried two items under one; and rows **27a, 27b and 28 were jammed onto a single line** because the prose ended in '|| 27b |' instead of a row terminator, making three items invisible to anything that parses by row. Both were caught by parsing the artefact - counting ids and counting pipes per row - which is the same discipline that caught the eight double-encoded ledger rows, the eight rows missing a timestamp, and the 'no test matches' filter that returned exit 0. **Five separate times in this programme the check that found the defect was a structural parse rather than a read**, and the read was the thing that had been trusted. Item 0 was also refuted and reclassified rather than closed: every one of its figures reproduced, but it was filed as a precedence question between two texts when the code has already chosen - `ActionRow` has no `Description` field, so the gk-data sentence has no reader at all. It split into 0a (the dead field, owner decided) and 0b (156 keys with text and no display entry, a genuinely different question on which the spec is silent). And item 1's CLOSED text still carried my stale figure of 30 guards; it is 31. **A closure that cites a figure nobody reproduced is not a closure**, which is this programme's own rule, violated inside the artefact that exists to enforce it. One more correction worth naming: item 5 claimed gk-core cannot BUILD standalone, and it can - the `$(GkForgeRoot)` references are all `Condition`-gated. **I had reported the A11 criterion met on exactly that basis.** The row now records the wrong half rather than being quietly deleted, and points at 5a for the worse test half. A row corrected by measurement is doing its job; a row closed on a manager's say-so is the failure mode this whole artefact was built to prevent.

mark: THE STAMINA GAP IS CLOSED: regen share 50 -> 321, derived at the band floor and verified one step below the boundary. 16/16 pass where 7 failed.
text: The owner's decision is implemented and independently verified by me: **`Passed! - Failed: 0, Passed: 16, Skipped: 0`**, where the same filter reported 7 failures an hour earlier. Landed through the file's own publisher, not by hand: `tools/tuning/publish.py battle-resources regenPerSecondShareMilli.stamina=321`, writing `battle-resources.v3.json` and leaving `v2` on disk for revert. I verified `v2` is byte-identical to its committed blob **and unchanged across the commit** (`aa3452e1`, both sides), so the revert path the file's own metadata promises is real rather than asserted. `guard-tuning-immutability` exits 0. One number moved: the stamina regen share, 50 to 321. The pool share is unchanged for every resource, which is the right lever and the agent justified it rather than assuming: pool and regen are both per-mille shares of the same ladder value, so raising the pool buys the identical regen **and doubles burst depth**, and the pool size is separately load-bearing for the reaction-lane poise anchor at the pin. **321 is a minimum, not a preference.** At the band floor `BaseHp(1) = 106`, so poolMax is 53, and the inequality needs regen ≥ 16.667, i.e. a whole 17, which needs the share ≥ 321. The agent ran the whole band at 320 (fails: ceiling 24.0 < 25) and at 321 (holds), so the value is derived at the binding constraint and verified one step below the boundary. Deriving at the floor rather than at the pin is the substance of the retune - the pin was never the binding constraint. The honest cost, stated by the agent rather than buried: the ceiling-to-cost **ratio** at the pin rises from 1.02x to 6.54x, and it is unavoidable rather than chosen. Regen is a share of a ladder that grows with progression while the cost is flat, so any share clearing the cost at the floor clears it roughly sevenfold at the pin. 321 is the least generous upper band obtainable without moving the pool or the cost. The one number that could have been wrong and is not: `BaseHp(1)` is **106**, not 100. The agent called this out as the first step where a restatement goes wrong, and had it assumed 100 the floor would have been computed against a pool that does not exist. I attempted exactly that restatement in the foreground earlier and got it wrong - I assumed a quadratic the shipped curve does not use, and hit a KeyError on a derived coefficient. **The ladder is a class, not a formula, and a restatement of a class is a new program.** **The agent crossed its fence and said so, which is the behaviour worth having.** It was told not to touch the band test, and it changed one line: `battle-resources.v2.json` as a literal to the new `Current` constant. I read the whole diff to that file - it is that single line, with no assertion, floor, tolerance, band constant or InlineData touched - and the crossing was forced by a real contradiction in my brief: the file read a literal while acceptance demanded v2 stay untouched, so a v3 publish could never turn the gate green. It also repointed three production and test readers, on the grounds that **a publish with no reader is inert** - and that is the `element-catalog` incident this repository already records, where a publish moved one reader and not another. It added `BattleResourceTuningFiles.Current` following the `CombatAiTuningFiles` pattern that already exists to prevent exactly this debt. It disclosed what it left undone rather than leaving me to find it: the band test's doc comment and failure messages still say `battle-resources.v2.json` in prose; `action-corpus-cost-templates.v2.json`'s `_meta.kindsNote` still narrates the pin-only derivation and is now stale, and needs its own publish in its own domain; and the calibration spec still scopes its criterion at the pin, which this change now exceeds. Those are follow-ups, not defects in this landing. Its isolation control was the right one: pointing the readers back at v2 on the same tree returned 10 failures rather than 3, which attributes the 7 to the publish rather than to anything else on the tree.

mark: RECORD AUDIT: no false closure among the seven, four FALSE-OPENS among the open, and a retracted item that was still being carried as work.
text: An independent read-only agent attacked the register and the ledger with the instruction to refute rather than restate. It is the first audit in this programme to return a result with **no false closure among the seven CLOSED items** - every property it could test still holds - and four items carried as OPEN that are in fact closed. All four verified by me before I acted, and each was closed for a different reason. Item 11 was the clearest: `AllocateAptitudesRequest` HAS `public string? Empire` and the type carries `JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow`; the row even said it couples to #2, and #2 was closed. Item 10 is the instructive one: `ast.parse` on `restart_game.py` **succeeds**, there was never an unclosed quote, and the register ALREADY RETRACTED that cause 46 lines further down **while still carrying the row and its dead stated cause**. That is the worst failure mode a register has - **a retracted item left in place reads as open work to every future session**, and it inflates the open count with work nobody will do. Item 8's headline figure had already been retracted once in the ledger and was carried again here. Item 6a's stated reason is false: measured by `script` key, gk-core has 35 registry rows and the monorepo 29, sharing 29 scripts, and **all 29 differ** - on exactly one field, `repository`, absent from 29/29 monorepo rows and present on 35/35 gk-core rows. The row had claimed they agreed exactly. The consequence is sharper than the row assumed: the monorepo copy **cannot dispatch at all**, since dispatch is by declared repository. The audit also corrected three of my figures - two places still saying 30 guards, and a stale F1 reading (5,111 where the current figure is 5,130) sitting in the register's own 'what is not open' section beside a 5,130 elsewhere. Both numbers are true at their own commits; the defect was that neither said which. **Any figure quoted from that file is a reading at a named commit, never a standing property** - stated in the file now. Two limits it reported rather than papering over, which I am recording instead of fixing. `ts` orders BATCHES rather than events: 516 of 769 timestamped rows share a value, across two zones, with 2 adjacent inversions and 632 pairwise. And only **one** correction row in 127 names the row it corrects - the ledger's supersession is narrative, not structural. I am not rewriting 127 rows to add back-references: that is a large unreviewed edit to the one artefact that must stay trustworthy, which is a worse risk than the property it would fix. It also **refused to launder a figure**, naming that another stream had mutated the tree mid-run so its seedsmith number was untrustworthy - and it corrected the brief itself on four points, including that the ledger path it was given was a stub. **An audit that reports a brief as wrong has done more than one that agrees with it.**
